Investigating Vanishing Gradients and Early-Layer Trainability Across Network Depth in Deep MLPs on BloodMNIST¶

Research Project - The Effects of Vanishing Gradients in Deep Neural Networks

Overview¶

This project investigates how network depth affects gradient propagation and early-layer trainability in multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) using the BloodMNIST dataset.

The study consists of two controlled experiments:

  • Stage A — Network Depth: Compare MLPs with 2, 5, 10, and 20 hidden layers under a fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.
  • Stage B — Activation Functions: Compare Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU at a fixed depth of 5 hidden layers using the same Xavier Uniform initialization and training protocol.

The experiments measure layer-wise RMS weight gradients, normalized first-layer weight displacement, training-loss dynamics, and validation accuracy and macro-F1 across three random seeds.

Part 1 — Data Pipeline & Experimental Configuration¶

1. Overview & Objective¶

Part 1 establishes the shared experimental configuration and prepares the BloodMNIST dataset for the gradient-vanishing study.

The goal is to ensure consistent data preprocessing, model input dimensions, training settings, and reproducibility controls across Stage A (network depth) and Stage B (activation functions).

BloodMNIST contains RGB images of size 28 × 28 from eight classes. Each image is represented as [B, 3, 28, 28] and flattened to [B, 2352] inside the MLP in Part 2, where B denotes batch size.

The official training, validation, and test splits are preserved. Normalization statistics are calculated from the training split only and then applied consistently to all three splits. The test split is reserved and is not used for the main experimental comparisons.

3. Important Objects & Their Roles¶

Object / Function Defined In Role
Config / cfg 1.2 Configuration class and instance containing model, training, and experiment settings.
set_seed() / device 1.2 Random-seed control and computing device selection.

Key distinctions:

  • Config defines experimental settings; cfg is its instance. The neural network class ConstantWidthMLP is defined separately in Part 2.
  • A Dataset provides image–label samples; a DataLoader organizes those samples into mini-batches. Neither performs model training.
  • get_first_batch(seed) checks DataLoader behavior, whereas make_train_loader(seed) in Part 5 creates fresh seeded DataLoaders for experimental runs.
  • Section 1.9 verifies flattening with images.flatten(start_dim=1); the actual MLP performs flattening internally using nn.Flatten().

5. Expected Outcome & Role in the Experiment¶

Part 1 produces a verified experimental configuration, training-derived normalization statistics, official BloodMNIST datasets, and DataLoaders ready for model construction and training.

Its role is to establish consistent data preparation and experimental controls, allowing subsequent comparisons to focus on the intended independent variables:

  • Stage A: Network depth.
  • Stage B: Activation function at fixed D5 depth.

No MLP training or hypothesis testing is performed in Part 1.

1.2 — Experimental Configuration & Reproducibility¶

Objective

Define a centralized experimental configuration and initialize the random-seed controls and computing device used throughout the BloodMNIST gradient-vanishing study.

Procedure

  1. Define a Config dataclass containing the dataset paths, batch sizes, MLP dimensions, activation and initialization settings, optimizer hyperparameters, convergence threshold, network depths, random seeds, and results directory.
  2. Implement set_seed(seed) to initialize Python, NumPy, and PyTorch random-number generators and configure available CuDNN reproducibility settings.
  3. Create the shared configuration object using cfg = Config().
  4. Select the available computing device (Apple MPS or CPU).
  5. Initialize the starting random seed and display the configuration, device, and PyTorch version.

Purpose

Centralize the experimental settings to improve consistency, reproducibility, and code maintainability.

The configuration defines the controlled conditions for the two main experiments:

Experiment Independent Variable Controlled Settings
Stage A — Depth Effect Number of hidden layers: D2, D5, D10, D20 Sigmoid activation, Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD settings, dataset preprocessing, and training duration
Stage B — Activation Effect Activation function: Sigmoid, Tanh, ReLU D5 architecture, Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD settings, dataset preprocessing, and training duration

Both stages use three random seeds (0, 1, 2) to assess variability across independent training runs.

The learning rate (cfg.lr = 0.1) is initially provisional, while cfg.loss_threshold is initially unset. Part 5 checks and finalizes these settings before the main experiments.

Expected Results

  • A Config class defining the shared experiment settings.
  • A cfg object containing the initial configuration values.
  • A reusable set_seed(seed) function.
  • A selected computing device (device).
  • Printed configuration and environment information for verification.

Role in the Experiment

Section 1.2 establishes the experimental controls reused throughout the notebook:

  • Part 2: Uses the configuration to construct MLP architectures with the specified dimensions, activation functions, and initialization.
  • Parts 3–4: Use the configured settings during training, validation, and gradient measurements.
  • Part 5: Performs the learning-rate pilot, finalizes the training protocol, and applies per-run seed control.
  • Part 6: Compares network depths under the fixed Stage A baseline.
  • Part 7: Compares activation functions at fixed D5 depth under a shared initialization rule.
  • Part 8: Verifies the recorded experimental settings and results before final reporting.

Important distinctions:

  • Config defines the experimental settings; cfg is an instance of that class.
  • Config is not the MLP architecture. The ConstantWidthMLP class is defined separately in Part 2.
  • set_seed() initializes random-number generators but does not guarantee complete determinism across all hardware and operations.
  • The initial seed establishes the starting random state; subsequent experimental runs explicitly use their assigned seeds.
  • Defining hyperparameters does not train a model. Model construction, training, and measurement are implemented in later parts.
In [ ]:
# Configuration: setup hyperparameters for the whole experiment
@dataclass
class Config:
    # Data
    data_dir: str = "./data"
    batch_size: int = 128
    eval_batch_size: int = 1024 

    # Model: 2352 -> 256 -> ... -> 256 -> 8
    input_dim: int = 3 * 28 * 28           # BloodMNIST: 3 x 28 x 28 = 2352
    hidden_dim: int = 256
    num_classes: int = 8  

    # Stage A baseline
    activation: str = "sigmoid"            # Stage A baseline: "sigmoid" | "tanh" | "relu"
    init: str = "xavier_uniform"           # "xavier_uniform" | "he_uniform"

    # Optimizer  
    optimizer: str = "sgd"                 # SGD, so gradient magnitude maps directly to weight update
    lr: float = 0.1                        # provisional; finalize after LR pilot check
    momentum: float = 0.0
    epochs: int = 20  
    weight_decay: float = 0.0

    # Convergence threshold (used for H2: epochs-to-threshold)
    loss_threshold: float = None           # set after pilot run, then freeze

    # Experiment. 
    depths: tuple = (2, 5, 10, 20)   # number of hidden layers
    seeds: tuple = (0, 1, 2)  

    #Results
    results_dir: str = "./results"


def set_seed(seed):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False


cfg = Config()
device = torch.device("mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")
set_seed(cfg.seeds[0])

print(cfg)
print("device:", device, "| torch:", torch.__version__)

1.3 — Load Raw Training Data & Compute RGB Normalization Statistics¶

Objective

Load the raw BloodMNIST training images and calculate per-channel RGB mean and standard deviation for subsequent image normalization.

Procedure

  1. Load the official training split into raw_train_dataset without applying a normalization transform.
  2. Compute the mean and standard deviation across all training images and spatial positions for each RGB channel.
  3. Divide the statistics by 255 to express them on the [0, 1] pixel-value scale.
  4. Display the resulting RGB mean and standard deviation.

Purpose

Estimate normalization statistics exclusively from the training set to prevent validation/test data leakage and establish a consistent preprocessing scale across all experimental conditions.

Expected Results

  • raw_train_dataset: Raw BloodMNIST training dataset.
  • train_mean: Three mean values corresponding to the R, G, and B channels.
  • train_std: Three standard deviation values corresponding to the R, G, and B channels.

Role in the Experiment

The training-derived statistics are reused in Section 1.4 to define the shared normalization transform, which is applied to the official training, validation, and test datasets in Section 1.5.

This ensures that Stage A (network depth) and Stage B (activation function) use the same input preprocessing, supporting controlled comparisons of gradient propagation and model trainability.

Important distinction: raw_train_dataset is used to calculate normalization statistics; the normalized train_dataset used for model training is created later in Section 1.5. No model training occurs in this section.

In [8]:
# Load raw training data (without normalization)
raw_train_dataset = BloodMNIST(
    split="train",
    root=cfg.data_dir,
    download=True
)

# Calculate per-channel mean and std from train images only
train_mean = raw_train_dataset.imgs.mean(axis=(0, 1, 2)) / 255.0
train_std = raw_train_dataset.imgs.std(axis=(0, 1, 2)) / 255.0

print("Train mean (RGB):", train_mean)
print("Train std  (RGB):", train_std)

1.4 — Define Image Preprocessing & Normalization¶

Objective

Define a consistent image preprocessing pipeline using the RGB normalization statistics calculated from the training set in Section 1.3.

Procedure

  1. Convert train_mean and train_std into Python lists: BLOODMNIST_MEAN and BLOODMNIST_STD.
  2. Create a transforms.Compose pipeline containing:
    • transforms.ToTensor(): Convert each RGB image to a PyTorch tensor with shape [3, 28, 28] and pixel values scaled to [0, 1].
    • transforms.Normalize(): Standardize each RGB channel using its training-derived mean and standard deviation.

Purpose

Apply the same preprocessing rules to all dataset splits, ensuring consistent input scaling for model training and evaluation without using validation or test data to estimate normalization statistics.

Expected Results

A reusable transform object that converts BloodMNIST images into normalized PyTorch tensors. The transform is defined here but is not yet applied to the official dataset objects.

Role in the Experiment

Section 1.4 connects the normalization statistics from Section 1.3 with the official datasets loaded in Section 1.5. The resulting preprocessing pipeline is shared across Stage A (network depth) and Stage B (activation function), helping maintain consistent input conditions for controlled comparisons of gradient propagation and trainability.

Important distinction: Section 1.3 computes normalization statistics; Section 1.4 defines the preprocessing transform; Section 1.5 attaches this transform to the official dataset objects.

In [9]:
# Convert train statistics to Python lists
BLOODMNIST_MEAN = train_mean.tolist()
BLOODMNIST_STD = train_std.tolist()

# Define image transforms
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize(
        mean=BLOODMNIST_MEAN,
        std=BLOODMNIST_STD
    )
])

1.5 — Load Official BloodMNIST Dataset Splits¶

Objective

Load the official BloodMNIST training, validation, and test splits using the shared preprocessing transform defined in Section 1.4.

Procedure

  1. Create train_dataset using split="train".
  2. Create val_dataset using split="val".
  3. Create test_dataset using split="test".
  4. Apply the same transform to all three datasets and use cfg.data_dir as the shared data directory.

Purpose

Preserve the official dataset partitions while ensuring consistent image preprocessing across training and evaluation. Keeping the splits separate prevents unintended overlap between model training and performance evaluation.

Expected Results

Three BloodMNIST dataset objects:

  • train_dataset: Provides training images and labels for model optimization.
  • val_dataset: Provides validation images and labels for evaluating learning progress without weight updates.
  • test_dataset: Reserves an independent dataset for potential final evaluation; it is not used in the main Stage A and Stage B analyses.

Each dataset returns image–label pairs with the same preprocessing applied to its images.

Role in the Experiment

Section 1.5 connects the preprocessing pipeline from Section 1.4 to the DataLoaders created in Section 1.6.

The same official dataset partitions are reused in both Stage A (network depth) and Stage B (activation function), allowing differences in gradient attenuation, trainability, and validation performance to be compared under consistent data conditions.

Important distinction: Section 1.5 creates dataset objects; Section 1.6 creates DataLoaders that organize examples from these datasets into mini-batches. No model training or evaluation is performed in this section.

In [10]:
# Load training dataset
train_dataset = BloodMNIST(
    split="train",
    root=cfg.data_dir,
    transform=transform,
    download=True
)

# Load validation dataset
val_dataset = BloodMNIST(
    split="val",
    root=cfg.data_dir,
    transform=transform,
    download=True
)

# Load test dataset
test_dataset = BloodMNIST(
    split="test",
    root=cfg.data_dir,
    transform=transform,
    download=True
)

1.6 — Create Training, Validation & Test DataLoaders¶

Objective

Create PyTorch DataLoaders for the official BloodMNIST splits, using appropriate batch sizes, shuffling rules, and random-seed controls.

Procedure

  1. Initialize a seeded torch.Generator using the first experimental seed (cfg.seeds[0]).
  2. Create train_loader with batch_size=cfg.batch_size (128) and shuffle=True, using the seeded generator.
  3. Create val_loader and test_loader with batch_size=cfg.eval_batch_size (1024) and shuffle=False.

Purpose

Organize the prepared datasets into mini-batches for efficient training and evaluation. Seeded training shuffling supports reproducible batch ordering under the same execution conditions, while disabling evaluation shuffling provides consistent sample ordering.

Expected Results

  • train_loader: Shuffled training mini-batches of up to 128 images.
  • val_loader: Validation mini-batches of up to 1024 images.
  • test_loader: Test mini-batches of up to 1024 images.

Each batch contains an image tensor and the corresponding classification labels.

Role in the Experiment

Section 1.6 connects the prepared datasets from Section 1.5 to the training and evaluation functions implemented in Part 3.

Part 5 introduces make_train_loader(seed) to create a fresh, independently seeded training DataLoader for each experimental run. Parts 6–7 then use this per-run training procedure to compare network depths and activation functions under consistent batching rules.

Important distinction: A DataLoader supplies batches but does not execute forward propagation, calculate loss, perform backpropagation, or update model parameters. These operations are implemented in the training pipeline.

In [11]:
# Set seed for training batch shuffling
seed = cfg.seeds[0]
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)

# Training DataLoader
train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset,
    batch_size=cfg.batch_size,
    shuffle=True,
    generator=g
)

# Validation DataLoader
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset,
    batch_size=cfg.eval_batch_size,
    shuffle=False
)

# Test DataLoader
test_loader = DataLoader(
    test_dataset,
    batch_size=cfg.eval_batch_size,
    shuffle=False
)

1.7 — Verify Official Dataset Split Sizes¶

Objective

Verify that the loaded BloodMNIST training, validation, and test datasets contain the expected numbers of samples.

Procedure

  1. Display the number of samples in train_dataset, val_dataset, and test_dataset using len().

1.10 — Verify Image Normalization & Numerical Validity¶

Objective

Inspect the training-derived RGB normalization statistics and verify that a preprocessed training batch contains numerically valid values.

Procedure

  1. Display BLOODMNIST_MEAN and BLOODMNIST_STD, calculated from the training dataset in Section 1.3.
  2. Assert that all three RGB standard deviations are positive.
  3. Compute and display the per-channel mean and standard deviation of the normalized image batch from Section 1.8.
  4. Assert that all image tensor values are finite (no NaN or infinity).

Purpose

Perform a preprocessing sanity check before model training. Positive standard deviations prevent division by zero during normalization, while finite-value checks help identify invalid model inputs.

Expected Results

  • Positive training-derived RGB standard deviations.
  • Finite normalized image values.
  • Batch-level RGB means and standard deviations displayed for inspection.
  • All assertions pass, and the code prints Normalization checks: OK.

Note: Batch-level means and standard deviations are not expected to equal exactly 0 and 1 because normalization parameters were calculated from the entire training set rather than the inspected mini-batch.

Role in the Experiment

This section checks the numerical validity of inputs produced using the transform defined in Section 1.4 and attached to the dataset in Section 1.5.

Consistent input normalization supports the controlled comparisons in Stage A (network depth) and Stage B (activation function), where input scaling can influence activation magnitudes, gradient measurements, and optimization behavior.

Important distinction: This section inspects normalization statistics and verifies numerical validity; it does not independently prove that every image was normalized correctly or that all batch statistics match the full training-set statistics.

1.11 — Inspect & Verify Class Distribution¶

Objective

  3. Display the class counts in a table and verify that their totals match the corresponding dataset sizes.
  4. Visualize the training-set class distribution using a horizontal bar chart.

Identify potential class imbalance, understand the representation of each class, and verify the consistency of the dataset labels and sample counts.

Role in the Experiment

This section provides exploratory data analysis and class-frequency information needed to interpret classification performance in the later experiments.

In Part 3, validation accuracy measures overall prediction correctness, while macro-F1 averages the F1 scores of the eight classes equally. Reporting both metrics helps assess classification performance when class frequencies are unequal.

The same dataset splits are used in Stage A (depth comparison) and Stage B (activation comparison), so the class distributions remain consistent across experimental conditions.

Important distinction: This section analyzes class frequencies; it does not rebalance the dataset, modify labels, calculate classification metrics, or train a model. Class counts matching dataset sizes verifies count consistency but does not independently establish label correctness.

It supports understanding the classification task before MLP construction in Part 2 and model training in Parts 3–7.

# Get training labels
train_labels = train_dataset.labels.reshape(-1)

# Prepare mean and std for undoing normalization
mean = torch.tensor(BLOODMNIST_MEAN).view(3, 1, 1)
std = torch.tensor(BLOODMNIST_STD).view(3, 1, 1)

# Create a figure with 8 images

for i in range(cfg.num_classes):

    # Get the normalized image
    image, label = train_dataset[int(idx)]

    # Undo normalization for visualization
    image = image * std + mean

    # Convert [C, H, W] to [H, W, C]
    image = image.permute(1, 2, 0)

    # Display image
    axes[i].imshow(image.clamp(0, 1).numpy())
    axes[i].set_title(f"Class {i}", fontsize=10)
    axes[i].axis("off")

1.13 — Verify DataLoader Shuffling Reproducibility¶

Objective

Verify that independently created training DataLoaders produce identical first mini-batches when initialized with the same random seed.

Procedure

  1. Define get_first_batch(seed) to create a training DataLoader with shuffle=True and a freshly seeded torch.Generator.
  2. Retrieve two first mini-batches using the same seed (42) and one using a different seed (43).
  3. Use torch.equal() and assertions to confirm that both images and labels are identical for the same seed.
  4. Display whether the first image batches differ when different seeds are used.

Purpose

Check that the seeded DataLoader shuffling procedure is reproducible under the same dataset and execution conditions, supporting consistent experimental comparisons.

Expected Results

  • Identical images and labels for the two first batches generated with seed 42.
  • All same-seed assertions pass, and the code prints Same seed reproduces the first batch: OK.
  • The different-seed comparison typically returns True, indicating different first-batch images; this comparison is displayed but not asserted.

Role in the Experiment

This section verifies the seeded shuffling mechanism introduced in Section 1.6.

Part 5 later defines make_train_loader(seed) to create a fresh training DataLoader for each experimental run. Parts 6–7 use this per-run procedure with seeds 0, 1, and 2 to support reproducible depth and activation comparisons.

Important distinction: This check verifies first-batch reproducibility, not full training determinism. It does not verify model initialization, optimizer updates, complete epoch ordering, or identical training results across devices. get_first_batch(seed) is an inspection helper; make_train_loader(seed) in Part 5 is used for the main experiments.

In [18]:
# Get the first batch using a specific seed
def get_first_batch(seed):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)

    loader = DataLoader(
        train_dataset,
        batch_size=cfg.batch_size,
        shuffle=True,
        generator=g
    )

    return next(iter(loader))


# Same seed
images_a, labels_a = get_first_batch(42)
images_b, labels_b = get_first_batch(42)

# Different seed
images_c, labels_c = get_first_batch(43)

# Verify reproducibility
assert torch.equal(images_a, images_b)
assert torch.equal(labels_a, labels_b)

print("Same seed reproduces the first batch: OK")
print(
    "Different seeds give different first batches:",
    not torch.equal(images_a, images_c)
)

Same seed reproduces the first batch: OK
Different seeds give different first batches: True

# Convert mean and std to arrays for broadcasting

std = np.array(BLOODMNIST_STD).reshape(3, 1, 1)

    plt.imshow(np_img)
    plt.axis("off")

Part 2 — Configurable Constant-Width MLP (Model Construction & Verification)¶

Objective:

Build a reusable, configurable Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture to investigate how network depth and hidden-layer activation functions affect gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, and learning behavior on BloodMNIST.

This part focuses on model construction, weight initialization, and architecture verification. No model training is performed in Part 2.

Model Architecture:

2352 → 256 → ... → 256 → 8

  • Input: 2,352 features from flattened RGB BloodMNIST images (3 × 28 × 28).
  • Hidden layers: Configurable number of Linear layers, each containing 256 neurons.
  • Hidden activations: Sigmoid, Tanh, or ReLU, applied after each hidden Linear layer.
  • Output layer: A Linear layer producing 8 raw logits, one for each BloodMNIST class.

Design Choices¶

  1. Configurable depth: Use a single ConstantWidthMLP class to construct networks with different numbers of hidden layers. The experiment compares D2, D5, D10, and D20 in Stage A, where D2 contains 2 hidden Linear layers, D5 contains 5, and so on. Each model contains depth + 1 Linear layers, including the output layer.

  2. Constant hidden width: Keep all hidden layers at 256 neurons to maintain a consistent hidden-layer width across network depths. Increasing depth introduces additional layers and parameters while preserving the same hidden width.

  3. Activation functions: Use Sigmoid as the baseline activation in Stage A (Part 6). Compare Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU at a fixed network depth in Stage B (Part 7). Each model uses one activation function consistently across all its hidden layers.

  4. Weight initialization: Apply Xavier Uniform initialization (gain = 1) to all Linear layers in both Stage A and Stage B, with all Linear biases initialized to zero. Keep the initialization rule fixed to support controlled comparisons. Alternative initialization schemes, including He Uniform, are not evaluated in the main experiment.

  5. Controlled architecture: Use only Linear layers and hidden-layer activation functions, without Batch Normalization, Dropout, or residual connections. This avoids introducing additional architectural components that could affect gradient propagation and complicate the controlled comparisons.

  6. Reproducibility: Set a random seed before model initialization to produce reproducible initial weights and biases under the same configuration. Use the same seed set across experimental conditions to support consistent comparisons.

  7. Layer-wise gradient analysis: Provide the linear_layers() method to access the model's Linear layers in input-to-output order. This supports the gradient-recording and parameter-measurement procedures implemented in Part 4.

  8. Raw output logits: Do not apply a hidden activation function or Softmax after the output Linear layer. Return raw logits with shape [batch_size, 8], as expected by PyTorch's nn.CrossEntropyLoss in Part 3.

Model Components¶

  • ConstantWidthMLP(nn.Module): Defines the configurable MLP architecture, including hidden Linear layers, activation functions, and the output Linear layer.
  • __init__(): Creates and initializes the model's layers and activation function.
  • forward(): Defines how input images are flattened and passed through the hidden layers and output layer.
  • linear_layers(): Provides ordered access to the Linear layers for subsequent gradient and parameter analysis.
  • build_model(): Creates a new model instance using the specified depth, activation function, and random seed.

These components are defined once and reused throughout the experiment rather than being reimplemented for each model configuration.

Model Verification¶

  • Verify the architecture and number of Linear layers for the selected network depths.
  • Check the number of trainable parameters.
  • Verify that a forward pass produces raw logits with shape [batch_size, 8].
  • Confirm that the selected activation function is correctly assigned to the hidden layers.
  • Verify Xavier Uniform initialization and zero-initialized biases.
  • Confirm reproducible initial parameters when models are constructed with the same random seed.

These checks validate model construction before the training and gradient-measurement pipeline is introduced.

Role in the Experiment & Connections to Other Parts¶

Part 2 establishes the shared neural network architecture used throughout the project.

  • Part 0 — Setup & Configuration: Supplies model dimensions, initialization settings, device configuration, and random seeds.
  • Part 1 — Data Pipeline: Supplies normalized BloodMNIST images with shape [batch_size, 3, 28, 28], which are flattened inside the model.
  • Part 3 — Training & Validation Pipeline: Uses the constructed MLP models with CrossEntropyLoss and SGD to train and evaluate classification performance.
  • Part 4 — Gradient & Trainability Measurements: Uses linear_layers() to access weight-gradient tensors and measure layer-wise RMS gradients and first-layer weight changes.
  • Part 5 — Pipeline Smoke Test & Pilot Configuration: Uses the model-building and training components to verify the complete pipeline and finalize the experimental training settings.
  • Part 6 — Stage A: Network Depth Experiment: Reuses the same model class to compare D2, D5, D10, and D20 with Sigmoid activation.
  • Part 7 — Stage B: Activation Function Experiment: Reuses the same model class at fixed depth D5 to compare Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU under Xavier Uniform initialization.
  • Part 8 — Multi-Seed Analysis & Final Report: Uses the recorded training and gradient results to evaluate the research hypotheses and report final findings.

Expected Result:

A verified, reproducible, configurable MLP architecture that can be reused across all experimental conditions without redefining the model class or changing the underlying model-construction procedure.

The purpose of Part 2 is to construct and verify the models, not to train them or evaluate gradient vanishing yet. Training begins in Part 3, gradient measurements are implemented in Part 4, and the main controlled experiments are conducted in Parts 6–7.

2.1 Define Configurable Constant-Width MLP¶

Objective: Define a reusable Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) class that supports different network depths while maintaining a constant hidden width of 256 neurons.

Model Architecture: 2352 → 256 → ... → 256 → 8

Procedure:

  1. Define the MLP class: Create ConstantWidthMLP, inheriting from PyTorch's nn.Module. The class serves as a reusable blueprint for constructing MLP models.

  2. Define init(): Specify the model's configuration, including:

depth: Number of hidden Linear layers, excluding the output layer.

input_dim: Number of input features (2352 for BloodMNIST).

hidden_dim: Number of neurons per hidden layer (256).

num_classes: Number of output classes (8).

activation: Hidden activation function (sigmoid, tanh, or relu).

  1. Create the model layers:

  • Use nn.Flatten() to convert input images from [B, 3, 28, 28] into [B, 2352].

  • Use nn.ModuleList() to register hidden Linear layers.

  • Use a for loop to create exactly depth hidden layers.

  • The first hidden layer receives 2352 features; subsequent hidden layers receive 256 features.

  • Create one output Linear layer mapping 256 features to 8 logits.

  1. Choose the activation function: Apply the same activation function after every hidden Linear layer. Use Sigmoid for the Stage A baseline and support Tanh/ReLU for Stage B.

  2. Define linear_layers(): Return all hidden and output Linear layers in input-to-output order for layer-wise gradient measurements in Part 4.

  3. Define forward(): Specify how input data passes through Flatten, the hidden Linear layers with activation functions, and the output Linear layer.

Expected Result:

A single MLP class capable of constructing:

  • D2: 2 hidden layers + 1 output Linear layer.

  • D5: 5 hidden layers + 1 output Linear layer.

  • D10: 10 hidden layers + 1 output Linear layer.

  • D20: 20 hidden layers + 1 output Linear layer.

All models have an input dimension of 2352, a hidden width of 256, and an output dimension of 8.

The output layer returns raw logits without a final Sigmoid or Softmax activation because nn.CrossEntropyLoss() expects logits.

Purpose: Establish one consistent architecture family for studying how increasing network depth affects gradient propagation and early-layer trainability.

Defining the class does not yet instantiate a specific D2/D5/D10/D20 model or train any parameters. Actual models will be created in later sections.

In [21]:
class ConstantWidthMLP(nn.Module):                    # Create a custom MLP class that inherits from nn.Module (the base class for neural networks in PyTorch)

    def __init__(                                       # __init__() defines and creates the model's layers (is called automatically when we create an MLP object).
                 self,                                  # self: refers to the current model object.
                 depth,                                 # depth: number of hidden Linear layers (not including output).
                 input_dim=2352,                        # input_dim: number of input features per image = 3*28*28.
                 hidden_dim=256,                        # hidden_dim: number of neurons in each hidden layer.
                 num_classes=8,                         # num_classes: number of output classes in BloodMNIST.     
                 activation="sigmoid"                   # activation: activation function used in all hidden layers.
                 ):

        super().__init__()                              # Initialize the parent class (nn.Module). This allows PyTorch to register and manage model layers. 

        if depth < 1:                                        # Check that the model has at least one hidden layer.
            raise ValueError("depth must be at least 1")     # raise ValueError stops execution if depth is invalid.

        # Flatten input images
        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()                      # Create a Flatten module, converts images from [B, 3, 28, 28] to [B, 2352], B is the batch size. self.flatten belongs to the current MLP object. 

        # Create hidden layers 
        self.hidden_layers = nn.ModuleList()             # Create an empty ModuleList to store hidden Linear layers. ModuleList registers each layer's weights and biases so that PyTorch can include them in model.parameters().

        for i in range(depth):                           # Create exactly 'depth' hidden Linear layers; range(depth) generates 0, 1, ..., depth-1. For depth=2, this loop runs twice (i=0 and i=1).
            in_features = input_dim if i == 0 else hidden_dim     # The first hidden layer receives 2352 input features. All later hidden layers receive 256 input features.This is a Python conditional expression: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false

            self.hidden_layers.append(                   # Create a Linear layer and append it to ModuleList.
                nn.Linear(in_features, hidden_dim)       # nn.Linear(in_features, hidden_dim) computes: output = input @ weight.T + bias
            )                                            # Each hidden layer has 256 output neurons. bias=True by default.

        # Choose activation function (The same activation type is used after every hidden layer)
        if activation == "sigmoid":                      # Stage A baseline: Sigmoid (maps inputs to values between 0 and 1)
            self.activation = nn.Sigmoid()
                                                         # Stage B comparison: Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.
        elif activation == "tanh":                       # Tanh maps inputs to values between -1 and 1.
            self.activation = nn.Tanh()

        elif activation == "relu":                       # Relu maps inputs to values between 0 and infinity. ReLU(x) = max(0, x).
            self.activation = nn.ReLU()

        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported activation: {activation}")    # Stop if an unsupported activation name is provided.

        # Create the final output Linear layer.
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, num_classes)            # Input: 256 features from the last hidden layer. Output: 8 logits, one for each BloodMNIST class. No activation is applied after this output layer,because CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits.

    # Return all Linear layers in input-to-output order (useful for measuring gradients in Part 4)
    def linear_layers(self):
        return [*self.hidden_layers, self.output_layer]   # unpacks the hidden layers from ModuleList. The output layer is then added as the final element. D2 returns: [hidden_layer_1, hidden_layer_2, output_layer]

    def forward(self, x):                                 # forward() defines how input data passes through the model, used when we run model(images). x: input tensor containing a batch of images.

        # Flatten each image into a one-dimensional feature vector, [B, 3, 28, 28] -> [B, 2352]. The batch dimension B is preserved.
        x = self.flatten(x)

        # Pass data through hidden layers one by one
        for layer in self.hidden_layers:         # 'layer' refers to the current Linear layer in ModuleList.
            x = self.activation(layer(x))        # First calculate the Linear layer output: layer(x). Then apply the chosen activation function.
                                                 # D2 runs this line twice:
                                                 # Hidden 1: [B, 2352] -> [B, 256] -> Sigmoid
                                                 # Hidden 2: [B, 256]  -> [B, 256] -> Sigmoid
                                                 # x is updated after every hidden layer.
         # Return raw logits
        x = self.output_layer(x)                 # Pass the last hidden layer's output to the output layer. [B, 256] -> [B, 8]. The result contains raw logits (not probabilities).

        return x                                 # Return the final logits to the caller.

2.2 Initialize Weights and Biases¶

Objective: Define a consistent initialization procedure for all Linear layers to control the initial weight distribution and biases across experimental conditions.

Procedure:

  1. Define a reusable function initialize_weights(model) that accepts a PyTorch model object.

  2. Iterate through the model's registered modules using model.modules().

  3. Identify Linear layers using isinstance(layer, nn.Linear).

  4. Apply Xavier Uniform initialization (gain = 1) to each Linear layer's weight matrix.

Xavier Uniform samples weights from:

$$ W \sim U(-a,a), \qquad a=\sqrt{\frac{6}{fan_{in}+fan_{out}}} $$

  1. Initialize every Linear layer's bias vector to zero using nn.init.zeros_().

  2. Apply the same initialization rule to all hidden and output Linear layers.

Expected Result:

  • All Linear weights are initialized using Xavier Uniform.

  • All Linear biases are initialized to zero.

  • The initialization procedure is consistent across D2, D5, D10, and D20.

  • Stage A and Stage B use the same Xavier initialization scheme.

Purpose: Reduce initialization-related differences between experimental conditions and ensure that the initialization procedure is explicitly documented and reproducible.

The initial weight values are randomly sampled, while biases start at zero. Both weights and biases remain trainable and may change during optimization.

PyTorch initializes Linear layers by default when they are created. This function explicitly replaces those initial values according to the experimental protocol.

Only Xavier Uniform initialization is used in this study. Comparisons involving other initialization schemes are outside the project's scope.

In [22]:
def initialize_weights(model):        # Define a function to initialize all Linear layers in a model. 'model' is the PyTorch neural network passed into the function.

    for layer in model.modules():     # model.modules() iterates through the model and its registered submodules, including nested hidden layers.

        if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):  # Check whether the current module is a Linear layer. isinstance(object, class) returns True or False. Flatten and activation modules are skipped because this initialization rule targets Linear parameters.

            nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight, gain=1.0)  # Initialize the layer's weight matrix using Xavier Uniform initialization with gain=1. 
                                                             # Xavier samples initial weights from U(-a, a), where a = sqrt(6 / (fan_in + fan_out)). 
                                                             # fan_in: number of inputs to the Linear layer.
                                                             # fan_out: number of outputs from the Linear layer.
                                                             # The trailing underscore (_) means that the function modifies the tensor in place.
            
            # Initialize all bias values to zero (applies to both hidden and output layers). zeros_() also modifies the existing tensor in place.
            nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)

2.3 Build MLP Model¶

Objective: Create a reusable function that instantiates a specific MLP architecture and applies the chosen activation function, random seed, and initialization procedure consistently.

Procedure:

  1. Define build_model(depth, seed, activation=None):

depth: Specifies the number of hidden layers.

seed: Controls random initialization.

activation: Optionally overrides the baseline activation.

  1. Choose the activation function: If no activation is provided, use cfg.activation (Sigmoid for the baseline).

  2. Set the random seed: Call torch.manual_seed(seed) before constructing the model.

  3. Create a model instance: Instantiate ConstantWidthMLP using the specified depth and activation, together with the input dimension, hidden width, and number of classes from cfg.

  4. Apply initialization: Call initialize_weights(model) to initialize all Linear weights with Xavier Uniform and set biases to zero.

  5. Return the model: Use return model to provide the newly created MLP object.

Expected Result:

  1. The function can instantiate models such as:

model_d2 = build_model(depth=2, seed=0)

model_d5 = build_model(depth=5, seed=0)

model_d10 = build_model(depth=10, seed=0)

model_d20 = build_model(depth=20, seed=0)

  1. It also supports different activation functions for Stage B:

model_sigmoid = build_model(depth=10, seed=0, activation="sigmoid")

model_tanh = build_model(depth=10, seed=0, activation="tanh")

model_relu = build_model(depth=10, seed=0, activation="relu")

Purpose: Standardize model construction across different depths, activations, and random seeds without repeatedly writing model creation and initialization code.

Using the same architecture, random seed, and initialization procedure produces reproducible initial parameters under the same execution conditions.

Using the same seed for different depths does not guarantee identical initial weights because the architectures differ.

Important: build_model() constructs and initializes the model; it does not train the model, compute classification loss, perform backpropagation, or update parameters.

In [23]:
# Define a reusable function to build an MLP model with controlled initialization
def build_model(depth, seed, activation=None):    # depth: number of hidden layers.
                                                  # seed: random seed used for model initialization.
                                                  # activation=None: use the baseline activation from cfg.
                                                  # If activation is explicitly provided, use that value instead.
    # Use baseline activation (cfg.activation) if none is specified
    if activation is None:                        # Stage A: cfg.activation = "sigmoid". 
        activation = cfg.activation               # 'is None' checks whether activation has the value None.

    # Set the PyTorch random seed before creating the model.
    torch.manual_seed(seed)        # This controls random weight initialization and allows the same model configuration to be reproduced (manual_seed also changes PyTorch's RNG state).

    # Create MLP
    model = ConstantWidthMLP(      # Create an object from the ConstantWidthMLP class.
        depth=depth,               # Pass the depth and activation selected for this model.
        input_dim=cfg.input_dim,   # Read input_dim, hidden_dim, num_classes from Config.
        hidden_dim=cfg.hidden_dim,
        num_classes=cfg.num_classes,
        activation=activation
    )

    # Initialize weights and biases
    initialize_weights(model)      # Apply Xavier Uniform to all Linear weight matrices and initialize all Linear biases to zero. This overwrites PyTorch's default Linear initialization.

    # Return the initialized model object
    return model                   # For example: model_d2 = build_model(depth=2, seed=0)

2.4 Check MLP Model D2 before training¶

Objective: Verify that the baseline D2 MLP is correctly constructed and can perform a forward pass on real BloodMNIST images before training.

Procedure:

  1. Create a D2 model with 2 hidden Linear layers, Sigmoid activation, and Xavier Uniform initialization.

  2. Print the model architecture to inspect its layers and dimensions.

  3. Select the first 8 normalized images from the BloodMNIST training dataset and combine them into a batch of shape [8, 3, 28, 28].

  4. Perform a forward pass in evaluation mode without gradient tracking.

  5. Verify that the model produces finite logits with shape [8, 8].

Expected Result:

Input shape: [8, 3, 28, 28]

Output shape: [8, 8]

No NaN or infinite output values.

Output Layer Verification:

The final output layer is nn.Linear(256, 8), producing 8 raw logits per image.

Unlike the hidden layers, no activation function (Sigmoid, Tanh, ReLU, or Softmax) is applied after the output layer.

This is intentional because nn.CrossEntropyLoss() expects raw logits and internally performs the necessary log-softmax computation.

The forward-pass check confirms the output shape [8, 8] and verifies that all logits are finite. The absence of a final activation is confirmed by inspecting the forward() implementation in Section 2.1.

Purpose: Detect architecture, tensor-shape, or forward-computation errors before implementing the training loop.

This is a forward-pass sanity check only. No loss, backward propagation, optimizer step, or weight update is performed.

In [25]:
# Create the baseline D2 MLP.
model_d2 = build_model(   # build_model() also applies Xavier Uniform initialization.
    depth=2,              # depth=2 means the model has 2 hidden Linear layers.
    seed=cfg.seeds[0]     # seed=cfg.seeds[0] uses the first experimental seed.
)

# Display the architecture of the D2 model (PyTorch prints all registered modules and their dimensions)
print(model_d2)

# Get 8 images directly from the BloodMNIST training dataset.
sample_images = torch.stack(
    [train_dataset[i][0] for i in range(8)]  # train_dataset[i] returns (image, label) for sample i. [0] selects the image, not its label. 
)                                            # 'for i in range(8)' retrieves images with indices 0 to 7.
                                             # The square brackets create a Python list of 8 image tensors. torch.stack() combines these 8 tensors into one batch.
                                             # Each image: [3, 28, 28]
                                             # Final batch: [8, 3, 28, 28]
                                             # The dataset transform from Part 1 already normalized them.
                              
# Forward pass through model D2 without gradient tracking
# 8 images BloodMNIST [8, 3, 28, 28] -> Flatten [8, 3*28*28] or [8, 2352] -> Hidden Layer 1 + Sigmoid [8, 256] -> Hidden Layer 2 + Sigmoid [8, 256] -> Output Linear Layer [8, 8]. Results are logits with shape [8, 8].
model_d2.eval()       # Switch the model to evaluation mode (good practice for model verification). In this MLP, there is no Dropout or BatchNorm,so eval() does not change the forward calculations.

with torch.no_grad():  # Disable gradient tracking for this forward-pass check. We are only checking model outputs, not training. 'with' creates a context in which no_grad() is active.

    logits = model_d2(sample_images)    # Pass the 8 images through model_d2. Calling model_d2(sample_images) invokes the model's forward() method through PyTorch's nn.Module mechanism.
                                        # Input:  [8, 3, 28, 28]
                                        # Output: [8, 8] (8 logits per image)

# Print the input and output tensor shapes.
print("Input shape:", sample_images.shape)
print("Output shape:", logits.shape)

# Verify that the output shape is correct [8, 8]
assert logits.shape == (8, cfg.num_classes)  # assert checks a condition. If the condition is False, Python raises AssertionError. cfg.num_classes = 8 for BloodMNIST.

# Verify that all output values are finite (output values are not NaN, +inf, or -inf)
assert torch.isfinite(logits).all()          # torch.isfinite(logits) checks for NaN and infinity.
                                             # .all() returns True only if every value is finite.

# Verify that the output layer is Linear (raw logits)
assert isinstance(model_d2.output_layer, nn.Linear)

print("Output layer: Linear (raw logits, no final activation) - OK")

print("D2 forward pass: OK")                 # This message is printed only if all checks pass.

  (hidden_layers): ModuleList(
    (0): Linear(in_features=2352, out_features=256, bias=True)
    (1): Linear(in_features=256, out_features=256, bias=True)
  )
  (activation): Sigmoid()
  (output_layer): Linear(in_features=256, out_features=8, bias=True)
)

2.5 Check models D2, D5, D10, D20¶

Objective: Confirm that the same configurable MLP class correctly constructs and runs networks with 2, 5, 10, and 20 hidden layers.

Procedure:

  1. Iterate over the configured depths: D2, D5, D10, and D20.

  2. Build a new model for each depth using the same hidden width, activation function, Xavier initialization rule, and random seed.

  3. Pass the same batch of 8 BloodMNIST images through each model.

  4. Verify that each network contains exactly depth + 1 Linear layers, including the output layer.

  5. Verify that every model returns finite logits with shape [8, 8].

Expected Result:

  • D2: 2 hidden layers + 1 output layer.

  • D5: 5 hidden layers + 1 output layer.

  • D10: 10 hidden layers + 1 output layer.

  • D20: 20 hidden layers + 1 output layer.

  • All models produce outputs with shape [8, 8].

Purpose: Ensure that changing the depth parameter correctly changes the number of hidden layers while preserving the required input and output dimensions.

These checks verify model construction and forward computation, not training performance.

In [26]:
# Loop through the depths defined in Config.
# Example: cfg.depths = (2, 5, 10, 20). The loop runs four times, creating one model per depth.
for depth in cfg.depths:
    model = build_model(              # Build a new model for the current depth. Each model uses:
        depth=depth,                  # - The same hidden width (256)
        seed=cfg.seeds[0]             # - The same baseline activation (Sigmoid)
    )                                 # - The same initialization rule (Xavier Uniform)
                                      # - The same experimental seed

    model.eval()                      # Set the model to evaluation mode for verification.

    with torch.no_grad():             # Perform a forward pass without tracking gradients.
        logits = model(sample_images) # Reuse the same 8 images from Section 2.4. The output should have shape [8, 8] for every depth.

    # Check the total number of Linear layers.
    assert len(model.linear_layers()) == depth + 1  # linear_layers() returns all hidden layers + output layer. D2 should have 3 Linear layers. D20 should have 21 Linear layers.

    # Check that the output has 8 logits per image.
    assert logits.shape == (8, cfg.num_classes)

    # Check that the output contains no NaN or infinity.
    assert torch.isfinite(logits).all()

    # Print the current model's depth and output shape.
    print(f"D{depth}: output shape = {logits.shape} - OK") # f"..." is a Python f-string. {depth} inserts the current depth into the text.

# Print the final message after all four models pass.
print("All MLP architectures: OK")

2.6 Verify Model Parameters & Bias Initialization¶

Objective: Verify that each MLP (D2, D5, D10, D20) has the correct number of parameters and that all Linear layer biases are initialized to zero before training.

Procedure:

  1. Count actual model parameters: Define count_params(model) to count all weight and bias values in the PyTorch model using model.parameters() and p.numel().

  2. Calculate expected parameters: Define expected_params(depth) to independently calculate the theoretical number of parameters based on the model architecture.

    For a Linear layer with bias=True:

    $$ \text{Parameters} = \text{in\_features}\times\text{out\_features}+\text{out\_features} $$

    For the constant-width MLP:

    $$ \begin{aligned} P(D) ={}& (2352\times256+256)\\ &+ (D-1)(256\times256+256)\\ &+ (256\times8+8) \end{aligned} $$

    Where:

    • First term: Parameters in the first hidden layer.
    • Second term: Parameters in the remaining D - 1 hidden layers.
    • Third term: Parameters in the output layer.
    • D: Number of hidden layers, excluding the output layer.

  3. Verify parameter counts: Compare the actual parameter count returned by count_params(model) with the expected count calculated by expected_params(depth). Use assert to confirm that both values match.

  4. Verify bias initialization: Iterate through all Linear layers using model.linear_layers() and confirm that every bias value is zero before training.

Expected Result:

Model Hidden Layers Total Linear Layers Total Parameters
D2 2 3 670,216
D5 5 6 867,592
D10 10 11 1,196,552
D20 20 21 1,854,472

All Linear layer biases should be initialized to zero.

Purpose:

  • Confirm that each MLP contains the expected number of trainable parameters.
  • Detect possible architecture errors, such as missing layers or incorrect layer dimensions.
  • Verify that the intended zero-bias initialization has been applied consistently.
  • Document how total parameter count increases with network depth, even though all hidden layers maintain a constant width of 256 neurons.

Important Notes:

  • Increasing depth adds more hidden Linear layers and therefore increases the total number of parameters.
  • Constant hidden width does not imply equal parameter counts across different network depths.
  • All weights are initialized using PyTorch's Xavier Uniform initialization, while biases are initialized to zero.
  • Zero-initialized biases remain trainable and may change during optimization.
  • Detailed empirical verification of each layer's initial weight standard deviation is outside the scope of this study.
  • These checks validate model structure and initial bias values; they do not evaluate training performance or gradient propagation.
In [ ]:
# Define a function to count all model parameters.
def count_params(model):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) # model.parameters() returns the trainable parameter tensors, including Linear weights and biases. For example, in model D2, they include Hidden 1 weights and bias, Hidden 2 weights and bias, Output weight and bias.
                                                      # p.numel() returns the number of scalar values in tensor p.
                                                      # The generator expression iterates through all parameters. sum() adds their element counts together.



# Calculate the expected number of parameters (This formula assumes the constant-width MLP architecture)
def expected_params(depth):  # Read model dimensions from Config.

    d = cfg.input_dim        # d: input dimension = 2352
    h = cfg.hidden_dim       # h: hidden width = 256
    c = cfg.num_classes      # c: output classes = 8

    first_hidden = d * h + h                     # First hidden layer: Linear(d, h). Weight matrix has h*d values. Bias vector has h values. Example: 2352*256 + 256
    other_hidden = (depth - 1) * (h * h + h)     # Remaining hidden layers: Linear(h, h). There are (depth - 1) such layers. Each has h*h weight values and h bias values.
    output = h * c + c                           # Output layer: Linear(h, c).  h*c weights and c biases.

    return first_hidden + other_hidden + output  # Total parameters = first hidden + other hidden + output.


# Check all four model depths and verify parameters & biases.
for depth in cfg.depths:

    model = build_model(depth=depth, seed=cfg.seeds[0])  # Create a model using the baseline configuration.

    actual = count_params(model)                         # Count parameters directly from the PyTorch model.

    expected = expected_params(depth)                    # Calculate parameters using the architecture formula.

    assert actual == expected                            # The actual parameter count must match the formula.

    # Verify all bias initialization are zero for every Linear layer
    for layer in model.linear_layers():
        assert torch.count_nonzero(layer.bias).item() == 0  # torch.count_nonzero() counts nonzero tensor elements. The expected number is 0 because biases start at zero. 
                                                            # .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number.

    print(f"D{depth}: {actual:,} parameters - OK")          # Print the total parameter count for this model.
                                                            # :, adds thousands separators to make large numbers readable.

D2: 670,216 parameters - OK
D5: 867,592 parameters - OK
D10: 1,196,552 parameters - OK
D20: 1,854,472 parameters - OK

2.7 Verify Model Initialization Reproducibility¶

Objective: Verify that models with identical architectures and random seeds receive identical initial parameters.

Procedure:

  1. Create two D10 models using the same random seed (seed=0).

  2. Create a third D10 model using a different seed (seed=1).

  3. Compare corresponding weights and biases across models using torch.equal().

  4. Verify that the two models created with the same seed have identical parameters.

  5. Verify that at least one parameter tensor differs when using different seeds.

Expected Result:

  • Same architecture + same seed → identical initial parameters.

  • Same architecture + different seeds → different initial weights.

Purpose: Verify that model initialization is reproducible under the same configuration.

Using the same seed across different depths does not imply identical weights because the architectures contain different numbers of parameters.

In Stage B, models with the same depth and seed will use identical initial parameters while changing only the activation function (Sigmoid, Tanh, or ReLU).

This test verifies initialization reproducibility, not full training reproducibility. DataLoader shuffling and other sources of randomness will be controlled during the experiments.

In [28]:
# Build three models with the same architecture and seeds (D10).
model_a = build_model(depth=10, seed=0)  # model_a and model_b use the same seed (0).
model_b = build_model(depth=10, seed=0)
model_c = build_model(depth=10, seed=1)  # model_c uses a different seed (1).

# Check that the same seed gives identical parameters (Check whether model_a and model_b (with same seed) have identical parameters)
same_seed = all(                # Require all parameter pairs to be identical for the same seed
    torch.equal(p1, p2)         # torch.equal(p1, p2) checks exact tensor equality
    for p1, p2 in zip(          # zip() pairs corresponding parameters from the two models
        model_a.parameters(),   # return weights and biases of model a
        model_b.parameters()    # return weights and biases of model b
    )
)                               # all() returns True if every parameter pair is identical.

# Check that different seeds give different parameters (Check whether model_a and model_c have any differences)
different_seed = any(           # any() returns True if at least one pair differs.
    not torch.equal(p1, p2)     # 'not torch.equal(...)' is True if a parameter pair differs.
    for p1, p2 in zip(
        model_a.parameters(),
        model_c.parameters()
    )
)

# Models with the same architecture and seed must match.
assert same_seed

# Different seeds should produce different initial parameters.
assert different_seed

# Print success if both checks pass.
print("Model initialization reproducibility: OK")

Model initialization reproducibility: OK

Part 3 — Training & Validation Pipeline¶

1. Overview & Objective¶

Part 3 implements a reusable training and validation pipeline for the configurable MLP architectures defined in Part 2.

The objective is to establish consistent optimization and evaluation procedures across network depths and activation functions, enabling controlled comparisons in Stage A and Stage B.

The training pipeline updates model parameters using mini-batch SGD, while the validation pipeline evaluates classification performance without parameter updates.

2. Workflow & Section Guide¶

Section Main Task Purpose
3.1 — Define CrossEntropyLoss Create nn.CrossEntropyLoss() for eight-class classification. Establish a consistent training and evaluation objective.
3.2 — Define SGD Optimizer Configure SGD using the shared learning rate, zero momentum, and zero weight decay. Apply a consistent parameter-update rule across experimental conditions.
3.3 — Implement train_one_epoch() Perform forward propagation, loss calculation, backpropagation, and SGD updates over training batches. Train model parameters and return sample-weighted mean training loss.
3.4 — Implement evaluate() Calculate validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1 without updating model parameters. Evaluate classification performance consistently across models.
3.5 — Short D2 Training Trial Run a limited training and full-validation check using a freshly initialized D2 model. Verify the integration of the data, model, training, and validation components.

3. Training Protocol¶

For each training mini-batch, train_one_epoch() performs:

  1. Prepare image tensors and integer class labels on the selected device.
  2. Clear previous gradients using optimizer.zero_grad().
  3. Generate logits using model(images).
  4. Calculate classification loss using nn.CrossEntropyLoss().
  5. Compute parameter gradients using loss.backward().
  6. Update weights and biases using optimizer.step().

The MLP returns eight raw logits per image. Softmax is not applied separately before CrossEntropyLoss.

The optimizer uses plain SGD with momentum and weight decay fixed at zero. The learning rate is initially provisional and is finalized through the pilot procedure in Part 5.

For each parameter (W), the SGD update is:

$$ W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta\frac{\partial L_t}{\partial W_t} $$

where $\eta$ is the learning rate and $L_t$ is the current mini-batch loss.

The training function returns the sample-weighted mean loss across processed batches:

$$ L_{\text{train}}= \frac{\sum_b B_bL_b}{\sum_b B_b} $$

where $B_b$ is the number of samples in batch $b$, and $L_b$ is its mean loss.

This accounts for unequal batch sizes, including the final batch of an epoch.

4. Validation Protocol & Metrics¶

The evaluate() function uses model.eval() and disables gradient tracking during validation.

Model parameters remain unchanged during evaluation.

Metric Definition Interpretation
Validation Loss Sample-weighted mean CrossEntropyLoss across validation batches. Measures classification loss on the validation split.
Validation Accuracy Proportion of correctly classified validation images. Measures overall classification correctness.
Validation Macro-F1 Unweighted mean of the eight class-specific F1 scores. Evaluates class-wise performance without weighting classes by frequency.

Macro-F1 is calculated from predictions collected across the complete validation dataset rather than averaging batch-level F1 scores.

The official test split remains reserved and is not used in the main experiments.

5. Short D2 Integration Trial¶

Section 3.5 verifies the training and validation pipeline using a newly initialized D2 model.

The trial performs two short training passes, each limited to five mini-batches, followed by evaluation on the complete validation split.

These are partial debugging passes, not full training epochs or main experimental runs.

The trial checks that model inputs, loss calculation, backpropagation, SGD updates, and validation metrics execute correctly.

6. Connections to Subsequent Parts¶

Part Connection to Part 3
Part 4 — Gradient Measurements Extends the training procedure with layer-wise RMS gradient recording and normalized first-layer weight displacement measurements.
Part 5 — Pilot & Pipeline Verification Integrates training, validation, and gradient recording into run_training(); verifies the pipeline and finalizes experimental settings.
Part 6 — Stage A Reuses the established procedures to compare D2, D5, D10, and D20.
Part 7 — Stage B Applies the same training and evaluation protocol to Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU at fixed D5 depth.
Part 8 — Final Reporting Summarizes and interprets the recorded training and validation results.

7. Expected Outcome & Role in the Experiment¶

Part 3 establishes reusable train_one_epoch() and evaluate() functions, a consistent classification objective, and an SGD optimization protocol.

These components provide the training-loss and validation-performance measurements needed to assess model trainability alongside the gradient and weight-change measurements introduced in Part 4.

The short D2 trial verifies basic pipeline execution; the controlled multi-seed experiments are conducted later in Parts 6–7.

3.1 — Define Cross-Entropy Loss¶

Objective: Define the loss function used to measure classification errors during MLP training and validation.

Procedure:

  1. Create a loss function using nn.CrossEntropyLoss().
  2. The loss function receives:
    • logits: Raw model outputs with shape [B, 8], where each image has 8 class scores.
    • labels: Ground-truth class indices with shape [B], containing integer values from 0 to 7.
  3. Compute a scalar loss representing the average classification error within a batch.
  4. Use the same loss function for training and validation.

Expected Result:

  • Input logits: [B, 8]
  • Input labels: [B]
  • Output: One scalar CrossEntropyLoss value.

Purpose: Provide the optimization objective that allows the model to compute gradients during backpropagation.

Important Notes:

  • The output layer must return raw logits without a final Sigmoid or Softmax.
  • nn.CrossEntropyLoss() internally performs the necessary log-softmax computation.
  • The loss function measures classification error but does not update model parameters. Parameter updates are performed later by the optimizer.
In [29]:
# Define the classification loss function
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # Computes mean cross-entropy from logits [B, 8] and integer labels [B]

3.2 — Define SGD Optimizer¶

Objective: Create an SGD optimizer to update the MLP's trainable parameters using gradients computed during backpropagation.

Procedure:

  1. Create a fresh baseline D2 model using build_model().
  2. Move the model to the configured computation device (CPU, CUDA, or MPS).
  3. Create an SGD optimizer using torch.optim.SGD().
  4. Pass model.parameters() to identify the weights and biases that will be optimized.
  5. Use the learning rate, momentum, and weight decay specified in cfg.

Expected Result:

  • A newly initialized D2 MLP ready for training.
  • An SGD optimizer connected to the D2 model's parameters.
  • No parameter updates until the training loop calls optimizer.step().

Purpose: Define a consistent optimization method for the controlled gradient-vanishing experiments.

For plain SGD without momentum or weight decay, parameter updates follow:

$$ W\_{t+1}=W_t-\eta\nabla_W L $$

where $\eta$ is the learning rate and $\nabla_W L$ is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights.

Important Notes:

  • SGD is used consistently across all experimental conditions.
  • The initial learning rate is provisional and will be checked during the learning-rate sanity pilot in Part 5.
  • The same primary learning rate will be used across depths in the main experiment.
  • Creating the optimizer does not update weights. Updates occur when optimizer.step() is called during training.
In [30]:
# Create a fresh D2 model for training (separate from the model checks in Part 2)
model_d2_train = build_model(
    depth=2,                       # D2 has 2 hidden Linear layers
    seed=cfg.seeds[0]              # Use the first experimental seed for this trial
).to(device)                       # Move model parameters to CPU, CUDA, or MPS

# Configure SGD using the experimental settings from Part 0

    momentum=cfg.momentum,         # 0.0 means standard SGD without momentum

)
