# Select early-training RMS gradients recorded during the first 10 batches of epoch 1.
fig1_epoch = 1                                           # Compare all depths at the same training epoch
fig1_data = stage_a_gradients_df.loc[
    stage_a_gradients_df["epoch"] == fig1_epoch
].copy()                                                 # Copy the selected records without modifying Section 6.3 data

assert len(fig1_data) == len(cfg.seeds) * sum(cfg.depths)  # 3 seeds × (2 + 5 + 10 + 20) = 111 records
assert np.isfinite(fig1_data["mean_grad_rms"]).all()      # All recorded gradient magnitudes must be finite
assert (fig1_data["mean_grad_rms"] >= 0).all()             # RMS gradients cannot be negative


# Find the last hidden-layer RMS gradient within each depth-seed run.
last_hidden = fig1_data.loc[
    fig1_data["layer"] == fig1_data["depth"],
    ["depth", "seed", "mean_grad_rms"]
].rename(columns={"mean_grad_rms": "last_hidden_rms"})    # Rename the reference gradient for clarity

assert len(last_hidden) == len(cfg.depths) * len(cfg.seeds)  # Exactly one reference for each of the 12 runs

# Match each hidden layer with its own run's reference, then calculate relative gradient magnitude.
fig1_data = fig1_data.merge(
    last_hidden,
    on=["depth", "seed"],                                 # Match using BOTH depth and seed to avoid mixing runs
    validate="many_to_one"                               # Many layers must match exactly one reference row
)

fig1_data["relative_grad_rms"] = (
    fig1_data["mean_grad_rms"]
    / fig1_data["last_hidden_rms"].replace(0, np.nan)    # RMS(layer l) / RMS(last hidden layer); avoid division by zero
)


# Calculate mean ± sample standard deviation across the three seeds for each depth and hidden layer.
fig1_summary = (
    fig1_data.groupby(["depth", "layer"], as_index=False)  # Group matching hidden layers within each depth
    .agg(
        grad_mean=("mean_grad_rms", "mean"),                # Mean absolute RMS gradient across seeds
        grad_std=("mean_grad_rms", "std"),                  # Sample std of absolute RMS gradients
        ratio_mean=("relative_grad_rms", "mean"),           # Mean of per-run relative gradient ratios
        ratio_std=("relative_grad_rms", "std")              # Sample std of per-run relative ratios
    )
)


# Create one Figure 1 containing absolute and relative gradient comparisons.
fig, (ax_abs, ax_rel) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5))  # Two complementary panels in one figure

for depth in cfg.depths:

    rows = fig1_summary.loc[
        fig1_summary["depth"] == depth
    ].sort_values("layer")                                # Arrange Hidden Layer 1 through the last hidden layer

    x = rows["layer"].to_numpy()                           # Horizontal axis: hidden-layer index
    grad_mean = rows["grad_mean"].to_numpy()                # Mean absolute RMS gradient for each layer
    grad_std = rows["grad_std"].fillna(0).to_numpy()        # Standard deviation across seeds
    ratio_mean = rows["ratio_mean"].to_numpy()              # Mean RMS gradient relative to the last hidden layer
    ratio_std = rows["ratio_std"].fillna(0).to_numpy()      # Standard deviation of the relative ratios

    # Panel (a): Plot absolute RMS gradients and their mean ± std bands.
    line, = ax_abs.plot(
        x, np.where(grad_mean > 0, grad_mean, np.nan),      # Log scale requires positive plotted values
        marker="o", markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.8,
        label=f"D{depth}"                                  # Identify each network by its number of hidden layers
    )

    color = line.get_color()                               # Reuse the same automatic color in both panels

    ax_abs.fill_between(
        x,
        np.where(grad_mean - grad_std > 0, grad_mean - grad_std, np.nan),  # Lower mean - std bound
        grad_mean + grad_std,                             # Upper mean + std bound
        color=color, alpha=0.16                            # Light shading for variability across seeds
    )

    # Panel (b): Plot relative gradients using the SAME depth color for easy comparison.
    ax_rel.plot(
        x, np.where(ratio_mean > 0, ratio_mean, np.nan),    # Last hidden layer has ratio 1 when defined
        marker="o", markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.8,
        color=color, label=f"D{depth}"
    )

    ax_rel.fill_between(
        x,
        np.where(ratio_mean - ratio_std > 0, ratio_mean - ratio_std, np.nan),  # Positive lower bound
        ratio_mean + ratio_std,                           # Upper mean + std bound
        color=color, alpha=0.16
    )


# Add scientific labels, logarithmic scales, and legends to both panels.
ax_abs.set_title("(a) Absolute RMS Gradient")
ax_abs.set_ylabel("RMS weight gradient (per parameter)")

ax_rel.set_title("(b) Relative to the Last Hidden Layer")
ax_rel.set_ylabel("RMS gradient / last hidden-layer RMS")
ax_rel.axhline(1.0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)  # Reference ratio of the last hidden layer

for ax in (ax_abs, ax_rel):
    ax.set_xlabel("Hidden-layer index (1 = closest to input)")
    ax.set_yscale("log")                                   # Show large differences in gradient orders of magnitude
    ax.grid(True, which="both", linestyle=":", alpha=0.3)  # Add light gridlines for easier reading
    ax.legend(title="Depth")                              # Identify D2, D5, D10, and D20

fig.suptitle(
    f"Figure 1 — Stage A Gradient Magnitude vs. Layer (Epoch {fig1_epoch})",
    fontsize=13
)
fig.tight_layout()                                        # Adjust spacing between panels and labels


# Save one publication-ready figure in both PNG and vector PDF formats.
fig1_dir = Path(cfg.results_dir) / "stage_a"               # Reuse the existing Stage A results folder
fig1_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)               # Create the folder if necessary

fig1_png = fig1_dir / "figure1_gradient_vs_layer.png"     # High-resolution image for reports and slides
fig1_pdf = fig1_dir / "figure1_gradient_vs_layer.pdf"     # Vector version for scalable report figures

fig.savefig(fig1_png, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")       # Save PNG at 300 dpi
fig.savefig(fig1_pdf, bbox_inches="tight")                # Save vector PDF
plt.show()                                                # Display Figure 1 in the notebook
plt.close(fig)                                            # Close the Matplotlib figure after display


# Display a compact table of first-hidden-layer gradients for comparing network depths.
fig1_first_layer = fig1_summary.loc[
    fig1_summary["layer"] == 1,
    ["depth", "grad_mean", "grad_std", "ratio_mean", "ratio_std"]
].copy()                                                   # One summary row for Hidden Layer 1 of each depth

print("=== Figure 1 — First Hidden-Layer Gradient Summary (Epoch 1) ===")
print(
    fig1_first_layer.to_string(
        index=False,
        float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3e}"          # Scientific notation preserves extremely small values
    )
)

# Report any exact-zero gradients, which cannot appear directly on logarithmic axes.
if (fig1_data["mean_grad_rms"] == 0).any():
    print("Note: Exact-zero RMS gradients are omitted from the log-scale curves.")

if (last_hidden["last_hidden_rms"] == 0).any():
    print("Note: Relative gradients are undefined when the last hidden-layer RMS is zero.")

print(f"\nFigure 1 saved to: {fig1_png}")
print(f"Vector version saved to: {fig1_pdf}")

6.4 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully generated Figure 1 using the recorded epoch-1 layer-wise RMS weight gradients from all 12 Stage A runs (4 depths × 3 random seeds).
  • Reused stage_a_gradients_df from Section 6.3 without retraining models or recomputing gradients through backpropagation.
  • Selected gradient measurements from the first 10 training batches of epoch 1 for each hidden layer.
  • Calculated two complementary metrics:
    • Absolute RMS gradient: The mean RMS weight gradient for each hidden layer, aggregated across three seeds.
    • Relative RMS gradient: The RMS gradient of each hidden layer divided by the RMS gradient of the last hidden layer within the same depth–seed run.
  • Calculated mean and sample standard deviation across the three random seeds for both metrics.
  • Created Figure 1 with two panels:
    • Panel (a): Absolute RMS Gradient vs. Hidden-Layer Index.
    • Panel (b): Relative RMS Gradient vs. Hidden-Layer Index.
  • Used logarithmic y-axes to display gradients spanning multiple orders of magnitude.
  • Saved the figure in both PNG and PDF formats under results/stage_a/.

Results — First Hidden-Layer Gradients (Epoch 1, Mean ± Std Across 3 Seeds):

Model Absolute RMS Gradient Relative RMS Gradient
D2 6.259e-04 ± 4.655e-05 4.070e-01 ± 4.482e-02
D5 8.823e-06 ± 7.251e-07 6.369e-03 ± 1.129e-03
D10 6.227e-09 ± 1.040e-09 4.837e-06 ± 6.791e-07
D20 3.664e-15 ± 5.195e-16 2.711e-12 ± 1.922e-13

Preliminary Observations:

  1. Strong depth-dependent gradient attenuation was observed. The mean RMS gradient of Hidden Layer 1 decreased from approximately 6.26e-04 in D2 to 3.66e-15 in D20, a difference of roughly 11 orders of magnitude.

  2. Panel (a) showed progressively smaller early-layer gradients in deeper networks. D5, D10, and D20 exhibited increasingly large differences between gradients in the first and last hidden layers.

  3. Panel (b) confirmed substantial relative gradient attenuation:

    • D2: The first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 40.7% of the last hidden-layer RMS gradient.
    • D5: Approximately 0.637%.
    • D10: Approximately 4.84e-04%.
    • D20: Approximately 2.71e-10%.

    For D20, the mean relative gradient at Hidden Layer 1 was approximately 2.71e-12, indicating extremely strong attenuation relative to Hidden Layer 20.

  4. The attenuation pattern was consistent across the three random seeds. The observed standard deviations were relatively small compared with the corresponding means, although three seeds are insufficient for strong statistical-significance claims.

  5. The logarithmic gradient profiles showed a systematic increase in gradient magnitude from early toward later hidden layers, especially for D10 and D20, consistent with progressive attenuation during backward gradient propagation.

Interpretation — H1 (Depth Effect):

The results provide strong empirical support for H1 under the fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

Increasing network depth was associated with substantially smaller early-layer RMS gradients, both in absolute magnitude and relative to the last hidden layer.

This behavior is consistent with the vanishing-gradient phenomenon in deep neural networks, where repeated multiplication by layer derivatives and weight matrices during backpropagation can strongly attenuate gradients before they reach earlier layers.

However, Figure 1 alone does not identify the separate contributions of activation saturation, initialization, or weight-matrix properties to the observed attenuation.

Connection to H2 (Early-Layer Trainability):

The gradient results align with the training-loss convergence patterns observed in Section 6.3:

  • D2 reached the training-loss threshold of 1.50 at epoch 2 for all three seeds.
  • D5 required 14–15 epochs.
  • D10 and D20 did not reach the threshold within 20 epochs.

With plain SGD and a fixed learning rate, smaller weight gradients correspond to smaller individual parameter-update magnitudes.

Therefore, the observed early-layer gradient attenuation provides a plausible mechanism contributing to the slower training-loss reduction in deeper networks.

However, Figure 1 measures gradients rather than cumulative parameter changes. The relationship between gradient attenuation and actual early-layer trainability must be evaluated directly using normalized first-layer weight changes in Section 6.7.

Limitations:

  • Figure 1 uses only epoch-1 gradient measurements; it does not show whether the attenuation pattern persists throughout training.
  • Epoch-1 gradients were measured during the first 10 training batches, when model parameters were already being updated.
  • Only hidden-layer weight gradients were analyzed; output-layer and bias gradients were excluded.
  • Relative RMS gradients quantify layer-wise attenuation but do not independently establish causality.
  • Mean ± standard deviation across three seeds describes variability but does not establish statistical significance.
  • The findings apply to the tested BloodMNIST MLP configurations and should not automatically be generalized to all neural network architectures.

Connection to Subsequent Sections:

  • Section 6.5: Examine how layer-wise gradient magnitudes evolve over the full 20 training epochs.
  • Section 6.6: Compare training-loss trajectories across depths.
  • Section 6.7: Evaluate cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes to investigate H2 directly.
  • Sections 6.8–6.9: Integrate gradient attenuation, trainability, convergence, and validation performance to evaluate H1/H2 and discuss limitations.

Figure 1 provides strong direct evidence of depth-dependent early-layer gradient attenuation under the controlled Stage A experimental conditions.

6.5 — Figure 2: Gradient Evolution During Training¶

Objective:

Visualize how layer-wise RMS weight gradients evolve throughout training in the deepest Stage A network (D20), and investigate whether the strong early-layer gradient attenuation observed in Figure 1 persists or changes across the 20 training epochs.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse the recorded gradient measurements:

    • Read stage_a_gradients_df from Section 6.3.
    • Select D20, the deepest MLP in Stage A and the network exhibiting the strongest early-layer gradient attenuation in Figure 1.
    • Include all 20 hidden layers, all 20 training epochs, and all three random seeds.
    • Each mean_grad_rms value represents the arithmetic mean of RMS weight gradients recorded during the first 10 training batches of a particular epoch.
    • Reuse the existing measurements without retraining the model or performing additional backpropagation.

  2. Aggregate the gradients across three random seeds:

    • Group records by hidden-layer index and epoch.
    • Calculate the arithmetic mean of mean_grad_rms across seeds 0, 1, and 2.
    • Preserve both layer and epoch identifiers to compare gradient magnitudes across network depth and training time.

  3. Prepare the layer × epoch heatmap:

    • Convert the aggregated measurements into a matrix:
      • Rows: Hidden Layers 1–20, ordered from the input toward the output.
      • Columns: Training Epochs 1–20.
      • Cell values: Mean RMS weight gradients across three seeds.
    • Apply a base-10 logarithmic transformation:

    $$ H_{l,e} = \log_{10}\left( \frac{1}{3} \sum_{s=0}^{2} G_{s,l,e} \right) $$

    where:

    • $l$: Hidden-layer index (1–20).

    • $e$: Training epoch (1–20).

    • $s$: Random seed (0, 1, 2).

    • $G_{s,l,e}$: Mean RMS weight gradient of hidden layer $l$ during the first 10 training batches of epoch $e$, for seed $s$.

    • $H_{l,e}$: Log10-transformed mean RMS gradient used for heatmap coloring.

    • Apply log10 after averaging the RMS gradients across seeds, rather than averaging their logarithms.

    • Preserve exact-zero gradients in the original data and display them as gray cells because log10(0) is undefined.

  4. Create and save Figure 2:

    • Plot one heatmap for D20.
    • X-axis: Training epoch (1–20).
    • Y-axis: Hidden-layer index (1 = closest to input; 20 = last hidden layer).
    • Cell color: Log10-transformed mean RMS gradient.
    • Use a single color scale across all layers and epochs.
    • Add a colorbar to identify the gradient magnitude represented by each color.
    • Save the figure in PNG and PDF formats under results/stage_a/.

  5. Inspect the gradient evolution:

    • Compare gradient magnitudes between early and late hidden layers at the same epoch.
    • Compare gradient magnitudes for the same hidden layer across different epochs.
    • Display the mean RMS gradients of Hidden Layers 1 and 20 at selected epochs (1, 10, and 20).

Purpose:

Determine whether gradient attenuation in the deepest MLP is persistent throughout training or changes as the model parameters are updated.

Figure 1 shows how gradients are distributed across hidden layers during early training. Figure 2 extends this analysis by examining the same phenomenon over the full training period.

The logarithmic transformation allows gradient magnitudes spanning several orders of magnitude to be visualized using a readable color scale.

Expected Results:

  • One heatmap showing gradient evolution in D20 across 20 hidden layers and 20 epochs.
  • A 20 × 20 matrix containing 400 aggregated gradient measurements.
  • A shared color scale representing log10(mean RMS weight gradient).
  • A compact numerical comparison of first-layer and last-hidden-layer gradients at epochs 1, 10, and 20.
  • Saved files:
    • figure2_gradient_evolution_d20.png
    • figure2_gradient_evolution_d20.pdf

Figure 2 will reveal whether early-layer gradients remain substantially smaller than later-layer gradients, increase during training, decrease further, or exhibit other patterns. No particular temporal pattern is assumed before inspecting the results.

Role in the Experiment:

Figure 2 provides additional evidence for:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Examine whether the early-layer gradient attenuation observed in the deepest model persists during training.

It also provides supporting context for:

  • H2 — Trainability Effect: Investigate whether persistently small gradients may be associated with limited early-layer parameter changes and slower training-loss reduction.

Figure 2 will be interpreted alongside:

  • Section 6.4: Figure 1 — Gradient Magnitude vs. Layer.
  • Section 6.6: Figure 3 — Training Loss Curves.
  • Section 6.7: Early-Layer Weight Change Analysis.
  • Sections 6.8–6.9: Integrated Stage A results and interpretation.

Interpretation Notes:

  • Each epoch-level measurement is based on the first 10 training batches, not every batch in the epoch.
  • The selected batches can differ across epochs because the training DataLoader shuffles the dataset.
  • The heatmap shows gradient magnitudes, not the direction of individual gradients or cumulative parameter updates.
  • Averaging across three seeds describes the overall pattern but does not display between-seed variability directly; Figure 1 provides complementary mean ± standard deviation comparisons.
  • The experiment does not use the BloodMNIST test split in this section.

6.5 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully generated Figure 2 using the recorded layer-wise RMS weight gradients from D20 across 20 training epochs and three random seeds.
  • Reused stage_a_gradients_df from Section 6.3 without retraining any models or recomputing gradients through backpropagation.
  • Selected 1,200 D20 gradient records (20 hidden layers × 20 epochs × 3 seeds).
  • Calculated the mean RMS weight gradient across three seeds for each hidden-layer/epoch combination.
  • Reshaped the aggregated results into a 20 × 20 matrix containing 400 mean gradient measurements.
  • Applied log10 to the mean RMS gradients for heatmap visualization.
  • Created one heatmap with:
    • X-axis: Training epoch (1–20).
    • Y-axis: Hidden-layer index (1 = closest to input; 20 = last hidden layer).
    • Color: log10(mean RMS weight gradient).
  • Saved Figure 2 in PNG and PDF formats under results/stage_a/.
  • Displayed the mean RMS gradients of Hidden Layers 1 and 20 at epochs 1, 10, and 20.

Results — D20 Gradient Evolution (Mean Across 3 Seeds):

Epoch Hidden Layer 1 RMS Hidden Layer 20 RMS
1 3.664e-15 1.362e-03
10 3.236e-15 9.118e-04
20 2.918e-15 8.794e-04

Preliminary Observations:

  1. Extremely small early-layer gradients persisted throughout training. Hidden Layer 1 maintained mean RMS gradients on the order of 1e-15 across the selected epochs.

  2. Later hidden layers maintained substantially larger gradients. Hidden Layer 20 exhibited mean RMS gradients on the order of 1e-3 to 1e-4 during the same training period.

  3. A strong gradient-magnitude difference was visible across network layers. The heatmap showed progressively larger gradients from the first hidden layer toward the last hidden layer, spanning approximately 11–12 orders of magnitude between Layers 1 and 20.

  4. The overall attenuation pattern remained persistent across 20 epochs. The horizontal color bands changed relatively little compared with the strong vertical gradient differences, indicating that early-layer gradients did not recover substantially during the observed training period.

  5. Gradient magnitudes did change over time. From epoch 1 to epoch 20, the mean RMS gradient decreased by approximately 20.4% in Hidden Layer 1 and 35.4% in Hidden Layer 20. These changes did not eliminate the large difference in gradient magnitude between the two layers.

Interpretation — H1 (Depth Effect):

Figure 2 provides evidence that the strong early-layer gradient attenuation observed in D20 persists throughout the 20-epoch training period.

Combined with Figure 1, which showed increasingly smaller early-layer gradients as network depth increased from D2 to D20, the results provide strong empirical support for H1 under the controlled Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

The observations are consistent with the vanishing-gradient phenomenon, in which gradients can become severely attenuated as they propagate backward through many network layers.

Figure 2 extends Figure 1 by examining the temporal persistence of gradient attenuation rather than comparing different network depths at a single epoch.

Connection to H2 (Early-Layer Trainability):

The persistent first-layer RMS gradients near 1e-15 suggest that SGD updates to early-layer weights may be extremely small under the fixed learning rate of 0.1.

This observation is consistent with the training-loss results from Section 6.3, where D20 did not reach the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50 within 20 epochs for any of the three seeds.

However, small gradients alone do not establish the total amount of parameter change or prove causality.

Section 6.7 will directly evaluate cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes to investigate whether the observed gradient attenuation corresponds to reduced early-layer trainability.

Limitations:

  • Figure 2 visualizes only D20; the effect of increasing depth is established primarily through the cross-depth comparison in Figure 1.
  • Each epoch-level value is calculated from the first 10 training batches, rather than all batches in the epoch.
  • Gradients are measured while training is in progress, not necessarily at the end of each epoch.
  • The heatmap averages measurements across three seeds and does not display seed-level standard deviations.
  • The heatmap represents RMS weight-gradient magnitudes, not gradient directions or cumulative weight changes.
  • The findings do not independently establish that vanishing gradients are the sole cause of poor optimization or classification performance.

Connection to Subsequent Sections:

  • Section 6.6: Compare training-loss trajectories across D2, D5, D10, and D20.
  • Section 6.7: Examine cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes to evaluate H2 directly.
  • Sections 6.8–6.9: Integrate gradient attenuation, training behavior, weight changes, and validation performance to assess H1/H2 and discuss limitations.

Figure 2 shows persistent and severe early-layer gradient attenuation in D20 throughout the observed training period.

6.6 — Figure 3: Training Loss Curves¶

Objective:

Visualize and compare the training-loss trajectories of D2, D5, D10, and D20 across 20 epochs to investigate whether increasing network depth is associated with slower training-loss reduction, prolonged plateaus, or greater optimization difficulty.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse the recorded training histories:

    • Read stage_a_history_df from Section 6.3, containing 240 training/validation history records (4 depths × 3 seeds × 20 epochs).
    • Select the recorded train_loss values for D2, D5, D10, and D20.
    • Each train_loss value represents the sample-weighted mean CrossEntropyLoss over all training batches processed during that epoch.
    • Keep the depth, seed, and epoch identifiers to preserve independent experimental runs.
    • Reuse the existing results without loading the dataset or retraining models.

  2. Calculate training-loss statistics across three seeds:

    • Group training losses by network depth and epoch.
    • Calculate the arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) across seeds 0, 1, and 2.
    • For each depth $d$ and epoch $e$:

    $$ \overline{L}_{d,e} = \frac{1}{3}\sum_{s=0}^{2}L_{d,s,e} $$

    $$ SD_{d,e} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{s=0}^{2}(L_{d,s,e}-\overline{L}_{d,e})^2}{3-1}} $$

    where:

    • $d$: Network depth (2, 5, 10, or 20 hidden layers).
    • $e$: Training epoch (1–20).
    • $s$: Random seed (0, 1, or 2).
    • $L_{d,s,e}$: Mean training loss for one independent run at epoch $e$.
    • $\overline{L}_{d,e}$: Mean training loss across the three seeds.
    • $SD_{d,e}$: Sample standard deviation across seeds.

  3. Create Figure 3 — Training Loss vs. Epoch:

    • Plot one curve per network depth.
    • X-axis: Training epoch (1–20).
    • Y-axis: Mean training CrossEntropyLoss.
    • Use the same depth colors as Figure 1 for consistency.
    • Add shaded bands representing mean ± 1 standard deviation across seeds.
    • Use a linear y-axis because CrossEntropyLoss is nonnegative and the observed values do not require a logarithmic scale.
    • Add a horizontal dashed line at the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.

  4. Review training-loss convergence behavior:

    • Compare the initial and final training losses of the four depths.
    • Examine the rate of loss reduction and identify any apparent plateaus.
    • Reuse stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 to report the number of seeds reaching the threshold and the mean ± standard deviation of epochs-to-threshold.
    • Keep threshold-attainment calculations at the individual-run level. Crossing the threshold on an averaged loss curve is not equivalent to averaging the first threshold-reaching epochs of individual runs.

  5. Save Figure 3:

    • Save the training-loss figure under results/stage_a/.
    • Export both PNG and PDF versions for subsequent analysis, presentation, and the technical report.

Purpose:

Assess whether networks with stronger early-layer gradient attenuation also exhibit slower reductions in training loss under the same controlled training conditions.

Training-loss trajectories provide an observable measure of optimization behavior. When examined alongside layer-wise gradients and normalized weight changes, they help investigate whether gradient attenuation is associated with reduced early-layer trainability.

Expected Results:

  • One Figure 3 containing four training-loss curves (D2, D5, D10, D20).
  • Each curve represents mean training loss across three seeds, with a mean ± standard deviation band.
  • A horizontal reference line indicating the fixed training-loss threshold of 1.50.
  • A compact summary of final training losses and epochs-to-threshold statistics.
  • Saved files:
    • figure3_training_loss_curves.png
    • figure3_training_loss_curves.pdf

The figure will show whether training-loss reduction differs across depths and whether deeper models exhibit slower learning or extended plateaus. No additional training is performed.

Role in the Experiment:

Figure 3 provides the main training-loss evidence for:

  • H2 — Trainability Effect: Whether conditions exhibiting stronger early-layer gradient attenuation are also associated with slower training-loss reduction and reduced optimization progress.

The figure complements:

  • Section 6.4 — Figure 1: Layer-wise gradient attenuation across network depths.
  • Section 6.5 — Figure 2: Persistence of gradient attenuation throughout training.
  • Section 6.7: Cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes.
  • Sections 6.8–6.9: Validation performance, convergence analysis, and integrated interpretation of H1/H2.

Interpretation Notes:

  • Training loss is measured during each epoch while model parameters are being updated; it is not a separate evaluation of the final epoch-end model.
  • The predefined threshold of 1.50 is a comparative training-loss milestone, not a stopping rule or proof of complete convergence.
  • A flat training-loss curve may indicate limited optimization progress, but it does not independently establish the underlying cause.
  • Mean ± standard deviation across three seeds describes observed variability, not statistical significance.
  • The relationship between gradient attenuation and slow training remains associative until examined alongside the weight-change measurements in Section 6.7.
  • The BloodMNIST test split remains untouched.

6.6 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully generated Figure 3 using the training-loss histories from all 12 completed Stage A runs (4 depths × 3 random seeds).
  • Reused stage_a_history_df and stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 without retraining models or recalculating losses through forward propagation.
  • Organized the training losses by network depth and epoch, producing 80 depth–epoch summary records (4 depths × 20 epochs).
  • Calculated mean and sample standard deviation of training loss across three random seeds for each depth and epoch.
  • Created one figure containing:
    • Four mean training-loss curves for D2, D5, D10, and D20.
    • Shaded regions representing mean ± 1 standard deviation across seeds.
    • A horizontal dashed line at the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.
  • Reused the per-run epochs-to-threshold statistics calculated in Section 6.3.
  • Saved Figure 3 as PNG and PDF files under results/stage_a/.

Results — Final Training Loss & Convergence (3 Seeds):

Model Final Training Loss (Mean ± Std) Seeds Reaching Threshold Epochs-to-Threshold (Mean ± Std)
D2 0.3963 ± 0.0065 3/3 2.00 ± 0.00
D5 1.2553 ± 0.0086 3/3 14.67 ± 0.58
D10 2.0114 ± 0.0013 0/3 Not reached
D20 2.0117 ± 0.0014 0/3 Not reached

Note: "Not reached" indicates that the predefined mean training-loss threshold of 1.50 was not reached within the 20-epoch training budget. It does not imply that the model could never improve with additional training or different experimental conditions.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. D2 exhibited rapid and sustained training-loss reduction. Its mean training loss decreased substantially throughout training, reaching approximately 0.3963 at epoch 20. All three seeds reached the threshold of 1.50 at epoch 2.

  2. D5 showed delayed training-loss reduction. The mean loss remained near its initial high level during approximately the first 9–10 epochs, followed by a more pronounced decline. All three seeds reached the threshold at epochs 14–15, requiring an average of 14.67 epochs compared with 2.00 epochs for D2.

  3. D10 exhibited a persistent high-loss plateau. Its training-loss curve remained nearly flat around 2.01, with a final mean training loss of 2.0114. None of its three runs reached the predefined threshold within 20 epochs.

  4. D20 showed similarly limited optimization progress. Its curve nearly overlapped with D10 and ended at a mean training loss of 2.0117. None of its three runs reached the threshold.

  5. The observed convergence patterns were relatively consistent across seeds. Final training-loss standard deviations were small within each depth. D5 showed some variation in its transition toward faster loss reduction, but all three runs eventually crossed the threshold.

Interpretation — H2 (Early-Layer Trainability):

Figure 3 provides evidence of increasingly difficult training-loss reduction as network depth increases under the fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

The loss trajectories complement the gradient measurements from earlier sections:

  • Figure 1 showed progressively smaller first-layer RMS gradients from D2 to D20.
  • Figure 2 showed persistent early-layer gradient attenuation in D20 throughout training.
  • Figure 3 showed progressively slower or nearly absent training-loss reduction as depth increased.

Together, these findings indicate a strong association between early-layer gradient attenuation and reduced optimization progress.

D5 required approximately 7.3 times as many epochs as D2 to reach the same predefined loss threshold. D10 and D20 did not reach the threshold within the 20-epoch budget.

The results support the convergence-related component of H2. However, the first-layer parameter-change component remains to be evaluated directly in Section 6.7.

Connection to H1 (Depth Effect):

Figure 3 does not directly measure gradient propagation. Instead, it provides optimization-context evidence for the depth-dependent gradient attenuation observed in Figures 1 and 2.

The strong differences in training-loss trajectories are consistent with the hypothesis that severe early-layer gradient attenuation may contribute to optimization difficulties in deeper MLPs.

However, these observations establish association rather than a unique causal explanation.

Limitations:

  • Training loss is measured during each epoch while model parameters are being updated, rather than from a separate epoch-end training evaluation.
  • The training-loss threshold of 1.50 is a predefined comparative milestone, not a stopping rule or a proof of complete convergence.
  • A high-loss plateau indicates limited observed optimization progress but does not independently establish its underlying cause.
  • Mean curves and standard-deviation bands describe three-seed variability; they do not provide statistical-significance tests.
  • Epochs-to-threshold is calculated separately for each run. Crossing the threshold on an aggregated mean curve is not equivalent to averaging the individual first-reaching epochs.
  • The findings apply to the tested MLP architectures and fixed training conditions; they should not be generalized automatically to all deeper neural networks.

Connection to Subsequent Sections:

  • Section 6.7: Evaluate cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes to investigate whether smaller gradients correspond to smaller parameter changes.
  • Section 6.8: Examine validation loss, validation accuracy, macro-F1, and convergence behavior across network depths.
  • Section 6.9: Integrate gradient attenuation, parameter changes, loss trajectories, and classification performance to evaluate H1 and H2 and discuss experimental limitations.

Figure 3 demonstrates substantial depth-dependent differences in training-loss reduction and provides strong supporting evidence for the convergence-related component of H2.

6.7 — Early-Layer Weight Change Analysis¶

Objective:

Compare cumulative normalized weight changes in the first hidden layer of D2, D5, D10, and D20 to investigate whether stronger early-layer gradient attenuation is associated with smaller parameter changes during training.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse the recorded first-layer weight changes:

    • Read stage_a_weights_df from Section 6.3, containing 240 records (4 depths × 3 seeds × 20 epochs).
    • Each record was calculated by GradientRecorder in Part 4, after all optimizer updates for the corresponding epoch.
    • Reuse stage_a_summary_df, which already contains the final first-layer weight-change mean and standard deviation across three seeds.
    • No models are created or retrained, and no new gradients or weight changes are computed from model parameters.

  2. Use the normalized cumulative first-layer weight-change metric:

    $$ \boxed{ C_{1,e} = \frac{\left\|W_1^{(e)}-W_1^{(0)}\right\|_F} {\left\|W_1^{(0)}\right\|_F} } $$

    where:

    • $W_1^{(0)}$: Weight matrix of Hidden Layer 1 immediately after initialization.
    • $W_1^{(e)}$: Weight matrix of Hidden Layer 1 after epoch $e$.
    • $\|\cdot\|_F$: Frobenius norm, equivalent to the L2 norm of the flattened weight matrix.
    • $C_{1,e}$: Normalized cumulative first-layer weight change after epoch $e$.

    This dimensionless metric measures how far the first-layer weights have moved from their initial values.

    It is not the individual SGD update of one batch, the change between consecutive epochs, or the sum of the magnitudes of all SGD updates.

  3. Examine weight changes throughout training:

    • Group stage_a_weights_df by network depth and epoch.
    • Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation across seeds 0, 1, and 2.
    • Examine the first-layer weight changes after epochs 1, 10, and 20.
    • Use the same 20-epoch training budget for all four depths.

  4. Compare final first-layer weight changes across network depths:

    • Reuse stage_a_summary_df to obtain the mean ± standard deviation of normalized first-layer weight change at epoch 20.
    • Include the epoch-1 first-layer RMS gradients from Figure 1 for comparison.
    • Compare whether networks with smaller early-layer RMS gradients also exhibit smaller cumulative first-layer weight changes.
    • Use scientific notation to preserve very small measurements.

  5. Interpret the results in relation to H2:

    • Identify whether D2, D5, D10, and D20 exhibit systematically different first-layer weight changes.
    • Compare the weight-change patterns with the gradient attenuation observed in Figures 1–2.
    • Connect these measurements to the training-loss convergence behavior observed in Figure 3.
    • Record any exact-zero weight changes without replacing them with artificial positive values.

Purpose:

Directly investigate the early-layer parameter-change component of H2.

Figures 1–2 measured gradient attenuation, while Figure 3 showed differences in training-loss reduction. Section 6.7 examines whether the early-layer weights actually moved less in models exhibiting stronger gradient attenuation.

Using normalized weight changes allows the parameter displacement to be interpreted relative to the magnitude of the initial weight matrix.

Expected Results:

  • One summary table comparing D2, D5, D10, and D20, containing:
    • First-layer RMS gradient at epoch 1 (mean ± std).
    • Final normalized first-layer weight change at epoch 20 (mean ± std).
    • Number of seeds reaching the predefined training-loss threshold.
  • One compact table of mean ± standard deviation of first-layer weight changes after epochs 1, 10, and 20.
  • Numerical evidence to assess whether stronger early-layer gradient attenuation is associated with smaller cumulative first-layer weight changes.
  • No additional figure, model training, or gradient recording.

The actual weight-change values will determine whether the observations support H2; no particular result is assumed in advance.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 6.7 provides direct parameter-change evidence for:

  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: Whether conditions exhibiting stronger early-layer gradient attenuation are associated with smaller normalized first-layer weight changes and slower training-loss reduction.

It connects three complementary measurements:

  • Figures 1–2: Layer-wise RMS gradients and gradient attenuation.
  • Section 6.7: Actual cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes.
  • Figure 3: Training-loss trajectories and epochs-to-threshold.

Interpretation Notes:

  • Smaller RMS gradients imply smaller individual plain-SGD update magnitudes under the same learning rate, but cumulative weight changes depend on the directions and accumulation of updates.
  • An exact-zero recorded weight change indicates that the stored first-layer weight matrix matches its initial matrix at the measurement precision. Extremely small updates may be lost because of floating-point rounding.
  • The weight-change metric measures displacement from initialization, not overall classification performance or complete network trainability.
  • The epoch-1 gradient measurement and epoch-20 cumulative weight change cover different time windows; their comparison is descriptive rather than a direct mathematical equality.
  • This analysis investigates association, not proof that gradient vanishing is the sole cause of optimization difficulties.
  • No additional training or test-set evaluation is performed.

Connection to Subsequent Sections:

  • Section 6.8: Compare validation loss, accuracy, macro-F1, and convergence behavior across network depths.
  • Section 6.9: Integrate gradient attenuation, first-layer weight changes, training-loss reduction, and validation performance to evaluate H1 and H2.

The complete Stage A measurements will also help inform the selection of a deep network for the Stage B activation-function comparison.

6.7 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully analyzed cumulative normalized first-hidden-layer weight changes from all 12 completed Stage A runs (4 depths × 3 random seeds).

  • Reused stage_a_weights_df and stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 without retraining models or recomputing gradients.

  • Used the normalized cumulative weight-change metric:

    $$ C_{1,e} = \frac{\|W_1^{(e)}-W_1^{(0)}\|_F} {\|W_1^{(0)}\|_F} $$

  • Aggregated weight-change measurements by network depth and epoch, calculating mean and sample standard deviation across three seeds.

  • Examined weight displacement from initialization after epochs 1, 10, and 20.

  • Compared final first-layer weight changes at epoch 20 with first-layer RMS gradients measured during epoch 1.

  • Verified consistency between the final weight-change records and previously calculated Stage A summary statistics.

  • Checked for exact-zero recorded first-layer weight changes.

  • No additional figure or training run was required.

Results — Cumulative Normalized First-Layer Weight Change (Mean Across 3 Seeds):

D5 2.318e-03 4.004e-02 1.090e-01
D10 1.519e-06 1.458e-05 2.740e-05
D20 0.000e+00 0.000e+00 0.000e+00

Results — Early-Layer Gradient vs. Final Weight Change (Mean ± Std Across 3 Seeds):

D2 6.259e-04 ± 4.655e-05 3.279e-01 ± 2.546e-03 3/3
D5 8.823e-06 ± 7.251e-07 1.090e-01 ± 4.262e-03 3/3

D20 3.664e-15 ± 5.195e-16 0.000e+00 ± 0.000e+00 0/3

Preliminary Observations:

  1. D2 exhibited substantial cumulative first-layer weight displacement. Its mean normalized weight change increased from 0.07854 after epoch 1 to 0.3279 after epoch 20.

  2. D5 showed smaller and more gradual first-layer weight displacement. Its normalized weight change increased from 0.002318 at epoch 1 to 0.1090 at epoch 20, remaining below D2 throughout the selected checkpoints.

  3. D10 exhibited extremely limited first-layer weight displacement. Its final normalized change was only 2.740e-05, approximately 12,000 times smaller than D2.

  4. D20 recorded zero cumulative first-layer weight displacement across all three seeds at epoch 20. The displayed checkpoints at epochs 1 and 10 were also zero. This does not imply that its mathematical gradients were zero.

  5. The results showed a consistent depth-dependent relationship: Networks with smaller early-layer RMS gradients also exhibited smaller cumulative first-layer weight changes under the fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD training configuration.

  6. The parameter-change results were consistent with the observed convergence behavior. D2 and D5 reached the predefined training-loss threshold in all three seeds, whereas D10 and D20 did not reach it within 20 epochs.

Interpretation — H2 (Early-Layer Trainability):

The results provide strong empirical support for the parameter-change component of H2.

As network depth increased, early-layer RMS gradients decreased by multiple orders of magnitude, while cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement also became substantially smaller.

Under plain SGD with a fixed learning rate, smaller gradients produce smaller individual parameter-update magnitudes. The recorded cumulative weight changes indicate that this gradient attenuation was associated with greatly reduced displacement of early-layer weights from their initialized values.

Combined with Figure 3, the findings support both components of H2:

  • Parameter-change effect: Stronger early-layer gradient attenuation was associated with smaller normalized first-layer weight changes.
  • Convergence effect: Networks exhibiting stronger attenuation and smaller weight changes also showed slower training-loss reduction or persistent high-loss plateaus.

The findings support an association between gradient attenuation and reduced early-layer trainability, but do not establish gradient vanishing as the sole causal mechanism.

Interpretation — H1 (Depth Effect):

Figures 1 and 2 provided direct evidence of depth-dependent gradient attenuation.

Section 6.7 complements those measurements by showing that deeper networks with extremely small first-layer gradients also exhibited much smaller changes in first-layer weights.

The combined evidence is consistent with vanishing gradients limiting the effective optimization of earlier layers in deep Sigmoid MLPs under the tested configuration.

Numerical Precision Considerations:

D20 recorded an exact-zero final normalized first-layer weight change in all three runs, despite having nonzero measured weight gradients.

One plausible explanation is floating-point rounding. With plain SGD (learning rate = 0.1), the mean RMS first-layer gradient of approximately 3.664e-15 during epoch 1 corresponds to a mean RMS update magnitude of approximately 3.664e-16 for the sampled steps.

Such updates may be too small to change many stored float32 weight values at their current magnitudes.

However, the recorded zero displacement alone does not establish that floating-point rounding was the only cause, nor does it prove that every individual SGD update was exactly zero.

Limitations:

  • The normalized weight-change metric measures cumulative displacement from initialization, not the sum of individual SGD update magnitudes.
  • It measures only Hidden Layer 1 and does not describe parameter changes throughout the entire network.
  • The gradient comparison uses epoch-1 measurements, whereas final cumulative weight changes are measured after 20 epochs. These quantities are related but are not mathematically equivalent.
  • Exact-zero recorded displacement may reflect finite numerical precision; additional numerical diagnostics would be required to establish its cause.
  • Three random seeds provide limited information about variability and do not establish statistical significance.
  • The observed relationships are associative and do not isolate all possible optimization mechanisms.

Connection to Subsequent Sections:

  • Section 6.8: Compare validation loss, validation accuracy, macro-F1, and convergence behavior across network depths.
  • Section 6.9: Integrate Figures 1–3, normalized first-layer weight changes, and validation performance to evaluate H1/H2 and discuss the main findings and limitations.
  • Part 7: Use the Stage A findings to select a suitable network depth for the controlled Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU comparison.

In 6.7, the results provide strong evidence that depth-dependent early-layer gradient attenuation is associated with greatly reduced first-layer weight displacement and slower optimization under the controlled Stage A experimental conditions.

6.8 — Validation Performance & Convergence¶

Objective:

Compare the final validation performance and training-loss convergence behavior of D2, D5, D10, and D20 under the same controlled Stage A experimental conditions.

Prepare one consolidated results table reporting training loss, validation loss, validation accuracy, validation macro-F1, and epochs-to-threshold across three random seeds.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse the recorded training and validation results:

    • Read stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3, which contains the aggregated results of all 12 Stage A runs (4 depths × 3 seeds).
    • Reuse the training and validation metrics recorded by run_training() during Sections 6.1–6.2.
    • Each model was trained for 20 full epochs using the same BloodMNIST training/validation splits, hidden width (256), Sigmoid activation, Xavier Uniform initialization, CrossEntropyLoss, SGD optimizer, learning rate (0.1), and batch size (128).
    • No models are retrained, and no new validation inference is performed.

  2. Compare final training and validation metrics:

    • Final training loss: Mean CrossEntropyLoss recorded during epoch 20.
    • Final validation loss: CrossEntropyLoss calculated over the complete validation split after epoch 20.
    • Final validation accuracy: Fraction of correctly classified validation images.
    • Final validation macro-F1: Unweighted mean of the eight class-specific F1 scores.
    • Report mean and sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) across three independent seeds for each depth.

  3. Compare training-loss convergence:

    • Reuse the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50, finalized in Part 5.
    • Report the number of seeds reaching the threshold within the 20-epoch training budget.
    • Report mean ± sample standard deviation of epochs-to-threshold among runs that reached it.
    • Display "Not reached" when none of the three runs reaches the threshold.
    • Do not replace unsuccessful runs with artificial epoch values or interpret threshold attainment as proof of full convergence.

  4. Create the Stage A Summary Results Table:

    • Present one row per network depth (D2, D5, D10, D20).
    • Display final training loss, validation loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1 as mean ± standard deviation.
    • Include epochs-to-threshold and threshold-attainment counts.
    • Use consistent formatting across the four models.
    • Preserve the original numeric results in stage_a_summary_df; create a separate formatted table for reporting.

  5. Save and review the results:

    • Save the consolidated results table as a CSV file under results/stage_a/.
    • Examine how validation performance changes with network depth.
    • Compare validation performance with the training-loss convergence patterns identified in Figure 3.
    • Relate these observations to the gradient attenuation and first-layer weight-change measurements from Sections 6.4–6.7.

Purpose:

Determine whether the optimization difficulties observed in deeper MLPs are accompanied by weaker classification performance on unseen validation images.

Training loss describes optimization progress on the training data, whereas validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1 describe performance on the held-out validation split.

Examining these measurements together provides a broader assessment of trainability and classification behavior than any single metric alone.

One Stage A Summary Results Table containing:

Epochs to Threshold Mean ± std of first-reaching epochs, or "Not reached"

The table will summarize performance and convergence across all four depths and three seeds.

Saved file:

  • stage_a_results_table.csv

No additional model training, validation evaluation, gradient recording, or figure generation is required.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 6.8 provides classification-performance and convergence evidence relevant to:

  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: Whether networks with stronger gradient attenuation and smaller first-layer weight changes also exhibit slower training-loss reduction and weaker validation performance.

The results complement:

  • Section 6.4 — Figure 1: Gradient magnitude across hidden layers and network depths.
  • Section 6.5 — Figure 2: Gradient evolution during training.
  • Section 6.6 — Figure 3: Training-loss trajectories and epochs-to-threshold.
  • Section 6.7: Cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes.

Together, these measurements will support the integrated interpretation of H1 and H2 in Section 6.9.

Interpretation Notes:

  • Final metrics are reported after a fixed 20-epoch training budget, rather than selecting the best-performing epoch separately for each model.
  • Training loss is accumulated during the epoch while parameters are updated; validation loss is evaluated after the epoch using the resulting model parameters.
  • Validation accuracy can conceal poor performance on individual classes; macro-F1 provides a complementary class-balanced evaluation.
  • Low validation performance does not independently establish vanishing gradients as the cause.
  • A small training–validation loss difference does not necessarily indicate good generalization, particularly when both losses remain high.
  • Epochs-to-threshold measures attainment of a predefined loss milestone, not complete mathematical convergence.
  • Results from three seeds describe run-to-run variability but do not establish statistical significance.
  • The BloodMNIST test split remains untouched.

    depth = int(row["depth"])                            # Number of hidden layers in the current model

    n_reached = int(row["seeds_reached_threshold"])      # Runs reaching mean training loss <= 1.50

    else:

        )

    results_rows.append({

        "Epochs to Threshold": threshold_text,           # First epoch reaching loss <= 1.50, summarized across seeds
        "Seeds Reached": f"{n_reached}/{n_seeds}"        # Preserve threshold-attainment information for every depth
    })

Note: All values are reported after the fixed 20-epoch training budget. "Not reached" means the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50 was not achieved within 20 epochs; it does not imply that the model could never improve under different conditions.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. D2 achieved the strongest training and validation performance. Its final mean training loss was 0.3963, validation loss was 0.5104, validation accuracy was 81.23%, and validation macro-F1 was 0.7851. All three seeds reached the training-loss threshold at epoch 2.

  2. D5 showed substantially weaker performance and slower training-loss reduction. Its mean validation accuracy was 46.63% and macro-F1 was 0.3377. Although all three seeds eventually reached the loss threshold, they required 14–15 epochs.

  3. D10 exhibited limited optimization progress and low validation performance. Its final mean training loss remained around 2.0114, validation accuracy was 18.20%, and macro-F1 was 0.0385. None of its three seeds reached the loss threshold within 20 epochs.

  4. D20 showed similarly limited optimization progress. Its final mean training loss was 2.0117, validation accuracy was 18.20%, and macro-F1 was 0.0385. None of its three seeds reached the threshold.

  5. D10 and D20 produced identical reported mean validation accuracy and macro-F1 values, including their standard deviations to four decimal places. This suggests similarly limited classification behavior, but their predicted-class distributions were not examined in this section.

  6. The depth-dependent performance differences were consistent across three seeds. D2 consistently outperformed D5, while D10 and D20 remained at substantially lower performance levels under the same experimental protocol.

Interpretation — Validation Performance & Convergence:

The results demonstrate substantial depth-dependent differences in both training-loss reduction and classification performance under the fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

D2 showed the strongest optimization progress and validation performance, while D5 learned more slowly and achieved weaker classification results. D10 and D20 exhibited persistent high-loss behavior and very low validation accuracy and macro-F1.

The small differences between training and validation losses for D10 and D20 should not be interpreted as evidence of strong generalization, because both training and validation performance remained poor.

Connection to H1 — Depth Effect:

Section 6.8 does not directly measure gradient propagation.

However, the deterioration in optimization and validation performance with increasing depth is consistent with the strong early-layer gradient attenuation documented in Figures 1 and 2.

The direct evidence for H1 remains the measured layer-wise RMS gradients.

Interpretation — H2 (Early-Layer Trainability):

The validation and convergence results complement the gradient and parameter-change measurements:

  • Gradient attenuation (Figures 1–2): Early-layer RMS gradients became substantially smaller as network depth increased.
  • Parameter changes (Section 6.7): Normalized first-layer weight displacement decreased markedly, reaching recorded zero displacement for D20 across all three seeds.
  • Training convergence (Figure 3): D2 reached the predefined training-loss threshold rapidly, D5 required considerably more epochs, and D10/D20 did not reach it within 20 epochs.
  • Validation performance (Section 6.8): Models exhibiting stronger attenuation and smaller early-layer weight changes also achieved weaker validation accuracy and macro-F1.

Together, these observations provide strong empirical support for the association between early-layer gradient attenuation, reduced parameter displacement, and slower optimization predicted by H2.

The poorer validation performance of deeper networks is consistent with these optimization difficulties, although the results do not establish gradient vanishing as their sole causal explanation.

Limitations:

  • The results describe the fixed 20-epoch training budget; different training durations could produce different outcomes.
  • The findings apply to the tested Sigmoid MLPs with Xavier initialization and plain SGD, not all deep neural networks.
  • Training loss and validation loss are measured at different points within an epoch: training loss is accumulated during parameter updates, while validation loss is evaluated after the epoch.
  • Low training–validation loss gaps do not necessarily indicate good generalization when both losses remain high.
  • Validation accuracy may obscure class-specific failures; macro-F1 provides complementary information but does not replace prediction-level diagnostics.
  • The predicted-class distributions of D10 and D20 were not examined.
  • The predefined loss threshold measures attainment of a comparative milestone, not complete convergence.
  • Three random seeds provide limited information about variability and do not establish statistical significance.
  • The observed associations do not isolate gradient vanishing as the only mechanism responsible for reduced optimization performance.

Connection to the Next Section:

Section 6.9 will integrate:

  • Figure 1 — Gradient Magnitude vs. Layer.
  • Figure 2 — Gradient Evolution During Training.
  • Figure 3 — Training Loss Curves.
  • Section 6.7 — Cumulative First-Layer Weight Changes.
  • Section 6.8 — Validation Performance & Convergence.

The combined evidence will be used to assess H1 and H2, identify limitations, and summarize the principal Stage A findings before the Stage B activation-function comparison.

In 6.8, the consolidated Stage A results table demonstrates substantial depth-dependent differences in validation performance and training-loss convergence under the controlled experimental conditions.

6.9 — Stage A Findings & Interpretation¶

Objective:

Integrate the gradient propagation, early-layer weight-change, training-loss convergence, and validation-performance results from Sections 6.4–6.8 to evaluate the two Stage A hypotheses:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Increasing network depth is expected to produce stronger gradient attenuation in hidden layers closer to the input, relative to later hidden layers.
  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: Conditions exhibiting stronger early-layer gradient attenuation are expected to show smaller normalized first-layer weight changes and slower training-loss convergence.

Summarize the principal Stage A findings under the controlled Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration without performing additional experiments.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse the completed Stage A results:

    • Use stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 for the aggregated results across D2, D5, D10, and D20.
    • Use fig1_summary from Section 6.4 for the first-to-last hidden-layer gradient RMS ratios.
    • Reference Figure 2 for the evolution of layer-wise gradients during training.
    • Reference Figure 3 for training-loss trajectories and the predefined convergence threshold.
    • Reference Sections 6.7–6.8 for normalized first-layer weight changes and validation performance.
    • Verify that all four depths and all three random seeds are represented.

  2. Evaluate H1 — Depth Effect:

    • Compare the epoch-1 RMS gradients of Hidden Layer 1 across network depths.
    • Compare the first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratios previously calculated for Figure 1.
    • Use the D20 gradient-evolution heatmap to determine whether severe early-layer gradient attenuation persisted during the 20-epoch training period.
    • Assess whether the observed gradient patterns are consistent with H1.

  3. Evaluate H2 — Early-Layer Trainability:

    • Compare the final cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes across depths.
    • Compare training-loss trajectories and final training losses.
    • Examine the number of seeds reaching the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.
    • Compare epochs-to-threshold among runs that reached it.
    • Assess whether stronger gradient attenuation is associated with smaller first-layer weight displacement and slower training-loss reduction.

  4. Review validation performance:

    • Compare final validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1 across the four depths.
    • Determine whether poorer optimization progress in deeper networks is accompanied by weaker validation classification performance.
    • Treat validation performance as complementary evidence rather than a direct measurement of gradient propagation.

  5. Summarize the Stage A conclusions and limitations:

    • Identify which experimental observations support H1 and H2.
    • Distinguish directly measured quantities from possible explanations.
    • Discuss finite numerical precision, especially the recorded zero first-layer weight changes in D20.
    • Acknowledge the limited model family, dataset, optimizer settings, training budget, and number of seeds.
    • Avoid interpreting associations as proof that vanishing gradients are the sole cause of optimization difficulties.

  6. Prepare the transition to Stage B:

    • Identify the trade-off between observing substantial gradient attenuation and retaining measurable learning progress.
    • Use the Stage A evidence to inform depth selection in Step 36.
    • Do not run the activation-function comparison or finalize the Stage B experimental results in this section.

Purpose:

Answer the primary research question:

How does increasing network depth affect layer-wise gradient propagation and the trainability of early layers in deep MLPs on BloodMNIST?

This section combines the complementary measurements collected throughout Stage A into one scientifically consistent interpretation.

Gradient RMS measurements describe backpropagated gradient magnitudes. Normalized first-layer weight changes describe cumulative parameter displacement from initialization. Training-loss trajectories and epochs-to-threshold describe optimization progress, while validation metrics describe classification performance on held-out images.

Expected Results:

  • A concise numerical summary of H1 and H2 evidence across D2, D5, D10, and D20.
  • A direct comparison of:
    • Epoch-1 first-layer RMS gradient.
    • Epoch-1 first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratio.
    • Final normalized first-layer weight change.
    • Final training loss.
    • Epochs-to-threshold and threshold-attainment counts.
    • Final validation accuracy and macro-F1.
  • A clear assessment of whether the observations support H1 and H2.
  • A discussion of experimental and numerical limitations.
  • Evidence to guide the selection of one deep network depth for the Stage B activation-function comparison.

No new figure, model training, validation inference, gradient recording, or additional statistical analysis is required.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 6.9 completes Stage A — Network Depth Experiment by integrating the evidence from:

  • Figure 1: Layer-wise gradient attenuation across network depths.
  • Figure 2: Gradient evolution across layers and epochs.
  • Figure 3: Training-loss trajectories and convergence behavior.
  • Section 6.7: Cumulative normalized first-hidden-layer weight changes.
  • Section 6.8: Final validation performance and convergence summary.

It provides the evidence-based assessment of H1 and H2 required by the project outline.

Interpretation Notes:

  • The first-to-last hidden-layer gradient ratio compares the RMS gradient of Hidden Layer 1 with that of the last hidden layer within each run. It is not a comparison between model parameters.
  • Epoch-level RMS gradients were calculated using the fixed gradient-sampling protocol established in Part 4.
  • Final normalized weight change measures displacement from initial weights, not the sum of individual SGD update magnitudes.
  • A recorded zero weight change does not imply that the corresponding mathematical gradients were zero.
  • The predefined loss threshold measures the first observed attainment of a training-loss milestone, not complete mathematical convergence.
  • Differences in validation accuracy and macro-F1 provide performance context but do not independently establish the cause of poor optimization.
  • Three seeds describe observed run-to-run variability but do not establish statistical significance.
  • The conclusions apply to the tested constant-width Sigmoid MLPs on BloodMNIST under the fixed Xavier initialization, plain SGD, and 20-epoch training budget.
  • H3, the activation-function hypothesis, has not yet been evaluated.

Connection to the Next Part:

  • Part 7, Step 36: Select one suitable deep network depth based on the Stage A findings.
  • Part 7, Steps 37–42: Hold depth and other controlled settings fixed while comparing Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU under the common Xavier initialization protocol.

Stage B will investigate whether changing the activation function alters gradient attenuation, convergence behavior, and classification performance at the selected depth.
