6.9 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation Summary:

  • Successfully consolidated the completed Stage A evidence from Sections 6.4–6.8 without additional model training, gradient computation, or validation inference.
  • Verified the availability of results from all four network depths (D2, D5, D10, D20), each evaluated across three independent random seeds.
  • Reused stage_a_summary_df for gradient magnitudes, cumulative first-layer weight changes, final losses, validation metrics, and threshold-attainment statistics.
  • Reused fig1_summary for the first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratios.
  • Integrated the observations from Figures 1–3 and Sections 6.7–6.8 to assess H1 and H2.

Results — Consolidated Stage A Evidence:

All models were trained for 20 epochs under the same controlled configuration: Sigmoid activation, Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD with learning rate 0.1, hidden width 256, and the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.

Measurement D2 D5 D10 D20
First-layer RMS gradient (Epoch 1) 6.259e-04 8.823e-06 6.227e-09 3.664e-15
First-to-last hidden-layer RMS ratio (Epoch 1) 4.070e-01 6.369e-03 4.837e-06 2.711e-12
Final normalized first-layer weight change 3.279e-01 1.090e-01 2.740e-05 0.000e+00
Final training loss 0.3963 1.2553 2.0114 2.0117
Epochs to threshold 2.00 ± 0.00 14.67 ± 0.58 Not reached Not reached
Seeds reaching threshold 3/3 3/3 0/3 0/3
Validation accuracy 0.8123 0.4663 0.1820 0.1820
Validation macro-F1 0.7851 0.3377 0.0385 0.0385

Values are means across three random seeds unless otherwise indicated. Standard deviations for the other metrics are reported in Sections 6.3–6.8. Epoch-1 gradient statistics were computed using the fixed sampling protocol of the first 10 training batches.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. Early-layer gradient magnitudes decreased sharply with increasing network depth. The mean first-layer RMS gradient decreased from 6.259e-04 in D2 to 3.664e-15 in D20, a difference of approximately 11 orders of magnitude.

  2. The relative gradient attenuation within each network became substantially stronger with depth. The first-to-last hidden-layer RMS ratio decreased from 4.070e-01 in D2 to 2.711e-12 in D20. These ratios compare early and late hidden layers within the same run, rather than gradients across different models.

  3. Severe early-layer attenuation persisted during training in D20. Figure 2 showed first-layer RMS gradients near 1e-15 throughout the sampled epochs, while last-hidden-layer RMS gradients remained approximately between 1e-3 and 1e-4. The gap persisted through epoch 20 under the recorded gradient-sampling protocol.

  4. First-layer parameter displacement decreased markedly with depth. Final cumulative normalized first-layer weight change decreased from 0.3279 in D2 to 0.1090 in D5 and 2.740e-05 in D10. D20 recorded an exact-zero final displacement across all three seeds.

  5. Training-loss reduction became substantially slower with depth. D2 reached the predefined loss threshold at epoch 2 in all three runs, whereas D5 required 14–15 epochs. Neither D10 nor D20 reached the threshold within the 20-epoch training budget.

  6. D10 and D20 exhibited persistent high-loss behavior. Their final mean training losses remained near 2.01, consistent with the nearly flat training-loss trajectories observed in Figure 3.

  7. Validation performance deteriorated substantially as depth increased. D2 achieved the highest mean validation accuracy (81.23%) and macro-F1 (0.7851), followed by D5 (46.63% accuracy; 0.3377 macro-F1). D10 and D20 both achieved only 18.20% accuracy and 0.0385 macro-F1.

Interpretation — H1: Depth Effect

H1 is strongly supported by the observed gradient measurements under the tested experimental conditions.

Figure 1 demonstrated that increasing network depth was associated with progressively smaller RMS gradients in hidden layers closer to the input.

The first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratios provide particularly direct evidence: the gradient magnitude near the input became much smaller relative to that of the last hidden layer as depth increased.

Figure 2 further showed that the severe early-layer attenuation observed in D20 persisted during the 20-epoch experiment, rather than appearing only at the beginning of training.

These findings are consistent with the vanishing-gradient phenomenon in deep Sigmoid networks, where repeated multiplication of backward-propagated derivatives and weight transformations can substantially reduce gradient magnitudes in earlier layers.

The evidence supports H1 for the tested constant-width Sigmoid MLPs, but does not establish that the same depth-dependent behavior would necessarily occur with different activations, initializations, optimizers, or architectures.

Interpretation — H2: Early-Layer Trainability

H2 is strongly supported by the observed associations between gradient attenuation, cumulative first-layer weight displacement, and training-loss convergence.

The models exhibiting stronger early-layer gradient attenuation also exhibited smaller normalized first-layer weight changes.

Under plain SGD with a common learning rate, smaller gradients correspond to smaller individual parameter-update magnitudes. The cumulative weight-change measurements indicate that severe gradient attenuation was accompanied by substantially reduced displacement of early-layer weights from initialization.

The convergence results show a consistent pattern:

  • D2 exhibited relatively large early-layer gradients, substantial first-layer weight displacement, and rapid training-loss reduction.
  • D5 exhibited stronger attenuation and smaller early-layer weight displacement, together with slower but measurable learning progress.
  • D10 exhibited extremely small early-layer gradients and weight changes, together with persistent high training loss.
  • D20 exhibited the strongest attenuation, zero recorded first-layer weight displacement, and persistent high training loss.

These patterns support the hypothesis that stronger early-layer gradient attenuation is associated with reduced early-layer trainability and slower optimization.

The validation results provide complementary evidence: the models exhibiting greater optimization difficulty also achieved substantially weaker classification performance on held-out validation images.

However, these associations do not establish gradient vanishing as the sole causal mechanism responsible for the differences in convergence and validation performance.

Numerical Precision Considerations:

D20 recorded zero cumulative first-layer weight displacement across all three seeds after 20 epochs, despite having nonzero measured first-layer gradients.

Under the fixed plain-SGD learning rate of 0.1, the measured epoch-1 first-layer RMS gradient of approximately 3.664e-15 corresponds to a mean RMS update magnitude of approximately 3.664e-16 for the sampled steps.

At this scale, floating-point rounding may prevent extremely small updates from changing stored float32 parameter values.

This is a plausible explanation for the recorded zero displacement, but the experiment did not directly isolate or verify floating-point rounding as its cause.

A zero recorded weight displacement must not be interpreted as proof that all mathematical gradients or all parameter updates were zero.

Overall Stage A Conclusion:

The Stage A experiments revealed a consistent depth-dependent pattern under the controlled Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration:

Increasing depth → Stronger early-layer gradient attenuation → Smaller observed first-layer weight displacement, accompanied by slower training-loss reduction and weaker validation performance.

The arrows summarize the direction of the observed patterns and should not be interpreted as proof of a fully isolated causal chain.

Together, Figures 1–3, the normalized first-layer weight-change analysis, and the validation-performance results provide strong empirical support for H1 and H2 within the tested experimental conditions.

Experimental Limitations:

  • The experiment used a single dataset (BloodMNIST) and one model family (constant-width fully connected MLPs).
  • Stage A held the activation function (Sigmoid), weight initialization (Xavier Uniform), optimizer (plain SGD), learning rate (0.1), and training budget (20 epochs) fixed.
  • Results may differ under other activation functions, initialization methods, optimizers, learning rates, or longer training schedules.
  • Gradient statistics were recorded using the predefined sampling protocol rather than every training batch.
  • First-layer weight displacement measures cumulative distance from initialization, not the sum of individual SGD update magnitudes or all-layer parameter trainability.
  • The exact-zero first-layer weight changes in D20 may involve finite floating-point precision and were not further diagnosed.
  • The threshold of 1.50 is a predefined comparative training-loss milestone, not a universal criterion for complete convergence.
  • Three random seeds provide limited information about variability and do not establish statistical significance.
  • Validation performance was used as complementary evidence; the BloodMNIST test split was not evaluated in Stage A.
  • The experiment demonstrates associations consistent with gradient vanishing but does not isolate gradient attenuation as the only cause of poor optimization in deeper networks.

Implications for Stage B — Activation Function Experiment:

Stage A identified a trade-off between network depth and measurable learning progress.

D5 showed substantial gradient attenuation while retaining the ability to reduce training loss and reach the predefined threshold across all three seeds.

D10 and D20 provided stronger examples of gradient attenuation but exhibited severe optimization limitations under Sigmoid.

These findings motivate selecting an appropriate deep network depth for a controlled comparison of Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.

The final Stage B depth selection will be documented in Step 36, with depth, initialization protocol, optimizer settings, dataset splits, and training budget controlled across the activation-function comparisons.

Now, Stage A — Network Depth Experiment is completed. H1 and H2 are strongly supported by the observed measurements within the specified experimental conditions. The results provide the basis for the Stage B activation-function comparison.

Part 7 — Stage B: Activation Function Experiment¶

1. Overview & Research Objective¶

Stage B investigates how hidden-layer activation functions affect gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, and optimization behavior in MLPs trained on BloodMNIST.

Building on the depth-dependent findings from Stage A, this experiment compares Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU at a fixed depth of five hidden layers (D5) under a common Xavier Uniform initialization and SGD training protocol.

The experiment addresses H3 — Activation Effect, examining whether activation choice is associated with differences in:

  • Layer-wise RMS weight-gradient magnitudes and relative attenuation.
  • Normalized first-layer weight displacement.
  • Training-loss reduction and epochs-to-threshold.
  • Validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1.

Stage B evaluates activation-dependent behavior at a single fixed depth. It does not directly test activation-by-depth interactions or initialization sensitivity.

2. Experimental Design & Controls¶

Independent variable: Hidden-layer activation function — Sigmoid, Tanh, or ReLU.

Fixed network architecture: D5, with five hidden Linear layers of width 256, an input dimension of 2,352, and eight output logits.

All five hidden layers within a model use the same activation function. The three configurations have identical architecture dimensions and 867,592 trainable parameters.

Component Experimental Setting
Dataset BloodMNIST, official training and validation splits
Preprocessing Shared normalization using training-derived RGB statistics
Network depth D5 — five hidden layers
Hidden width 256
Input / output dimensions 2352 / 8
Weight initialization Xavier Uniform, gain = 1
Bias initialization Zeros
Loss function CrossEntropyLoss
Optimizer SGD
Learning rate 0.1
Momentum / weight decay 0.0 / 0.0
Training batch size 128
Training duration 20 complete epochs
Random seeds 0, 1, 2
Gradient recording First 100 global steps; first 10 batches per epoch
Training-loss threshold 1.50

The same initialization rule and random-seed set are used across all activation conditions. Section 7.2 verifies that corresponding untrained models initialized with the same seed have identical Linear weights and biases.

Initialization control: Xavier Uniform is maintained for all three activations, including ReLU. This allows activation choice to be compared under a shared initialization rule, although that rule is not necessarily optimal for every activation.

The official test split remains unused in the Stage B analysis.

Reusing the Stage A Sigmoid Baseline¶

Stage B reuses the three completed D5 + Sigmoid runs from Stage A rather than retraining them.

The results are organized as:

  • stage_a_runs[(depth, seed)]: Completed Stage A results, including the D5 Sigmoid baseline.
  • stage_b_runs[(activation, seed)]: Stage B results indexed by activation function and random seed.

The full Stage B comparison contains nine activation–seed result entries:

  • 3 reused runs: D5 + Sigmoid, seeds 0–2.
  • 6 new runs: D5 + Tanh and D5 + ReLU, seeds 0–2.

Each new run uses a freshly initialized model, its own optimizer, a seeded training DataLoader, and the established gradient-recording protocol.

Sections 7.1–7.4 establish the controlled activation comparison and complete the required runs.

Sections 7.5–7.6 organize and analyze the recorded measurements.

Section 7.7 interprets the results in relation to H3.

4. Measurements & Analysis¶

Stage B uses the measurement definitions and logging protocol established in Part 4 and applied in Stage A.

Measurement Analysis Research Role
Layer-wise RMS weight gradients Compare absolute gradient magnitudes across the five hidden layers. Evaluate activation-dependent gradient behavior.
First-to-last gradient ratio Compare first-layer RMS relative to last-layer RMS within each run. Quantify relative early-layer gradient attenuation.
Gradient evolution Examine layer-wise RMS gradients across training epochs. Assess whether activation-related differences persist during training.
Normalized first-layer weight displacement Compare the net movement of first-layer weights from initialization. Examine early-layer trainability.
Training-loss trajectories Compare training-loss reduction across epochs. Assess optimization progress.
Epochs-to-threshold Identify the first epoch reaching mean training loss ≤ 1.50. Compare the predefined learning-progress milestone.
Validation metrics Compare validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1. Evaluate classification performance on the validation split.

Statistical reporting: Each activation condition is evaluated across three random seeds. Principal metrics are summarized using the mean and sample standard deviation, where applicable.

First-to-last gradient ratios are calculated separately for each run before aggregation across seeds.

Interpretation: Relative gradient ratios and absolute gradient magnitudes describe different properties. A larger ratio does not necessarily imply a larger absolute first-layer gradient or better validation performance.

Likewise, normalized weight displacement measures net parameter movement from initialization, not the total magnitude of all SGD updates.

The observed differences characterize activation-dependent behavior under the tested D5–Xavier–SGD protocol; they do not establish a universally superior activation function.

Stage A and Stage B investigate complementary experimental factors:

Stage B contributes evidence about activation choice at fixed D5 depth, complementing the depth-dependent findings established in Stage A.

7.1 — Depth Selection for Stage B¶

Objective:

Select one fixed MLP depth for Stage B based on the completed Stage A results. The selected network should exhibit substantial early-layer gradient attenuation while retaining measurable training progress.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 and fig1_summary from Section 6.4.
  2. Compare D5, D10, and D20 using:
    • First-layer gradient RMS at epoch 1.
    • First-to-last hidden-layer gradient RMS ratio.
    • Final normalized first-layer weight change.
    • Final training loss and epochs-to-threshold.
    • Final validation accuracy and macro-F1.
  3. Examine whether each candidate reached the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50 across the three seeds.
  4. Select one depth that exhibits substantial gradient attenuation while remaining trainable under the fixed experimental conditions.
  5. Store the selected depth in stage_b_depth for all subsequent Stage B runs.

Purpose:

Choose a scientifically justified network depth for the controlled activation-function comparison without introducing additional training experiments or modifying the Stage A results.

Expected Results:

  • D5 is expected to show substantial gradient attenuation while retaining measurable learning progress.
  • D10 and D20 are expected to show more severe gradient attenuation but limited optimization progress under Sigmoid.
  • D5 is expected to provide the most suitable balance between gradient attenuation and trainability for Stage B.

Role in the Experiment:

This section completes the experimental roadmap and establishes the fixed network depth for Stage B.

Once the depth is selected, Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU will be compared under the same architecture, initialization rule, optimization settings, dataset splits, training budget, and random-seed set.

No additional model training or gradient computation is performed in this section.

In [56]:
# Select the deep-network candidates using the completed Stage A results.
candidate_depths = (5, 10, 20)

candidate_summary = stage_a_summary_df.loc[
    stage_a_summary_df["depth"].isin(candidate_depths),
    [
        "depth",
        "n_seeds",
        "grad_rms_l1_epoch1_mean",
        "weight_change_l1_final_mean",
        "train_loss_mean",
        "seeds_reached_threshold",
        "epochs_to_threshold_mean",
        "val_accuracy_mean",
        "val_macro_f1_mean"
    ]
].copy()


# Reuse the first-to-last hidden-layer gradient ratios from Stage A Figure 1.
gradient_ratios = fig1_summary.loc[
    fig1_summary["layer"] == 1,
    ["depth", "ratio_mean"]
].rename(
    columns={"ratio_mean": "first_to_last_gradient_ratio"}
)

candidate_summary = candidate_summary.merge(
    gradient_ratios,                 # Add the existing gradient-ratio measurements.
    on="depth",                     # Match each candidate by network depth.
    validate="one_to_one"           # Require exactly one matching ratio per depth.
).sort_values("depth")

assert set(candidate_summary["depth"]) == set(candidate_depths)
assert (candidate_summary["n_seeds"] == len(cfg.seeds)).all()


# Display the evidence for selecting the Stage B network depth.
print("=== Section 7.1 — Stage B Depth Selection ===")
print(f"Candidate depths: {candidate_depths}")
print(f"Training-loss threshold: {cfg.loss_threshold:.2f}")
print("Results: Mean across 3 seeds\n")

with pd.option_context("display.float_format", "{:.4e}".format):
    display(candidate_summary)


# Select D5 based on gradient attenuation and measurable training progress.
stage_b_depth = 5

selected = candidate_summary.set_index("depth").loc[stage_b_depth]

d2_ratio = fig1_summary.loc[
    (fig1_summary["depth"] == 2) &
    (fig1_summary["layer"] == 1),
    "ratio_mean"
].iloc[0]

# Confirm that D5 exhibits attenuation and reaches the loss threshold.
assert stage_b_depth in cfg.depths
assert selected["first_to_last_gradient_ratio"] < d2_ratio
assert selected["seeds_reached_threshold"] == len(cfg.seeds)

print(f"\nSelected Stage B Depth: D{stage_b_depth}")
print("Reason: Substantial gradient attenuation with measurable learning progress.")
print(f"First-to-last gradient ratio: {selected['first_to_last_gradient_ratio']:.3e}")
print(f"Final training loss: {selected['train_loss_mean']:.4f}")
print(f"Seeds reaching threshold: {int(selected['seeds_reached_threshold'])}/{len(cfg.seeds)}")
print("\nStage B depth selection: COMPLETE")

7.1 — Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully reviewed the completed Stage A results for the three candidate network depths: D5, D10, and D20.
  • Reused stage_a_summary_df from Section 6.3 and fig1_summary from Section 6.4 without retraining models or recalculating gradients.
  • Compared early-layer RMS gradients, relative gradient attenuation, cumulative first-layer weight changes, training-loss convergence, and validation performance.
  • Evaluated each candidate using the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50 and results from three random seeds.
  • Selected D5 as the fixed network depth for Stage B based on the balance between substantial gradient attenuation and measurable training progress.
  • Stored the selected depth in stage_b_depth = 5.

Results — Depth Selection Evidence (Mean Across 3 Seeds):

Metric D5 D10 D20
First-layer RMS gradient (epoch 1) 8.823e-06 6.227e-09 3.664e-15
First-to-last gradient ratio 6.369e-03 4.837e-06 2.711e-12
Final normalized first-layer weight change 0.1090 2.740e-05 0.0000
Final training loss 1.2555 2.0114 2.0117
Seeds reaching loss ≤ 1.50 3/3 0/3 0/3
Mean epochs-to-threshold 14.67 Not reached Not reached
Validation accuracy 46.63% 18.20% 18.20%
Validation macro-F1 0.3377 0.0385 0.0385

Values are means across three seeds. Epoch-1 RMS gradients were measured using the first 10 training batches of each run. The gradient ratios are means of per-seed ratios. Full standard deviations are available in the Stage A analyses. "Not reached" means the threshold was not reached within 20 epochs.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. D5 exhibited substantial gradient attenuation while retaining measurable learning progress.

    • The first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 0.637% of the last hidden-layer RMS gradient.
    • The final normalized first-layer weight change was approximately 0.1090.
    • All three seeds reached the predefined training-loss threshold within 14–15 epochs.
    • The mean final training loss decreased to approximately 1.2555.

  2. D10 exhibited much stronger gradient attenuation and limited learning progress.

    • The first-layer RMS gradient decreased to approximately 6.227e-09.
    • The final normalized first-layer weight change was only 2.740e-05.
    • The mean final training loss remained approximately 2.0114.
    • None of the three seeds reached the loss threshold within 20 epochs.

  3. D20 exhibited the strongest gradient attenuation and the most severe early-layer trainability limitations.

    • The first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 3.664e-15.
    • The recorded cumulative first-layer weight change was zero across all three seeds.
    • The mean final training loss remained approximately 2.0117.
    • Extremely small SGD updates may have been affected by floating-point precision; the zero recorded displacement does not establish that mathematical gradients were zero.

  4. D5 achieved better validation performance than D10 and D20.

    • D5 achieved approximately 46.63% validation accuracy and 0.3377 macro-F1.
    • D10 and D20 achieved approximately 18.20% validation accuracy and 0.0385 macro-F1.
    • These performance measurements complement the gradient and convergence evidence but do not independently establish gradient vanishing.

Interpretation — Connection to H1 and H2:

H1 — Depth Effect:

The Stage A gradient measurements showed substantially stronger early-layer attenuation as network depth increased.

D5 exhibited meaningful attenuation, while D10 and D20 exhibited increasingly severe attenuation.

Section 7.1 reuses this evidence to identify a depth that demonstrates gradient vanishing without requiring the strongest possible attenuation.

H2 — Early-Layer Trainability:

The Stage A results showed that stronger gradient attenuation was associated with smaller cumulative first-layer weight changes and slower training-loss reduction.

D5 retained measurable parameter displacement and reached the training-loss threshold across all three seeds.

In contrast, D10 and D20 exhibited extremely small recorded first-layer weight changes and did not reach the threshold within the fixed training budget.

These findings support the H2 associations observed in Stage A, but do not establish gradient attenuation as the sole cause of the optimization differences.

Depth Selection — D5:

D5 is selected for Stage B because it provides a suitable balance between gradient attenuation and trainability.

Although D10 and D20 exhibit stronger gradient vanishing, their Sigmoid baselines show very limited training progress.

D5 provides an interpretable comparison condition: its Sigmoid baseline exhibits substantial gradient attenuation while still demonstrating measurable learning.

The objective is not to select the network with the highest classification accuracy or the most extreme gradient attenuation. It is to select a sufficiently deep network that supports a meaningful controlled activation-function comparison.

Role in Stage B — Connection to H3:

Stage B will use D5 as the fixed architecture and compare three activation functions:

  • D5 + Sigmoid + Xavier Uniform.
  • D5 + Tanh + Xavier Uniform.
  • D5 + ReLU + Xavier Uniform.

All three conditions will use the same architecture, initialization rule, dataset splits, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, random-seed set, and gradient-logging protocol.

The existing D5 + Sigmoid results from Stage A will serve as the baseline and will be reused without retraining.

Stage B will investigate H3 by examining how changing the activation function affects gradient propagation, early-layer weight displacement, training-loss convergence, and classification performance at the selected depth.

Limitations:

  • The depth selection is based on the tested Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration and the fixed 20-epoch training budget.
  • D10 and D20 might show different convergence behavior under other training configurations or longer training.
  • The recorded zero first-layer weight displacement in D20 may reflect numerical precision limitations and has not been independently diagnosed.
  • Selecting D5 does not imply that D5 is universally optimal for activation-function comparisons.
  • Stage B will evaluate activation differences at D5; its results should not automatically be generalized to all network depths.

Conclusion:

Selected Stage B depth: D5 (5 hidden Linear layers).

D5 demonstrates substantial early-layer gradient attenuation while maintaining measurable parameter changes and training-loss reduction.

The selection is supported by the completed Stage A evidence and satisfies the depth-selection criterion.

In 7.1, the Stage B network depth is finalized.

7.2 — Controlled Activation Comparison Setup¶

Objective:

Establish and verify the controlled experimental conditions for Stage B, using the D5 network selected in Section 7.1.

The independent variable is the hidden-layer activation function: Sigmoid, Tanh, or ReLU.

All other experimental conditions remain fixed so that differences in gradient propagation, early-layer weight changes, convergence, and validation performance can be examined under a common training protocol.

Procedure:

  1. Define the Stage B activation conditions:

    • Sigmoid + Xavier Uniform.
    • Tanh + Xavier Uniform.
    • ReLU + Xavier Uniform.

  2. Reuse the fixed experimental configuration:

    • Network depth: D5 (5 hidden Linear layers).
    • Hidden width: 256 neurons.
    • Input dimension: 2,352.
    • Output dimension: 8 classes.
    • Dataset: BloodMNIST, using the same official splits and preprocessing.
    • Weight initialization: Xavier Uniform (gain = 1).
    • Bias initialization: zeros.
    • Loss function: CrossEntropyLoss.
    • Optimizer: SGD (learning rate = 0.1, momentum = 0, weight decay = 0).
    • Training batch size: 128.
    • Training duration: 20 epochs.
    • Random seeds: 0, 1, 2.
    • Gradient logging: first 100 training steps and first 10 batches per epoch.
    • Training-loss threshold: 1.50.

  3. Verify activation handling and model consistency:

    • Reuse build_model() to construct D5 models with Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.
    • Confirm that each model uses the requested activation function.
    • Confirm that all models have the same number of hidden layers and trainable parameters.
    • Confirm that corresponding models initialized with the same seed have identical initial Linear weights and biases.

  4. Reuse the completed Sigmoid baseline:

    • Retrieve D5 + Sigmoid results for seeds 0, 1, and 2 from stage_a_runs.
    • Store the existing run results in stage_b_runs using (activation, seed) as the dictionary key.
    • Do not retrain Sigmoid or modify its recorded results.

  5. Prepare the remaining activation conditions:

    • Tanh and ReLU will be trained in Sections 7.3–7.4 using the existing run_training() function.
    • No model training is performed in Section 7.2.

Purpose:

Establish a fair and reproducible activation-function comparison while reusing the model architecture, initialization, training pipeline, gradient recorder, and completed Stage A baseline.

Using the same Xavier initialization rule prevents the main experiment from simultaneously changing both activation and initialization schemes.

Using the same random seeds also allows corresponding activation conditions to begin with identical initial Linear parameters and reproducible training-data shuffling.

Expected Results:

  • All three D5 models should contain five hidden Linear layers and one output Linear layer.
  • All models should have identical architecture dimensions and trainable parameter counts.
  • The requested activation functions should be correctly assigned.
  • Corresponding models constructed with the same seed should have identical initial Linear weights and biases.
  • All three D5 + Sigmoid runs should be available from Stage A.
  • stage_b_runs should contain the three reused Sigmoid runs, ready for the addition of Tanh and ReLU results.

Role in the Experiment:

It connects the depth-selection decision in Section 7.1 to the activation-function experiments in Sections 7.3–7.7.

Stage A varied network depth while keeping Sigmoid fixed. Stage B reverses this approach by fixing network depth at D5 and varying only the hidden-layer activation function.

This controlled comparison will provide the evidence needed to investigate H3 — Activation Effect.

In [57]:
# Define the activation conditions and reuse the fixed Stage A training settings.
stage_b_activations = ("sigmoid", "tanh", "relu")
stage_b_seeds = tuple(cfg.seeds)

assert stage_b_depth == 5                         # Use D5 selected from Stage A in Section 7.1.
assert cfg.init == "xavier_uniform"               # Keep the same Xavier initialization rule.
assert cfg.lr == 0.1                              # Preserve the learning rate finalized in Part 5.
assert cfg.epochs == 20                           # Keep the same training budget for all activations.
assert cfg.loss_threshold == 1.50                 # Reuse the predefined convergence threshold.

print("=== Section 7.2 — Controlled Activation Comparison Setup ===")
print(f"Fixed network depth: D{stage_b_depth}")
print(f"Activation functions: {stage_b_activations}")
print(f"Random seeds: {stage_b_seeds}")
print(f"Initialization: {cfg.init}")
print(f"Optimizer: SGD | LR: {cfg.lr} | Epochs: {cfg.epochs}")
print(f"Training-loss threshold: {cfg.loss_threshold:.2f}")


# Build one untrained D5 model per activation using the same random seed.
# This verifies the architecture and initialization before the main comparison.
verification_seed = stage_b_seeds[0]

stage_b_models = {
    activation: build_model(                    # Reuse the existing model builder from Part 2.
        depth=stage_b_depth,                    # Fix the architecture at five hidden layers.
        seed=verification_seed,                 # Use the same seed for comparable initial parameters.
        activation=activation                   # Change only the hidden-layer activation function.
    )
    for activation in stage_b_activations
}

reference_model = stage_b_models["sigmoid"]      # Use Sigmoid as the reference architecture.

for activation, model in stage_b_models.items():
    assert len(model.hidden_layers) == stage_b_depth    # Verify exactly five hidden Linear layers.
    assert isinstance(                         # Verify that the requested activation was assigned.
        model.activation,
        {"sigmoid": nn.Sigmoid, "tanh": nn.Tanh, "relu": nn.ReLU}[activation]
    )

    assert sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) == sum(
        p.numel() for p in reference_model.parameters()
    )                                           # All activations must have identical parameter counts.

    for (name, parameter), (ref_name, ref_parameter) in zip(
        model.named_parameters(), reference_model.named_parameters()
    ):
        assert name == ref_name                 # Match corresponding weights and biases by name.
        assert torch.equal(parameter, ref_parameter)   # Confirm identical initial parameter values.

    print(
        f"{activation.capitalize():7s} | "
        f"Hidden layers: {len(model.hidden_layers)} | "
        f"Parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,} | "
        "Initialization: MATCH"
    )


# Reuse the completed D5 + Sigmoid runs from Stage A without retraining.
# The dictionary key (activation, seed) will also be used for future Tanh/ReLU runs.
stage_b_runs = {}

for seed in stage_b_seeds:
    assert (stage_b_depth, seed) in stage_a_runs   # Ensure the completed Stage A baseline exists.
    stage_b_runs[("sigmoid", seed)] = stage_a_runs[(stage_b_depth, seed)]

assert len(stage_b_runs) == len(stage_b_seeds)     # Exactly three Sigmoid baseline runs are reused.

print(f"\nReused Sigmoid baseline runs: {len(stage_b_runs)}")
print(f"Stage B run keys: {list(stage_b_runs.keys())}")


# Confirm that Stage B is ready for training the remaining activation conditions.
remaining_activations = tuple(
    activation for activation in stage_b_activations if activation != "sigmoid"
)

print(f"\nRemaining activations to train: {remaining_activations}")
print(f"Remaining training runs: {len(remaining_activations) * len(stage_b_seeds)}")
print("Stage B activation setup: COMPLETE")

7.2 - Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Results:

The controlled activation comparison setup was completed successfully.

The experimental configuration was verified as follows:

  • Selected network depth: D5 (five hidden layers).
  • Activation functions: Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.
  • Model architecture: Identical across all three activation conditions.
  • Trainable parameters: 867,592 per model.
  • Weight initialization: Xavier Uniform.
  • Initial parameter consistency: All three models constructed with the same seed had identical initial weights and biases.
  • Optimizer: SGD with learning rate 0.1.
  • Training duration: 20 epochs.
  • Random seeds: 0, 1, and 2.
  • Training-loss threshold: 1.50.
  • Reused baseline: Three completed D5 + Sigmoid runs from Stage A.
  • Remaining experiments: Six training runs (Tanh and ReLU, each with three seeds).

All implemented architecture, activation-handling, and initialization-consistency checks passed.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. Controlled architecture: All three activation conditions use the same D5 network architecture and contain 867,592 trainable parameters. Therefore, model depth, hidden width, and parameter count are not additional experimental variables.

  2. Matched initialization: Corresponding models constructed with the same random seed have identical initial weights and biases. This reduces initialization-related variation when comparing activation functions.

  3. Single independent variable: The activation function is the only intended experimental variable. Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU are evaluated under the same Xavier initialization rule and fixed training configuration.

  4. Baseline reuse: All three D5 + Sigmoid runs were successfully retrieved from Stage A. No additional Sigmoid training is required.

  5. Training readiness: The remaining six Tanh and ReLU runs can proceed using the existing model-building, training, validation, and gradient-measurement pipeline.

Interpretation:

Section 7.2 establishes the experimental controls required to investigate H3 — Activation Effect.

By holding network architecture, initialization, optimizer, learning rate, training duration, and random seeds fixed, Stage B is designed to examine how the choice of hidden-layer activation function affects gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, convergence, and classification performance.

Using identical initial Linear parameters across corresponding activation conditions helps reduce initialization randomness as a potential confounding factor.

Importantly, identical initial parameters do not imply identical forward activations, gradients, or optimization trajectories. These quantities may differ because Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU apply different nonlinear transformations.

The successful setup does not provide new empirical evidence for H1, H2, or H3. Instead, it establishes the conditions needed for a controlled investigation of H3.

Connection to Other Sections:

  • Section 7.1: Selected D5 based on Stage A results showing substantial gradient attenuation while retaining measurable learning progress.
  • Section 7.2: Verified the controlled activation comparison and reused the completed Sigmoid baseline.
  • Sections 7.3–7.4: Train the remaining activation conditions using the existing experimental pipeline.
  • Later Stage B analysis: Compare layer-wise gradients, early-layer weight changes, convergence, and validation performance to evaluate H3.

Conclusion:

The Stage B experimental setup is complete. All three activation conditions share the same verified architecture and initialization protocol, and the completed Sigmoid baseline has been successfully reused.

The experiment is ready to proceed with Tanh and ReLU training.

7.3 — Single-Seed Activation Comparison¶

Objective

Conduct the initial Stage B comparison of Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU at a fixed depth of D5 using random seed 0 and the experimental protocol established in Section 7.2.

Procedure

  1. Reuse the completed D5 + Sigmoid baseline from Stage A without retraining.
  2. Execute two new D5 training runs using seed 0: one with Tanh and one with ReLU.
  3. Use the existing run_training() function with the same Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD optimizer, learning rate, training duration, and gradient-recording protocol.
  4. Store the new results in stage_b_runs using (activation, seed) as the dictionary key.
  5. Verify that all three activation conditions have complete training histories and recorded measurements.

Recorded Measurements

  • Training loss by epoch.
  • Validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1.
  • Layer-wise RMS weight gradients.
  • Normalized first-layer weight displacement.
  • Epochs-to-threshold using the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.

Verification

The two new runs are checked for completion of 20 training epochs and availability of the expected training, validation, gradient, and weight-displacement records.

Together with the reused Sigmoid baseline, these results establish the initial three-condition activation comparison at seed 0.

The remaining seeds (1 and 2) are completed in Section 7.4 before the multi-seed analysis in Sections 7.5–7.7.

In [58]:
# Reuse the completed Sigmoid baseline and prepare the two new activation runs.
stage_b_seed = stage_b_seeds[0]                       # Seed 0: the first controlled activation comparison.
assert stage_b_seed == 0                             # Section 7.3 is specifically the seed-0 experiment.
assert ("sigmoid", stage_b_seed) in stage_b_runs       # The Sigmoid baseline must already exist from Stage A.

print("=== Section 7.3 — Single-Seed Activation Comparison ===")
print(f"Fixed depth: D{stage_b_depth} | Seed: {stage_b_seed} | Epochs: {cfg.epochs}")
print(f"Activations: {stage_b_activations}")
print(f"Initialization: {cfg.init} | Optimizer: {cfg.optimizer.upper()} | LR: {cfg.lr:g}")
print("Sigmoid baseline: REUSED from Stage A")


# Train Tanh and ReLU independently using the existing training and gradient-recording pipeline.
for activation in remaining_activations:

    run_key = (activation, stage_b_seed)             # Identify each run by its activation and seed.

    if run_key in stage_b_runs:
        print(f"\nSkipping {activation.upper()} (seed={stage_b_seed}): already completed.")
        continue                                    # Preserve an existing run if this cell is executed again.

    print(f"\nTraining D{stage_b_depth} + {activation.upper()} (seed={stage_b_seed})...")

    result = run_training(
        depth=stage_b_depth,                         # Keep five hidden layers for every activation.
        seed=stage_b_seed,                           # Match the Sigmoid baseline's random seed.
        activation=activation,                       # Change only the hidden-layer activation function.
        lr=cfg.lr,                                   # Reuse the fixed learning rate from Stage A.
        epochs=cfg.epochs,                           # Train for all 20 epochs.
        max_batches=None                             # Use every training batch; no debugging limit.
    )

    # Check that training produced the complete history and gradient/weight-change records.
    history = result["history"]                      # Training and validation metrics for each epoch.
    epoch_gradients = result["epoch_gradients"]      # Mean RMS gradient for each hidden layer and epoch.
    weight_changes = result["weight_changes"]       # Normalized first-layer weight change after each epoch.

    assert result["run_config"]["activation"] == activation  # Confirm the requested activation was used.
    assert result["run_config"]["depth"] == stage_b_depth     # Confirm the fixed D5 architecture.
    assert result["run_config"]["seed"] == stage_b_seed       # Confirm the intended random seed.
    assert result["run_config"]["max_batches"] is None       # Confirm full training, not a partial debug run.

    assert len(history) == cfg.epochs                        # One history entry per completed epoch.
    assert len(epoch_gradients) == stage_b_depth * cfg.epochs # Five layers × 20 epochs = 100 records.
    assert len(weight_changes) == cfg.epochs                 # One first-layer weight-change record per epoch.
    assert len(result["step_records"]) > 0                   # Early-step gradient measurements are available.

    assert all(
        np.isfinite(row[metric])
        for row in history
        for metric in ("train_loss", "val_loss", "val_accuracy", "val_macro_f1")
    )                                                       # Ensure all training/validation metrics are finite.

    assert all(np.isfinite(row["mean_grad_rms"]) for row in epoch_gradients)
    assert all(np.isfinite(row["first_layer_weight_change"]) for row in weight_changes)

    # Store the verified run and display its final training and validation performance.
    stage_b_runs[run_key] = result                    # Preserve the complete result for Sections 7.4–7.7.
    last_epoch = history[-1]                         # Read the metrics after the final training epoch.

    print(
        f"D{stage_b_depth} + {activation.upper()} complete | "
        f"Train loss: {last_epoch['train_loss']:.4f} | "
        f"Val loss: {last_epoch['val_loss']:.4f} | "
        f"Val acc: {last_epoch['val_accuracy']:.4f} | "
        f"Val macro-F1: {last_epoch['val_macro_f1']:.4f}"
    )


# Verify that Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU are all available for the first random seed.
for activation in stage_b_activations:
    assert (activation, stage_b_seed) in stage_b_runs  # Every activation must have a completed seed-0 run.

print(f"\nStage B seed-{stage_b_seed} comparison:")
for activation in stage_b_activations:
    final_metrics = stage_b_runs[(activation, stage_b_seed)]["history"][-1]

    print(
        f"{activation.capitalize():7s} | "
        f"Train loss: {final_metrics['train_loss']:.4f} | "
        f"Val acc: {final_metrics['val_accuracy']:.4f} | "
        f"Val macro-F1: {final_metrics['val_macro_f1']:.4f}"
    )

print(f"\nStage B stored runs: {len(stage_b_runs)} / {len(stage_b_activations) * len(stage_b_seeds)}")
print("Stage B single-seed activation comparison: COMPLETE")

7.3 - Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully reused the completed D5 + Sigmoid baseline for seed 0 from Stage A.
  • Trained D5 + Tanh and D5 + ReLU independently for 20 complete epochs using seed 0.
  • Preserved the fixed architecture, Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD optimizer, learning rate of 0.1, and existing BloodMNIST data pipeline.
  • Reused the existing run_training() function and gradient-recording infrastructure.
  • Verified that training histories, gradient records, and normalized first-layer weight-change records were generated successfully.
  • Stored both new runs in stage_b_runs without modifying the existing Sigmoid baseline.
  • Completed the first single-seed comparison of all three activation functions.

Results — Seed 0, Epoch 20:

Metric Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
Final training loss 1.2604 0.1212 0.1474
Final validation loss Not displayed 0.4436 0.8238
Final validation accuracy 44.86% 86.27% 78.91%
Final validation macro-F1 0.3133 0.8458 0.7665

All results correspond to the D5 architecture, random seed 0, and the final epoch of the fixed 20-epoch training budget.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. Tanh and ReLU achieved substantially lower training losses than Sigmoid.

    • Sigmoid finished with a training loss of 1.2604.
    • Tanh and ReLU achieved training losses of 0.1212 and 0.1474, respectively.
    • Both alternatives demonstrated substantially stronger optimization progress under the fixed training protocol.

  2. Tanh achieved the strongest validation performance in the seed-0 comparison.

    • Tanh reached 86.27% validation accuracy and 0.8458 macro-F1.
    • ReLU reached 78.91% validation accuracy and 0.7665 macro-F1.
    • Sigmoid reached 44.86% validation accuracy and 0.3133 macro-F1.

  3. Tanh also achieved lower validation loss than ReLU.

    • Tanh: 0.4436.
    • ReLU: 0.8238.
    • The observed validation-loss gap was smaller for Tanh than for ReLU at epoch 20, although this alone does not establish a generalization advantage across seeds.

  4. All required experimental records were successfully generated.

    • Training and validation histories were recorded.
    • Layer-wise RMS gradients were recorded using the existing measurement protocol.
    • Normalized first-layer weight changes were recorded.
    • The results are available for the multi-seed analyses in later sections.

Interpretation — Connection to H3:

The single-seed results provide preliminary evidence that hidden-layer activation choice has a substantial effect on optimization behavior and validation performance at fixed network depth.

Both Tanh and ReLU outperformed Sigmoid in final training loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1.

Tanh also outperformed ReLU on these displayed metrics for seed 0.

These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that activation functions influence the trainability of deep MLPs.

However, the displayed results do not yet establish whether Tanh or ReLU provides better gradient propagation than Sigmoid.

The recorded layer-wise RMS gradients and normalized first-layer weight changes must be examined before drawing conclusions about the gradient-vanishing mechanism.

Connection to H1 and H2:

  • H1: Not directly retested because network depth is fixed at D5.
  • H2: The training-loss differences provide additional context for trainability, but the activation-specific gradient and parameter-displacement measurements have not yet been analyzed.
  • H3: The observed optimization and validation differences provide preliminary support for an activation effect under the controlled experimental configuration.

Limitations:

  • The comparison currently includes only one random seed.
  • The results reflect a fixed 20-epoch training budget and learning rate of 0.1.
  • All activations use Xavier Uniform initialization, which is not necessarily optimal for ReLU.
  • Final training and validation metrics alone do not identify the mechanism responsible for the observed differences.
  • The results do not establish that Tanh is universally superior to ReLU or Sigmoid.

Conclusion:

The first controlled activation-function comparison was completed successfully.

For seed 0, both Tanh and ReLU demonstrated substantially better optimization and validation performance than Sigmoid, with Tanh achieving the strongest results among the three activations.

These findings provide preliminary evidence relevant to H3, while the gradient-propagation and early-layer trainability mechanisms remain to be evaluated using the recorded measurements.

Five of the nine Stage B runs are now available.

7.4 — Complete Multi-Seed Stage B Runs¶

Objective:

Complete the controlled activation-function experiment by training the remaining D5 + Tanh and D5 + ReLU models using random seeds 1 and 2.

Extend the single-seed comparison from Section 7.3 to three random seeds per activation function, while preserving the fixed experimental configuration established in Section 7.2.

Procedure:

  1. Reuse completed Stage B runs:

    • Retain the three D5 + Sigmoid baseline runs reused from Stage A.
    • Retain the D5 + Tanh and D5 + ReLU runs for seed 0 completed in Section 7.3.
    • Do not retrain or overwrite existing results.

  2. Train the remaining activation–seed combinations:

    • D5 + Tanh, seed 1.
    • D5 + Tanh, seed 2.
    • D5 + ReLU, seed 1.
    • D5 + ReLU, seed 2.
    • Reuse the existing run_training() function and the fixed Stage B configuration.

  3. Preserve the controlled experimental conditions:

    • Network depth: D5.
    • Hidden width: 256.
    • Activation functions: Tanh and ReLU for the remaining runs.
    • Weight initialization: Xavier Uniform (gain = 1).
    • Optimizer: SGD with learning rate 0.1.
    • Training duration: 20 complete epochs per run.
    • Dataset: BloodMNIST with the same official splits, normalization, and DataLoaders.
    • Gradient and weight-change recording: identical to Stage A and Section 7.3.

  4. Verify the newly completed runs:

    • Confirm the intended depth, activation, seed, and full training configuration.
    • Confirm that each run contains 20 epochs of training and validation history.
    • Confirm that layer-wise RMS gradient records, early-step gradient records, and normalized first-layer weight-change records are available.
    • Check the recorded numerical values for NaN or infinite values.

  5. Store and verify the complete Stage B results:

    • Add each verified run to stage_b_runs, indexed by (activation, seed).
    • Confirm that all nine combinations of three activations and three seeds are present.
    • Display final training loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1 for every completed run.
    • Preserve the complete records for subsequent aggregation and analysis.

Purpose:

Evaluate whether the preliminary activation-related differences observed in Section 7.3 are consistent across multiple random seeds.

Using three seeds per activation reduces reliance on a single random initialization and training trajectory.

The complete experiment will allow the reporting of mean and standard deviation for gradient propagation, early-layer weight displacement, convergence behavior, and validation performance.

Expected Results:

  • Four additional D5 models complete 20 training epochs each.
  • No previously completed runs are retrained or overwritten.
  • stage_b_runs contains nine complete runs:
    • Sigmoid: seeds 0, 1, 2.
    • Tanh: seeds 0, 1, 2.
    • ReLU: seeds 0, 1, 2.
  • All runs contain the training, validation, gradient, and weight-change records required by the existing analysis pipeline.
  • The resulting multi-seed dataset is ready for mean ± standard deviation analysis.

The relative performance of Tanh and ReLU across all three seeds is not assumed in advance.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 7.4 completes the training component and provides the full experimental dataset required to investigate H3 — Activation Effect.

Stage A evaluated the effect of network depth while holding Sigmoid fixed.

Stage B holds network depth at D5 and varies the activation function, using the same initialization and training protocol.

By completing all three random seeds, this section prepares the experiment for a more reliable comparison of activation-dependent gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, convergence, and classification performance.

Connection to Other Sections:

  • Section 7.1: Selected D5 based on the completed Stage A evidence.
  • Section 7.2: Established and verified the controlled activation comparison.
  • Section 7.3: Completed the initial seed-0 activation comparison.
  • Section 7.4: Completes the remaining Tanh and ReLU training runs.
  • Sections 7.5–7.7: Aggregate, visualize, and interpret the completed multi-seed results to evaluate H3.

Notes:

No additional network depths, activation functions, initialization methods, optimizers, learning-rate searches, gradient metrics, or figures are introduced.

This section performs only the four remaining training runs and verifies the completeness of the Stage B results.

7.4 - Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation:

  • Successfully completed the four remaining Stage B training runs:
    • D5 + Tanh, seeds 1 and 2.

  • Reused the existing run_training() function and the fixed Stage B configuration.

  • Confirmed that all nine activation–seed combinations are present in stage_b_runs.

The preliminary mean and sample standard deviation values were calculated from the displayed four-decimal run results. Section 7.5 will calculate the official summaries directly from the stored run records.

Preliminary Observations:

  1. All Stage B training runs were completed successfully.

    • Nine of nine activation–seed combinations are available.
    • All four newly trained runs completed 20 epochs.
    • The required training and gradient-measurement records were verified.

  2. Tanh and ReLU consistently achieved lower final training losses than Sigmoid.

    • Sigmoid final training losses ranged from 1.2455 to 1.2606.
    • Tanh final training losses ranged from 0.1212 to 0.3287.
    • ReLU final training losses ranged from 0.1474 to 0.2871.
    • Both alternative activations demonstrated substantially greater optimization progress under the fixed training protocol.

  3. Tanh achieved the highest validation accuracy and macro-F1 across all three seeds.

    • Mean validation accuracy was approximately 86.21%.
    • Mean validation macro-F1 was approximately 0.8441.
    • Tanh also showed relatively small variation in validation accuracy across the three seeds.

  4. ReLU also substantially outperformed Sigmoid.

    • Mean validation accuracy was approximately 81.70%, compared with 46.63% for Sigmoid.
    • Mean validation macro-F1 was approximately 0.7946, compared with 0.3377 for Sigmoid.
    • ReLU exhibited greater seed-to-seed variation in validation accuracy than Tanh.

  5. Optimization outcomes varied across random seeds.

    • Tanh seed 1 had a higher final training loss than Tanh seeds 0 and 2.
    • ReLU seed 2 had a higher final training loss than ReLU seeds 0 and 1.
    • These differences illustrate why multiple random seeds are useful even when validation performance is relatively consistent.

Interpretation — Connection to H3:

The completed three-seed experiment provides consistent evidence that hidden-layer activation choice affects optimization and validation performance at fixed network depth.

Under the D5 + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration, both Tanh and ReLU achieved substantially lower final training losses and higher validation performance than Sigmoid across all three seeds.

Tanh achieved the strongest observed validation accuracy and macro-F1 among the three activation functions.

These findings support the performance-related aspect of H3.

However, the current output does not yet establish whether Tanh or ReLU reduces gradient attenuation relative to Sigmoid.

Layer-wise RMS gradients, first-to-last gradient ratios, normalized first-layer weight changes, and convergence measurements must be analyzed before evaluating the gradient-propagation mechanism.

Connection to H1 and H2:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Not directly retested. Network depth remained fixed at D5 throughout Stage B.
  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: The training-loss results provide additional evidence of differences in optimization behavior, but the gradient and weight-displacement measurements have not yet been compared across activations.
  • H3 — Activation Effect: The multi-seed results provide consistent evidence of activation-dependent optimization and validation performance under the controlled experimental configuration.

Limitations:

  • Only three random seeds were evaluated.
  • The results apply to the selected D5 architecture and the fixed 20-epoch training budget.
  • All activation conditions used Xavier Uniform initialization, which may not be optimal for ReLU.
  • Final-epoch performance does not fully describe convergence trajectories.
  • Higher validation performance alone does not demonstrate improved gradient propagation.
  • The results do not establish that Tanh is universally superior to ReLU or Sigmoid.

Conclusion:

Section 7.4 successfully completed the full Stage B training dataset.

Both Tanh and ReLU consistently outperformed Sigmoid in final training loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1 across all three random seeds.

Tanh achieved the strongest observed validation performance under the tested configuration.

These findings provide consistent preliminary evidence for the activation-performance component of H3. The gradient-propagation and early-layer trainability components remain to be evaluated using the recorded measurements.

All 9/9 Stage B runs are available.

7.5 — Organize & Aggregate Stage B Results¶

Objective:

Organize the measurements collected from all nine completed Stage B runs into analysis-ready Pandas DataFrames and calculate mean ± sample standard deviation across three random seeds for each activation function.

Prepare the gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, convergence, and validation performance measurements needed to evaluate H3 — Activation Effect under the fixed D5 + Xavier Uniform + SGD experimental configuration.

Procedure:

  1. Retrieve and verify the completed Stage B runs:

    • Reuse stage_b_runs from Sections 7.2–7.4.
    • Include three activation functions (Sigmoid, Tanh, ReLU), each evaluated with seeds 0, 1, and 2.
    • Verify the fixed D5 architecture, Xavier Uniform initialization, SGD settings, training duration, and batch size.
    • Preserve all previously recorded measurements without retraining models or recomputing gradients.

  2. Organize the recorded measurements into DataFrames:

    • stage_b_history_df: Training loss, validation loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1 for each activation, seed, and epoch.
    • stage_b_gradient_df: Layer-wise mean RMS weight gradients for each activation, seed, epoch, and hidden layer. Each epoch-level gradient is the arithmetic mean of the RMS measurements from the first 10 training batches.
    • stage_b_weights_df: Cumulative normalized weight changes of Hidden Layer 1 after each epoch, measured relative to its initial weights.

    Preserve the original activation, seed, epoch, and hidden-layer identifiers to avoid mixing measurements from different runs.

  3. Calculate one summary for each independent training run:

    • Extract final training loss, validation loss, validation accuracy, and validation macro-F1 after epoch 20.

    • Extract the mean RMS weight gradients of Hidden Layer 1 and Hidden Layer 5 at epoch 1.

    • Calculate the first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratio for each run:

      R = RMS(Hidden Layer 1) / RMS(Hidden Layer 5)

    • Extract the final cumulative normalized first-layer weight change after epoch 20.

    • Identify the first epoch when mean training loss reaches the predefined threshold of 1.50.

    • Record missing values (NaN) when the threshold is not reached within 20 epochs.

    • Store these measurements in stage_b_run_df, containing one row per activation–seed combination.

  4. Aggregate measurements across three random seeds:

    • Group the per-run summaries by activation function.
    • Calculate arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) for:
      • Final training loss.
      • Final validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1.
      • First-layer RMS gradient at epoch 1.
      • First-to-last hidden-layer gradient ratio at epoch 1.
      • Final normalized first-layer weight change.
      • Epochs-to-threshold.
    • Count how many seeds reached the predefined training-loss threshold.
    • Calculate gradient ratios separately within each run before averaging the ratios across seeds.
    • Calculate epochs-to-threshold statistics only from runs that reached the threshold.
    • Store the results in stage_b_summary_df, containing one row per activation function.

  5. Verify the organized results:

    • Confirm that all nine activation–seed combinations are represented.
    • Confirm that every run contains 20 training epochs.
    • Confirm that each epoch contains five hidden-layer gradient measurements.
    • Confirm that each epoch-level gradient measurement uses the first 10 training batches.
    • Check for duplicate records, missing measurements, and non-finite numerical values.
    • Preserve the complete records for subsequent analysis.

  6. Save and display the results:

    • Save the complete Stage B run records and the compact per-run and activation-level summary tables.
    • Display the per-run and multi-seed summaries without changing the precision of the underlying measurements.
    • Preserve the original stage_b_runs dictionary and the recorded first-100-step gradients.

Purpose:

Convert the recorded measurements from individual training runs into a consistent, reproducible format suitable for comparing activation functions.

Keeping individual seed results separate before aggregation preserves information about run-to-run variability.

Reporting mean ± sample standard deviation helps determine whether observed activation-dependent differences are reasonably consistent across the three random seeds.

Combining gradient attenuation, cumulative first-layer weight displacement, training-loss convergence, and validation performance provides a more informative evaluation of activation effects than classification accuracy alone.

Expected Results:

DataFrame Expected Rows Description
stage_b_history_df 180 9 runs × 20 epochs
stage_b_gradient_df 900 9 runs × 20 epochs × 5 hidden layers
stage_b_weights_df 180 One normalized first-layer weight-change record per run and epoch
stage_b_run_df 9 One summary per activation–seed combination
stage_b_summary_df 3 One aggregated summary per activation

The complete Stage B dataset should contain:

  • Nine completed training runs.
  • Three random seeds per activation function.
  • Valid gradient, weight-change, convergence, and validation measurements.
  • Mean and sample standard deviation for the principal metrics.
  • Correct handling of runs that did not reach the training-loss threshold.

The results should remain consistent with the existing D5 + Sigmoid measurements reused from Stage A.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 7.5 implements the data organization and multi-seed aggregation component.

It connects the completed activation-function training runs in Sections 7.3–7.4 to the quantitative analysis of gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, convergence, and classification performance in Section 7.6.

The same gradient measurement, normalized weight-change, and convergence definitions used in Stage A are retained to preserve methodological consistency.

The aggregated results will support the final evaluation of H3 in Section 7.7.

Connection to H1, H2, and H3:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Not directly retested because network depth remains fixed at D5. The Stage B results complement the depth-dependent findings from Stage A.
  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: Organizes gradient attenuation, cumulative first-layer weight displacement, and convergence measurements to examine their relationship under different activation conditions.
  • H3 — Activation Effect: Provides the multi-seed measurements necessary to compare Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU under a common Xavier Uniform initialization and fixed training protocol.

Notes:

This section performs data extraction, organization, verification, aggregation, and result preservation only.

No additional model training, gradient backpropagation, network architectures, activation functions, initialization methods, optimizers, figures, or statistical hypothesis tests are introduced.

The BloodMNIST test split remains untouched.

# Verify that all nine Stage B runs are available before processing their measurements.
expected_runs = {
    (activation, seed)
    for activation in stage_b_activations
    for seed in stage_b_seeds
}

assert set(stage_b_runs) == expected_runs             # Require all 3 activations × 3 random seeds.
assert cfg.loss_threshold is not None                 # The convergence threshold must be frozen from Part 5.

print("=== Section 7.5 — Organize & Aggregate Stage B Results ===")
print(f"Completed runs: {len(stage_b_runs)}")
print(f"Fixed depth: D{stage_b_depth}")
print(f"Activations: {stage_b_activations}")
print(f"Random seeds: {stage_b_seeds}")
print(f"Training-loss threshold: {cfg.loss_threshold:.2f}")


# Prepare containers for the recorded measurements and one summary per training run.
history_rows = []           # Training/validation metrics for every epoch.
gradient_rows = []          # Layer-wise RMS gradients averaged over the first 10 batches per epoch.
weight_rows = []            # Cumulative first-layer weight changes after each epoch.
run_summary_rows = []       # Final metrics and convergence information for each activation–seed run.


# Extract measurements from the completed runs without retraining or modifying the models.
for activation in stage_b_activations:
    for seed in stage_b_seeds:

        result = stage_b_runs[(activation, seed)]     # Retrieve the existing result for this activation and seed.
        settings = result["run_config"]               # Configuration actually used for this training run.

        # Confirm that only the activation function differs between corresponding conditions.
        assert settings["depth"] == stage_b_depth
        assert settings["activation"] == activation
        assert settings["seed"] == seed
        assert settings["initialization"] == cfg.init
        assert settings["learning_rate"] == cfg.lr
        assert settings["epochs"] == cfg.epochs
        assert settings["batch_size"] == cfg.batch_size
        assert settings["momentum"] == cfg.momentum
        assert settings["weight_decay"] == cfg.weight_decay
        assert settings["max_batches"] is None        # None means all training batches were processed.

        history = result["history"]                   # Training/validation metrics recorded after each epoch.
        gradients = result["epoch_gradients"]         # One mean RMS gradient per hidden layer and epoch.
        weight_changes = result["weight_changes"]     # One cumulative first-layer weight change per epoch.

        assert len(history) == cfg.epochs
        assert len(gradients) == stage_b_depth * cfg.epochs
        assert len(weight_changes) == cfg.epochs
        assert len(result["step_records"]) == 100 * stage_b_depth  # First 100 steps × five hidden layers.

        # Organize epoch-level training and validation metrics using the original record fields.
        for row in history:
            history_rows.append({
                "activation": activation,             # Independent variable in Stage B.
                "seed": seed,                         # Random seed identifying this independent run.
                "epoch": row["epoch"],                # Recorded epoch number, starting at 1.
                "train_loss": row["train_loss"],      # Mean training CrossEntropyLoss during this epoch.
                "val_loss": row["val_loss"],          # Validation CrossEntropyLoss after this epoch.
                "val_accuracy": row["val_accuracy"],  # Correct predictions / total validation samples.
                "val_macro_f1": row["val_macro_f1"]   # Mean of the eight class-specific F1 scores.
            })

        # Organize the gradient and first-layer weight-change measurements already recorded in Part 4.
        for row in gradients:
            gradient_rows.append({
                "activation": activation,
                "seed": seed,
                "epoch": row["epoch"],
                "layer": row["layer"],                 # Hidden-layer position, counted from the input.
                "mean_grad_rms": row["mean_grad_rms"], # Mean of RMS weight gradients from sampled batches.
                "batches": row["batches"]              # Number of sampled batches contributing to the mean.
            })

        for row in weight_changes:
            weight_rows.append({
                "activation": activation,
                "seed": seed,
                "epoch": row["epoch"],
                "first_layer_weight_change": row["first_layer_weight_change"]  # ||W1(t)-W1(0)|| / ||W1(0)||.
            })

        # Extract the first and last hidden-layer RMS gradients from epoch 1.
        first_grad = next(
            row["mean_grad_rms"] for row in gradients
            if row["epoch"] == 1 and row["layer"] == 1
        )                                              # Hidden Layer 1 is closest to the input.

        last_grad = next(
            row["mean_grad_rms"] for row in gradients
            if row["epoch"] == 1 and row["layer"] == stage_b_depth
        )                                              # Hidden Layer 5 is closest to the output.

        assert last_grad > 0                           # The denominator must be positive for a valid ratio.

        gradient_ratio = first_grad / last_grad        # Relative RMS gradient: Hidden Layer 1 / Hidden Layer 5.

        # Find the first epoch when mean training loss reaches the predefined threshold.
        reached_epoch = next(
            (
                row["epoch"] for row in history
                if row["train_loss"] <= cfg.loss_threshold
            ),
            np.nan                                     # Missing value if the threshold was never reached.
        )

        final = history[-1]                            # Final epoch's training/validation measurements.
        final_weight = weight_changes[-1]              # Final cumulative first-layer weight displacement.

        assert final["epoch"] == cfg.epochs
        assert final_weight["epoch"] == cfg.epochs

        # Store one compact summary for this completed activation–seed training run.
        run_summary_rows.append({
            "activation": activation,
            "seed": seed,
            "train_loss": final["train_loss"],
            "val_loss": final["val_loss"],
            "val_accuracy": final["val_accuracy"],
            "val_macro_f1": final["val_macro_f1"],
            "weight_change_l1_final": final_weight["first_layer_weight_change"],
            "reached_threshold": not pd.isna(reached_epoch), # True if loss <= threshold in any epoch.
            "epochs_to_threshold": reached_epoch,            # First qualifying epoch, or NaN.
            "grad_rms_l1_epoch1": first_grad,                 # First hidden-layer mean RMS at epoch 1.
            "grad_rms_last_epoch1": last_grad,                # Last hidden-layer mean RMS at epoch 1.
            "first_to_last_gradient_ratio": gradient_ratio   # Calculated separately for each seed.
        })


# Convert the collected measurements into structured, analysis-ready Pandas DataFrames.
stage_b_history_df = pd.DataFrame(history_rows)         # One row per activation, seed, and epoch.
stage_b_gradient_df = pd.DataFrame(gradient_rows)       # One row per activation, seed, epoch, and layer.
stage_b_weights_df = pd.DataFrame(weight_rows)          # One cumulative weight-change record per epoch.
stage_b_run_df = pd.DataFrame(run_summary_rows)         # One final summary per independent run.


# Verify the expected record counts and ensure no run/epoch/layer measurements are duplicated.
n_runs = len(expected_runs)

assert len(stage_b_history_df) == n_runs * cfg.epochs
assert len(stage_b_gradient_df) == n_runs * cfg.epochs * stage_b_depth
assert len(stage_b_weights_df) == n_runs * cfg.epochs
assert len(stage_b_run_df) == n_runs

assert not stage_b_history_df.duplicated(["activation", "seed", "epoch"]).any()
assert not stage_b_gradient_df.duplicated(["activation", "seed", "epoch", "layer"]).any()
assert not stage_b_weights_df.duplicated(["activation", "seed", "epoch"]).any()

# Verify complete epoch/layer coverage and the original fixed gradient-recording protocol.
expected_epochs = set(range(1, cfg.epochs + 1))
expected_layers = set(range(1, stage_b_depth + 1))

for _, group in stage_b_history_df.groupby(["activation", "seed"]):
    assert set(group["epoch"]) == expected_epochs     # Every run must contain epochs 1–20.

for _, group in stage_b_gradient_df.groupby(["activation", "seed", "epoch"]):
    assert set(group["layer"]) == expected_layers     # Each epoch must contain hidden layers 1–5.

assert (stage_b_gradient_df["batches"] == 10).all()    # Every epoch-level RMS mean uses 10 batches.

# Reject non-finite measurements while allowing very small or exactly zero gradient magnitudes.
history_metrics = ["train_loss", "val_loss", "val_accuracy", "val_macro_f1"]

assert np.isfinite(stage_b_history_df[history_metrics].to_numpy()).all()
assert np.isfinite(stage_b_gradient_df["mean_grad_rms"].to_numpy()).all()
assert np.isfinite(stage_b_weights_df["first_layer_weight_change"].to_numpy()).all()
assert np.isfinite(stage_b_run_df["first_to_last_gradient_ratio"].to_numpy()).all()

assert (stage_b_gradient_df["mean_grad_rms"] >= 0).all()             # RMS magnitudes cannot be negative.
assert (stage_b_weights_df["first_layer_weight_change"] >= 0).all()  # Normalized displacement is nonnegative.


# Aggregate the principal metrics across three seeds for each activation.
# Pandas std() uses sample standard deviation (ddof=1) by default.
stage_b_summary_df = (
    stage_b_run_df.groupby("activation", as_index=False, sort=False)
    .agg(
        n_seeds=("seed", "nunique"),                           # Number of independent seeds.

        seeds_reached_threshold=("reached_threshold", "sum"),  # Number reaching loss <= 1.50.

        train_loss_mean=("train_loss", "mean"),                # Mean final training loss.
        train_loss_std=("train_loss", "std"),                  # Variation across seeds.

        val_loss_mean=("val_loss", "mean"),                    # Mean final validation loss.
        val_loss_std=("val_loss", "std"),

        val_accuracy_mean=("val_accuracy", "mean"),            # Mean validation accuracy.
        val_accuracy_std=("val_accuracy", "std"),

        val_macro_f1_mean=("val_macro_f1", "mean"),            # Mean validation macro-F1.
        val_macro_f1_std=("val_macro_f1", "std"),

        grad_rms_l1_epoch1_mean=("grad_rms_l1_epoch1", "mean"), # Mean early RMS gradient at Hidden Layer 1.
        grad_rms_l1_epoch1_std=("grad_rms_l1_epoch1", "std"),

        first_to_last_gradient_ratio_mean=("first_to_last_gradient_ratio", "mean"),  # Mean of per-run ratios.
        first_to_last_gradient_ratio_std=("first_to_last_gradient_ratio", "std"),

        weight_change_l1_final_mean=("weight_change_l1_final", "mean"),  # Mean final relative W1 displacement.
        weight_change_l1_final_std=("weight_change_l1_final", "std"),

        epochs_to_threshold_mean=("epochs_to_threshold", "mean"),  # Mean among runs reaching the threshold.
        epochs_to_threshold_std=("epochs_to_threshold", "std")     # NaN if fewer than 2 runs reached it.
    )
)

assert len(stage_b_summary_df) == len(stage_b_activations)
assert (stage_b_summary_df["n_seeds"] == len(stage_b_seeds)).all()
assert stage_b_summary_df["seeds_reached_threshold"].between(0, len(stage_b_seeds)).all()


# Save the complete run records and compact CSV summaries, following the Stage A results structure.
stage_b_output_dir = Path(cfg.results_dir) / "stage_b"
stage_b_output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

torch.save(stage_b_runs, stage_b_output_dir / "stage_b_runs.pt")  # Preserve all histories and recorder outputs.
stage_b_run_df.to_csv(stage_b_output_dir / "stage_b_run_summary.csv", index=False)
stage_b_summary_df.to_csv(stage_b_output_dir / "stage_b_summary.csv", index=False)


# Report the organized record counts, then display the full-precision data in readable tables.
print("\n=== Stage B Organized Results ===")
print(f"Training/validation history: {len(stage_b_history_df)} rows")
print(f"Layer-wise RMS gradients: {len(stage_b_gradient_df)} rows")
print(f"First-layer weight changes: {len(stage_b_weights_df)} rows")
print(f"Per-run summaries: {len(stage_b_run_df)} rows")
print(f"Activation-level summaries: {len(stage_b_summary_df)} rows")

# Use four significant digits for display only; the DataFrames retain full numerical precision.
with pd.option_context("display.float_format", lambda value: f"{value:.4g}"):
    print("\n=== Stage B Per-Run Results ===")
    display(stage_b_run_df)

    print("\n=== Stage B Multi-Seed Summary (Mean ± Sample SD) ===")
    display(stage_b_summary_df)

print(f"\nResults saved to: {stage_b_output_dir}")
