7.5 - Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation & Data Verification:

Stage B results were successfully organized and aggregated without additional model training.

The completed dataset contains:

  • 9 training runs: 3 activation functions × 3 random seeds.
  • 180 epoch-history records: Training and validation measurements across 20 epochs.
  • 900 layer-wise gradient records: Five hidden-layer RMS gradient measurements per epoch.
  • 180 first-layer weight-change records: Cumulative normalized weight displacement after each epoch.
  • 9 per-run summaries: One for each activation–seed combination.
  • 3 activation-level summaries: Mean and sample standard deviation across three seeds.

The expected activation–seed combinations, epoch and layer coverage, gradient-recording batch counts, and numerical measurements passed the implemented validation checks.

The complete Stage B results and summary tables were saved to results/stage_b.

Results — Multi-Seed Activation Comparison:

All three seeds reached the predefined training-loss threshold for each activation. Statistics were calculated from the original full-precision run records using sample standard deviation (ddof = 1).

Preliminary Observations:

1. Sigmoid exhibited substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation.

  • Sigmoid's mean first-to-last RMS gradient ratio was approximately 0.006369 (0.64%).
  • Tanh and ReLU achieved ratios of approximately 0.474989 (47.50%) and 0.495396 (49.54%), respectively.
  • The mean ratio was approximately 74.6 times higher for Tanh and 77.8 times higher for ReLU relative to Sigmoid.
  • The difference between Sigmoid and the other activations was consistently observed across all three seeds.

These results indicate substantially less relative attenuation between the first and last hidden-layer weight gradients for Tanh and ReLU at epoch 1.

2. Tanh and ReLU also exhibited much larger absolute first-layer gradients.

  • Sigmoid: 8.823e-6.
  • Tanh: 0.003338.
  • ReLU: 0.001991.

The mean first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 378 times larger for Tanh and 226 times larger for ReLU than for Sigmoid.

Although ReLU had a slightly higher relative gradient ratio than Tanh, Tanh had a larger absolute first-layer RMS gradient.

Therefore, absolute gradient magnitude and relative gradient attenuation must be interpreted as complementary measurements rather than interchangeable quantities.

3. Early-layer parameter displacement differed substantially across activations.

The mean final normalized first-layer weight changes were:

  • Sigmoid: 0.108987.
  • Tanh: 0.398082.
  • ReLU: 0.403325.

Tanh and ReLU exhibited approximately 3.65 and 3.70 times the cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement observed with Sigmoid.

This indicates that the first hidden-layer weight matrices moved substantially farther from initialization under Tanh and ReLU.

The metric measures net parameter displacement relative to initialization, not the total magnitude of all SGD updates or the amount of useful representation learning.

4. Tanh and ReLU reached the training-loss threshold substantially earlier.

  • Sigmoid reached the predefined training-loss threshold in 14–15 epochs.
  • Tanh and ReLU reached the same threshold by the end of epoch 1 in all three seeds.
  • Final training losses were also substantially lower for Tanh and ReLU.

This demonstrates faster attainment of the predefined optimization milestone under Tanh and ReLU.

However, reaching a training loss of 1.50 does not imply complete convergence. The threshold does not distinguish the subsequent learning speeds of Tanh and ReLU because both had already reached it during the first epoch.

5. Tanh achieved the strongest observed validation performance.

The mean validation accuracies were:

  • Sigmoid: 46.63%.
  • Tanh: 86.21%.
  • ReLU: 81.70%.

Mean validation macro-F1 followed the same ordering:

  • Sigmoid: 0.3377.
  • Tanh: 0.8441.
  • ReLU: 0.7946.

Tanh also achieved the lowest mean validation loss (0.4301).

These findings indicate that Tanh produced the strongest observed validation performance among the tested activation functions under the fixed experimental conditions.

6. Gradient propagation and validation performance did not have identical rankings.

ReLU had a slightly higher mean first-to-last gradient ratio and final first-layer weight displacement than Tanh.

However, Tanh exhibited a larger absolute first-layer RMS gradient and achieved better validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1.

This distinction is important: stronger relative gradient propagation or greater parameter displacement does not automatically guarantee better classification performance.

Interpretation — H1: Depth Effect

H1 was investigated in Stage A by comparing D2, D5, D10, and D20 with Sigmoid fixed.

Stage B does not directly retest H1 because all activation conditions use D5.

Nevertheless, Stage B demonstrates that the severity of gradient attenuation at a fixed depth can differ substantially with activation choice.

The Stage A depth findings should therefore be interpreted within the Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration used in that experiment.

Interpretation — H2: Early-Layer Trainability

Stage A found that stronger early-layer gradient attenuation was associated with smaller first-layer weight displacement and slower training-loss reduction as network depth increased.

Stage B provides complementary evidence under a fixed depth:

  • Sigmoid exhibited much smaller first-layer gradients.
  • Sigmoid showed stronger relative gradient attenuation.
  • Sigmoid had smaller cumulative first-layer weight displacement.
  • Sigmoid reached the predefined loss threshold later and achieved higher final training loss.

These findings are consistent with the proposed relationship between gradient attenuation and reduced early-layer trainability.

However, activation choice influences several aspects of network behavior simultaneously. The observed associations do not establish gradient attenuation as the sole causal mechanism behind the optimization differences.

Interpretation — H3: Activation Effect

The results support a substantial activation-dependent difference in gradient propagation, early-layer weight displacement, optimization, and validation performance at the selected D5 depth.

Under common Xavier Uniform initialization and SGD settings, both Tanh and ReLU exhibited considerably less first-to-last gradient attenuation than Sigmoid.

ReLU showed a slightly higher mean relative gradient ratio than Tanh, consistent with the directional expectation of H3 at D5. However, the difference was modest and only three seeds were evaluated.

The experiment does not directly establish how activation differences change with increasing depth, because Stage B evaluates only one fixed depth.

The results therefore support the activation-effect component of H3 under the tested conditions, without establishing a general activation-by-depth relationship.

Limitations:

  • Only one dataset and one fixed network depth were used in Stage B.
  • Only three random seeds were evaluated.
  • All activations used Xavier Uniform initialization with gain = 1, which is not necessarily optimal for ReLU.
  • Gradient ratios were calculated from the first 10 training batches of epoch 1 and summarize relative weight-gradient magnitudes, not exact gradient-signal transmission.
  • Cumulative first-layer weight change measures net displacement from initialization rather than total SGD update magnitude.
  • The training-loss threshold is a predefined optimization milestone, not proof of complete convergence.
  • Activation saturation and dead-neuron diagnostics were not measured.
  • No statistical significance tests were performed, and the findings should not be generalized to all network architectures or training configurations.

Conclusion:

Section 7.5 successfully organized and aggregated the complete nine-run Stage B experiment.

The results provide consistent evidence that Sigmoid exhibits substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation, smaller first-layer weight displacement, slower training-loss reduction, and weaker validation performance than Tanh and ReLU under the tested D5 configuration.

Tanh achieved the strongest observed validation performance, while ReLU had a slightly higher mean relative gradient ratio and final normalized first-layer weight displacement.

Together, the measurements provide substantial evidence for activation-dependent differences relevant to H3 and complement the gradient-vanishing and trainability findings from Stage A.

All Stage B measurements are organized, aggregated, verified, and saved.

7.6 — Activation Effects on Gradient Propagation & Trainability¶

Objective:

Compare how Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU affect gradient propagation, early-layer weight displacement, training-loss convergence, and validation performance in the fixed D5 MLP.

Use the completed three-seed Stage B measurements to examine the relationships between activation choice, gradient attenuation, and trainability under the common Xavier Uniform initialization and SGD training protocol.

Procedure:

  1. Compare layer-wise gradient propagation at epoch 1:

    • Reuse stage_b_gradient_df from Section 7.5.
    • Examine the absolute RMS weight gradients across all five hidden layers.
    • Normalize each hidden-layer RMS gradient by the RMS gradient of Hidden Layer 5 within the same activation–seed run.
    • Calculate mean ± sample standard deviation across three seeds for each activation and hidden layer.
    • Compare the resulting absolute and relative gradient profiles.

  2. Examine gradient evolution during training:

    • Reuse the recorded epoch-level gradient measurements from all 20 epochs.
    • Track the first hidden layer's RMS gradient across epochs.
    • Track the first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratio across epochs.
    • Calculate mean ± sample standard deviation across seeds at each epoch.
    • Examine whether the early-layer attenuation observed at epoch 1 persists or changes during training.

  3. Compare early-layer trainability:

    • Reuse stage_b_weights_df from Section 7.5.
    • Examine the cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement relative to initialization.
    • Compare how the recorded displacement evolves during training.
    • Use the final normalized weight-change measurements from stage_b_summary_df to summarize the three-seed comparison.

  4. Compare training-loss convergence:

    • Reuse stage_b_history_df and stage_b_summary_df.
    • Examine training-loss trajectories throughout the fixed 20-epoch budget.
    • Compare final training losses and the number of epochs needed to reach the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.
    • Distinguish threshold attainment from complete convergence.

  5. Compare validation performance:

    • Examine validation loss, validation accuracy, and macro-F1 across the three activation functions.
    • Compare final mean ± sample standard deviation across three seeds.
    • Evaluate whether differences in validation performance correspond to the observed differences in gradient propagation and first-layer weight displacement.

  6. Verify and present the comparison:

    • Preserve the individual activation–seed measurements before aggregation.
    • Create stage_b_layer_profile_df for the epoch-1 layer-wise gradient comparison.
    • Create stage_b_dynamics_df for the 20-epoch training and gradient-dynamics comparison.
    • Check consistency between the new analysis views and the existing Section 7.5 summary.
    • Display the gradient profiles, selected training-epoch measurements, and principal multi-seed results.

Purpose:

Investigate activation-dependent differences using several complementary measurements instead of relying only on final validation accuracy.

Layer-wise RMS gradients measure the magnitude of weight-gradient signals associated with individual hidden layers.

First-to-last RMS gradient ratios quantify relative gradient attenuation within a network.

Cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes describe parameter displacement from initialization, while training-loss trajectories and epochs-to-threshold describe optimization progress.

Validation loss, accuracy, and macro-F1 provide additional evidence about classification performance on held-out data.

Together, these measurements support an evidence-based analysis of activation-dependent gradient propagation and trainability.

Expected Results:

Based on the aggregated results from Section 7.5:

  • Sigmoid is expected to exhibit substantially smaller early-layer RMS gradients and stronger relative gradient attenuation than Tanh and ReLU.
  • Tanh and ReLU are expected to show larger cumulative first-layer weight displacement than Sigmoid.
  • Tanh and ReLU are expected to reach the predefined training-loss threshold earlier and achieve lower final training losses.
  • Tanh is expected to show the strongest observed final validation accuracy and macro-F1 among the three activations.
  • ReLU is expected to show a slightly higher mean first-to-last gradient ratio than Tanh at epoch 1, while Tanh shows a larger absolute first-layer RMS gradient.

These are expectations based on the completed Stage B measurements, not assumptions about universal activation-function performance.

The gradient-evolution analysis will determine whether the epoch-1 patterns persist throughout training.

Role in the Experiment:

This section completes the quantitative activation-function comparison.

It extends the single-run and multi-seed results from Sections 7.3–7.5 into a coordinated analysis of gradient propagation, parameter displacement, convergence, and classification performance.

The comparisons provide the experimental evidence needed to evaluate H3 — Activation Effect in Section 7.7.

Connection to H1, H2, and H3:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Not directly retested because network depth remains fixed at D5. The results provide context for interpreting the depth-dependent findings from Stage A.
  • H2 — Early-Layer Trainability: Examines whether activation conditions with stronger early-layer gradient attenuation also show smaller first-layer weight displacement and slower optimization progress.
  • H3 — Activation Effect: Compares the three activation functions under the same initialization and training configuration to evaluate differences in gradient attenuation and trainability.

Notes:

This section reuses only the measurements and metrics already defined in Parts 3–5 and organized in Section 7.5.

It does not introduce additional training runs, network architectures, activation functions, initialization methods, optimizers, learning-rate experiments, mechanism diagnostics, or new report figures.

The quantitative findings will be interpreted and synthesized in Section 7.7.

# Verify that the completed Stage B measurements are available for analysis.
assert len(stage_b_run_df) == len(stage_b_activations) * len(stage_b_seeds)
assert len(stage_b_summary_df) == len(stage_b_activations)
assert len(stage_b_history_df) == len(stage_b_run_df) * cfg.epochs
assert len(stage_b_gradient_df) == len(stage_b_run_df) * cfg.epochs * stage_b_depth
assert len(stage_b_weights_df) == len(stage_b_run_df) * cfg.epochs

print("=== Section 7.6 — Activation Effects on Gradient Propagation & Trainability ===")
print(f"Fixed depth: D{stage_b_depth}")
print(f"Activations: {stage_b_activations}")
print(f"Random seeds: {stage_b_seeds}")
print("Analysis: Gradient propagation, gradient evolution, weight changes, and convergence")


# Normalize each layer's recorded RMS gradient by the last hidden layer of the same run and epoch.
# This preserves the per-run normalization used in Stage A before averaging across seeds.
last_layer_gradients = stage_b_gradient_df.loc[
    stage_b_gradient_df["layer"] == stage_b_depth,
    ["activation", "seed", "epoch", "mean_grad_rms"]
].rename(
    columns={"mean_grad_rms": "last_layer_grad_rms"}
)

assert (last_layer_gradients["last_layer_grad_rms"] > 0).all()  # Avoid division by zero.

relative_gradients = stage_b_gradient_df.merge(
    last_layer_gradients,
    on=["activation", "seed", "epoch"],                 # Match the same run and training epoch.
    validate="many_to_one"                             # Five hidden layers share one last-layer reference.
)

relative_gradients["relative_grad_rms"] = (
    relative_gradients["mean_grad_rms"]
    / relative_gradients["last_layer_grad_rms"]        # Relative RMS = RMS(layer) / RMS(last hidden layer).
)


# Compare absolute and relative gradients across the five hidden layers at epoch 1.
# Aggregate each hidden-layer measurement across the three random seeds.
stage_b_layer_profile_df = (
    relative_gradients.loc[relative_gradients["epoch"] == 1]
    .groupby(["activation", "layer"], as_index=False, sort=False)
    .agg(
        grad_rms_mean=("mean_grad_rms", "mean"),        # Mean absolute RMS weight gradient.
        grad_rms_std=("mean_grad_rms", "std"),          # Sample SD across three seeds.
        relative_grad_rms_mean=("relative_grad_rms", "mean"), # Mean relative to last hidden layer.
        relative_grad_rms_std=("relative_grad_rms", "std")
    )
)

assert len(stage_b_layer_profile_df) == len(stage_b_activations) * stage_b_depth


# Extract the first-layer gradient magnitude and attenuation ratio at every epoch.
# These records allow gradient evolution to be compared throughout the 20-epoch training budget.
first_layer_gradients = relative_gradients.loc[
    relative_gradients["layer"] == 1,
    ["activation", "seed", "epoch", "mean_grad_rms", "relative_grad_rms"]
].rename(
    columns={
        "mean_grad_rms": "grad_rms_l1",                 # First hidden-layer RMS gradient at each epoch.
        "relative_grad_rms": "gradient_ratio"          # First-to-last RMS gradient ratio at each epoch.
    }
)


# Combine the already recorded gradients, weight changes, and training histories.
# Each merge matches the same activation, random seed, and epoch without changing measurements.
stage_b_epoch_records = stage_b_history_df.merge(
    stage_b_weights_df,
    on=["activation", "seed", "epoch"],
    validate="one_to_one"                             # Each run has one weight-change record per epoch.
).merge(
    first_layer_gradients,
    on=["activation", "seed", "epoch"],
    validate="one_to_one"                             # Each run has one first-layer gradient record per epoch.
)

assert len(stage_b_epoch_records) == len(stage_b_history_df)


# Aggregate gradient evolution, weight displacement, loss, and validation performance by epoch.
# Keep both the mean and sample SD so comparisons do not depend on a single random seed.
stage_b_dynamics_df = (
    stage_b_epoch_records
    .groupby(["activation", "epoch"], as_index=False, sort=False)
    .agg(
        grad_rms_l1_mean=("grad_rms_l1", "mean"),       # First-layer RMS gradient over training.
        grad_rms_l1_std=("grad_rms_l1", "std"),

        gradient_ratio_mean=("gradient_ratio", "mean"), # First-to-last gradient attenuation over training.
        gradient_ratio_std=("gradient_ratio", "std"),

        weight_change_l1_mean=("first_layer_weight_change", "mean"), # Cumulative W1 displacement.
        weight_change_l1_std=("first_layer_weight_change", "std"),

        train_loss_mean=("train_loss", "mean"),        # Mean training-loss trajectory.
        train_loss_std=("train_loss", "std"),

        val_loss_mean=("val_loss", "mean"),            # Mean validation-loss trajectory.
        val_loss_std=("val_loss", "std"),

        val_accuracy_mean=("val_accuracy", "mean"),    # Validation accuracy across seeds.
        val_accuracy_std=("val_accuracy", "std"),

        val_macro_f1_mean=("val_macro_f1", "mean"),    # Validation macro-F1 across seeds.
        val_macro_f1_std=("val_macro_f1", "std")
    )
)

assert len(stage_b_dynamics_df) == len(stage_b_activations) * cfg.epochs


# Confirm that the new analysis views agree with the independent run summaries from Section 7.5.

for activation in stage_b_activations:

    summary = stage_b_summary_df.loc[

    ].iloc[0]                                        # The existing three-seed summary for this activation.

    first_epoch = stage_b_dynamics_df.loc[

    ].iloc[0]                                        # Measurements averaged across seeds at epoch 1.

    final_epoch = stage_b_dynamics_df.loc[

        & (stage_b_dynamics_df["epoch"] == cfg.epochs)
    ].iloc[0]                                        # Measurements averaged across seeds at epoch 20.

    assert np.isclose(
        first_epoch["grad_rms_l1_mean"],

    )                                                # Epoch-1 first-layer RMS must match Section 7.5.

    assert np.isclose(
        first_epoch["gradient_ratio_mean"],
        summary["first_to_last_gradient_ratio_mean"]

    assert np.isclose(

7.6 - Results, Preliminary Observations & Interpretation¶

Implementation & Verification:

The activation-function comparison was completed successfully using the existing Stage B measurements, without additional model training or gradient computation.

Two analysis-ready DataFrames were created:

  • stage_b_layer_profile_df: 15 records (3 activations × 5 hidden layers), containing absolute and last-layer-normalized RMS gradients at epoch 1, summarized across three seeds.
  • stage_b_dynamics_df: 60 records (3 activations × 20 epochs), containing mean ± sample standard deviation for gradient RMS, gradient ratios, cumulative first-layer weight changes, training/validation losses, validation accuracy, and macro-F1.

A compact snapshot of epochs 1, 5, 10, and 20 was displayed to examine representative stages of training without generating additional figures.

The consistency checks confirmed that the epoch-1 gradient measurements and final-epoch training/validation metrics agreed with the independent summaries from Section 7.5.

Results — Layer-Wise Gradient Propagation (Epoch 1):

The table below reports mean RMS gradients normalized by the last hidden layer within each activation–seed run, followed by averaging across three seeds.

Hidden Layer Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 — First 0.006369 0.4750 0.4954
2 0.01569 0.6773 0.7505
3 0.05673 0.7342 0.8134
4 0.2400 0.8581 0.8931
5 — Last 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000

The final hidden layer has a normalized value of 1 by definition.

Preliminary Observation 1 — Sigmoid exhibited substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation.

At epoch 1, the mean relative RMS gradients decreased sharply toward the input under Sigmoid.

The first hidden-layer RMS gradient was approximately 0.64% of the last hidden-layer RMS gradient.

In comparison:

  • Tanh: approximately 47.50%.
  • ReLU: approximately 49.54%.

The layer-wise profiles show that this difference is not restricted to the first hidden layer. Sigmoid exhibited substantially lower relative gradient magnitudes throughout the earlier hidden layers.

Tanh and ReLU displayed more moderate attenuation across the five-layer network.

These measurements provide direct evidence of activation-dependent differences in gradient propagation under the fixed D5 configuration.

Preliminary Observation 2 — Absolute gradient magnitudes also differed substantially.

At epoch 1, the mean first-layer RMS gradients were:

  • Sigmoid: 8.823e-6.
  • Tanh: 0.003338.
  • ReLU: 0.001991.

The Tanh and ReLU first-layer RMS gradients were approximately 378 and 226 times larger than Sigmoid's, respectively.

Tanh had the larger absolute first-layer gradient, whereas ReLU had the slightly higher relative first-to-last gradient ratio.

This distinction indicates that absolute gradient magnitude and relative gradient attenuation describe related but different properties of gradient propagation.

Results — Gradient Evolution During Training:

The mean first-to-last gradient ratios across three seeds changed as follows:

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 0.006369 0.4750 0.4954
5 0.007930 1.053 1.194
10 0.02637 1.234 1.283
20 0.4069 1.574 1.653

Preliminary Observation 3 — Gradient attenuation was not constant throughout training.

Sigmoid showed extremely strong first-to-last gradient attenuation during early training.

Its relative gradient ratio increased from approximately 0.006369 at epoch 1 to 0.4069 at epoch 20.

This indicates that the relative early-layer gradient magnitude increased substantially as training progressed, although it remained lower than the corresponding last-layer gradient at the final epoch.

Tanh and ReLU showed ratios above 1 at later epochs, indicating that their first hidden-layer RMS gradients exceeded those of their last hidden layers in those epoch-level measurements.

A ratio above 1 does not independently indicate exploding gradients. It represents a relative comparison between two layers, and may increase because the first-layer gradient grows, the last-layer gradient decreases, or both.

The gradient-evolution results therefore need to be interpreted together with absolute gradient magnitudes and training-loss trajectories.

Results — Early-Layer Weight Displacement:

The mean cumulative normalized first-layer weight changes were:

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 0.002318 0.08846 0.08107
5 0.01285 0.2074 0.2046
10 0.04004 0.2889 0.2869
20 0.1090 0.3981 0.4033

Preliminary Observation 4 — Tanh and ReLU produced substantially larger early-layer parameter displacement.

Sigmoid exhibited very small first-layer weight displacement during the early training epochs.

At epoch 1, the mean normalized displacement was approximately 0.002318 for Sigmoid, compared with 0.08846 for Tanh and 0.08107 for ReLU.

By epoch 20, the values increased to:

  • Sigmoid: 0.1090.
  • Tanh: 0.3981.
  • ReLU: 0.4033.

These results show that the first-layer weights moved substantially farther from initialization under Tanh and ReLU.

The metric measures cumulative net displacement from initialization, not the total magnitude of all individual SGD updates or the quality of learned representations.

Results — Training-Loss Convergence:

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 2.034 1.214 1.310
5 2.020 0.5121 0.6149
10 1.986 0.3149 0.4151
20 1.2555 0.1934 0.1992

Preliminary Observation 5 — Tanh and ReLU achieved substantially faster training-loss reduction.

Sigmoid showed limited training-loss reduction during the first 10 epochs, with the mean loss remaining near 2.0.

In contrast, Tanh and ReLU achieved considerably lower training losses early in training and continued improving throughout the 20-epoch budget.

All three seeds using Tanh or ReLU reached the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50 by epoch 1.

Sigmoid reached the same threshold after approximately 14.67 ± 0.58 epochs.

These results indicate faster attainment of the predefined optimization milestone under Tanh and ReLU.

However, the threshold represents a fixed learning-progress milestone, not complete convergence.

Results — Validation Performance:

Mean validation accuracy across three seeds:

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 0.1587 0.6269 0.6433
5 0.1713 0.7321 0.7784
10 0.2255 0.8144 0.7917
20 0.4663 0.8621 0.8170

Final validation macro-F1:

  • Sigmoid: 0.3377.
  • Tanh: 0.8441.
  • ReLU: 0.7946.

Final mean validation loss:

  • Sigmoid: 1.2689.
  • Tanh: 0.4301.
  • ReLU: 0.6748.

Preliminary Observation 6 — Tanh achieved the strongest final validation performance.

ReLU achieved slightly higher mean validation accuracy than Tanh at epochs 1 and 5.

However, Tanh achieved higher accuracy at epochs 10 and 20.

At the final epoch, Tanh also obtained the highest macro-F1 and lowest validation loss.

These results show that the ranking of activation functions can change during training.

Moreover, ReLU had a slightly higher final first-to-last gradient ratio and normalized first-layer weight displacement than Tanh, but Tanh achieved stronger validation performance.

Therefore, relative gradient magnitude and cumulative parameter displacement do not uniquely determine classification performance.

Interpretation — H1: Depth Effect

H1 was tested in Stage A by varying network depth under the fixed Sigmoid activation.

Section 7.6 does not directly retest the depth hypothesis because all Stage B networks have five hidden layers.

However, the results demonstrate that gradient propagation at the same network depth can differ substantially depending on activation choice.

This provides important context for the Stage A findings: depth-related gradient attenuation should be interpreted within the activation function and training configuration used in the experiment.

Interpretation — H2: Early-Layer Trainability

The Stage A results associated stronger early-layer gradient attenuation with smaller first-layer weight changes and slower training-loss reduction as depth increased.

Section 7.6 provides complementary evidence at fixed depth.

Compared with Tanh and ReLU, Sigmoid exhibited:

  • Smaller absolute first-layer gradients.
  • Stronger relative gradient attenuation during early training.
  • Smaller cumulative first-layer weight displacement.
  • Slower training-loss reduction.
  • Weaker validation performance.

Together, these measurements are consistent with the proposed association between severe gradient attenuation and limited early-layer trainability.

However, activation functions influence forward representations and optimization dynamics as well as backward gradients. The observed differences do not establish gradient attenuation as the sole cause of the performance differences.

Interpretation — H3: Activation Effect

The Section 7.6 results provide substantial evidence for activation-dependent differences in gradient propagation and trainability under the fixed D5 + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration.

Both Tanh and ReLU exhibited substantially less early-layer attenuation than Sigmoid at epoch 1, together with larger first-layer weight displacement, faster training-loss reduction, and stronger validation performance.

ReLU showed slightly higher mean relative gradient ratios than Tanh at epoch 1 and the selected later epochs. However, Tanh showed larger absolute first-layer RMS gradients at epoch 1 and better final validation performance.

These observations support the activation-effect component of H3 in the tested setting.

Because Stage B uses only one fixed depth, the experiment does not establish how activation-dependent differences vary systematically with network depth.

Limitations & Interpretation Boundaries:

  • The analysis is limited to one dataset, one MLP depth, three activation functions, and three random seeds.
  • All activation functions use common Xavier Uniform initialization with gain = 1.
  • RMS weight-gradient magnitudes are summaries of parameter gradients, not direct measurements of every backpropagated signal.
  • A first-to-last gradient ratio above 1 does not by itself demonstrate exploding gradients.
  • Small gradients late in training do not necessarily indicate harmful gradient vanishing.
  • Cumulative normalized weight displacement does not measure total SGD update magnitude or representation quality.
  • The predefined loss threshold indicates attainment of a learning milestone, not complete optimization convergence.
  • No activation saturation, dead-neuron, or initialization-sensitivity experiments were performed.
  • The findings should not be generalized to all network architectures or training configurations.

Conclusion:

Section 7.6 completed the controlled multi-seed comparison of gradient propagation, early-layer trainability, convergence, and validation performance.

Sigmoid exhibited substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation and slower learning than Tanh and ReLU, particularly during early training.

Tanh and ReLU maintained larger early-layer gradients, produced greater first-layer parameter displacement, and achieved substantially better optimization and validation outcomes under the tested conditions.

Tanh achieved the strongest final validation performance, while ReLU exhibited slightly higher relative gradient ratios and final first-layer weight displacement.

The combined evidence supports meaningful activation-dependent differences relevant to H3, while demonstrating that gradient propagation, parameter displacement, and classification performance should be evaluated as complementary rather than interchangeable measurements.

Quantitative Stage B activation comparisons are available.

7.7 — Stage B Findings & Interpretation¶

Objective:

Synthesize the completed Stage B results and evaluate H3 — Activation Effect, using the controlled comparison of Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU in the D5 Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) trained on BloodMNIST.

Examine whether the observed differences in gradient propagation are accompanied by differences in early-layer parameter displacement, training-loss convergence, and validation performance.

Distinguish findings directly supported by the experimental measurements from interpretations and limitations that require further investigation.

Procedure:

  1. Review the completed Stage B measurements:

    • Use the nine completed activation–seed runs from Sections 7.3–7.4.
    • Reuse the multi-seed summaries from Section 7.5.
    • Review the layer-wise gradient profiles and training dynamics from Section 7.6.
    • Do not conduct additional training or calculations.

  2. Evaluate gradient propagation:

    • Compare absolute RMS weight gradients across the five hidden layers.
    • Compare first-to-last hidden-layer gradient ratios.
    • Examine how early-layer gradients and relative attenuation change during training.
    • Identify which activation conditions exhibit more severe early-layer gradient attenuation.

  3. Evaluate early-layer trainability:

    • Compare cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement.
    • Examine whether conditions with stronger gradient attenuation also show smaller parameter displacement.
    • Consider the relationship between gradient measurements and optimization progress.

  4. Evaluate convergence and classification performance:

    • Compare training-loss trajectories and final training losses.
    • Compare epochs-to-threshold using the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50.
    • Compare validation loss, validation accuracy, and macro-F1.
    • Examine whether the activation with the strongest relative gradient propagation also achieves the strongest validation performance.

  5. Evaluate H3 and connect Stage B to Stage A:

    • Determine which aspects of H3 are supported by the controlled activation comparison.
    • Explain how the Stage B observations complement the depth-dependent gradient-vanishing findings from Stage A.
    • Identify which conclusions cannot be established from a single fixed network depth and common initialization scheme.

  6. Document limitations and conclude Stage B:

    • Summarize the principal findings.
    • Discuss experimental and measurement limitations.
    • State the conclusion within the tested configuration without claiming universal activation superiority.

Purpose:

Provide an evidence-based interpretation of the activation-function experiment rather than relying on a single performance metric.

The central goal is to understand how activation choice relates to gradient propagation and early-layer trainability, and whether differences in these measurements correspond to differences in optimization and classification performance.

Expected Results:

Based on the completed analyses in Sections 7.5–7.6:

  • Sigmoid is expected to exhibit substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation than Tanh and ReLU, especially during early training.
  • Tanh and ReLU are expected to show larger cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement.
  • Tanh and ReLU are expected to demonstrate faster training-loss reduction and earlier attainment of the predefined loss threshold.
  • Tanh is expected to achieve the strongest observed final validation performance.
  • ReLU is expected to exhibit a slightly higher relative first-to-last gradient ratio than Tanh, although the difference is modest.
  • Gradient propagation, parameter displacement, and validation performance are not expected to have identical rankings across activation functions.

The interpretation must remain limited to the tested D5 + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration.

Role in the Experiment:

This section completes and concludes Part 7.

Stage A investigated the effect of increasing network depth under a fixed Sigmoid activation.

Stage B investigated the effect of changing the activation function while holding network depth and the remaining training conditions fixed.

Together, the two stages examine complementary aspects of gradient vanishing and early-layer trainability.

The resulting findings will be integrated into the final project report in Part 8.

7.7.1 — Summary of the Experimental Evidence¶

Controlled Configuration:

Principal Results — Mean ± Sample SD Across Three Seeds:

First-layer RMS gradient, epoch 1 8.823e-6 ± 7.251e-7 0.003338 ± 0.000107 0.001991 ± 0.000266
First-to-last gradient ratio, epoch 1 0.006369 ± 0.001129 0.474989 ± 0.037617 0.495396 ± 0.021509

7.7.2 — Finding 1: Activation Choice Substantially Affected Gradient Propagation¶

Primary observation:

Sigmoid exhibited much stronger early-layer gradient attenuation than Tanh and ReLU.

At epoch 1, the first-to-last hidden-layer RMS gradient ratios were:

  • Sigmoid: 0.006369.
  • Tanh: 0.474989.
  • ReLU: 0.495396.

These correspond to first-layer RMS gradients of approximately 0.64%, 47.50%, and 49.54% of the respective last-layer RMS gradients.

The relative ratios for Tanh and ReLU were approximately 74.6 and 77.8 times the Sigmoid ratio.

The absolute first-layer RMS gradients also differed substantially:

  • Tanh's mean first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 378 times that of Sigmoid.
  • ReLU's mean first-layer RMS gradient was approximately 226 times that of Sigmoid.

The layer-wise results from Section 7.6 showed that Sigmoid's strong relative attenuation extended across multiple early hidden layers rather than occurring only at Hidden Layer 1.

Interpretation:

Under the fixed D5 configuration, Tanh and ReLU maintained substantially larger early-layer weight-gradient magnitudes than Sigmoid during early training.

This finding is consistent with the theoretical expectation that activation derivatives influence gradient propagation during backpropagation.

Sigmoid derivatives are bounded above by 0.25 and can become much smaller in saturated regions. Repeated derivative multiplication may contribute to attenuation in deep networks.

Tanh and ReLU exhibit different derivative behavior, which can produce different gradient propagation patterns.

However, the experiment did not directly measure activation saturation or isolate the contribution of individual derivative terms. These mechanisms are therefore theoretical explanations consistent with the observations, not independently verified causal mechanisms.

7.7.3 — Finding 2: Gradient Attenuation Changed During Training¶

Primary observation:

The first-to-last gradient ratios evolved throughout the 20-epoch training period.

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 0.006369 0.4750 0.4954
5 0.007930 1.053 1.194
10 0.02637 1.234 1.283
20 0.4069 1.574 1.653

Sigmoid exhibited severe relative attenuation during early training, followed by a substantial increase in its first-to-last gradient ratio.

Tanh and ReLU also showed increasing ratios, exceeding 1 at the selected later epochs.

Interpretation:

Gradient propagation is dynamic rather than constant throughout training.

The increase in Sigmoid's ratio indicates that its first-layer RMS gradient became larger relative to its last-layer RMS gradient over time.

However, an increasing ratio does not necessarily indicate that absolute gradients are increasing.

Likewise, a ratio above 1 does not independently demonstrate exploding gradients. It indicates that the first-layer RMS gradient exceeds the last-layer RMS gradient within the normalized comparison.

These results emphasize the importance of interpreting relative gradient ratios alongside absolute gradient magnitudes and training-loss trajectories.

The early-training gradient measurements are particularly informative because Sigmoid initially exhibited very small early-layer gradients while its training loss remained high.

7.7.4 — Finding 3: Activation Choice Was Associated with Early-Layer Parameter Displacement¶

Primary observation:

The cumulative normalized first-layer weight displacement differed substantially across activation conditions.

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 0.002318 0.08846 0.08107
5 0.01285 0.2074 0.2046
10 0.04004 0.2889 0.2869
20 0.1090 0.3981 0.4033

At epoch 20:

  • Tanh exhibited approximately 3.65 times the normalized first-layer displacement of Sigmoid.
  • ReLU exhibited approximately 3.70 times the normalized first-layer displacement of Sigmoid.

Interpretation:

The first hidden-layer weights moved substantially farther from their initialization under Tanh and ReLU than under Sigmoid.

These differences are consistent with the larger early-layer gradients observed under Tanh and ReLU.

Under plain SGD, each individual weight update is proportional to the corresponding gradient and the fixed learning rate.

Nevertheless, the cumulative normalized weight-change metric represents net parameter displacement from initialization.

It does not measure the total magnitude of all updates, the fraction of weights that changed, or the quality of learned representations.

The results support an association between gradient attenuation and early-layer parameter displacement, without establishing gradient attenuation as the sole cause of the observed optimization differences.

7.7.5 — Finding 4: Activation Choice Substantially Affected Optimization Progress¶

Primary observation:

Tanh and ReLU achieved much faster training-loss reduction than Sigmoid.

Mean training losses at selected epochs were:

Epoch Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
1 2.034 1.214 1.310
5 2.020 0.5121 0.6149
10 1.986 0.3149 0.4151
20 1.2555 0.1934 0.1992

The predefined training-loss threshold was 1.50.

All Tanh and ReLU runs reached this threshold by epoch 1, whereas Sigmoid reached it in epochs 14–15.

The mean epochs-to-threshold were:

  • Sigmoid: 14.67 ± 0.58.
  • Tanh: 1.00 ± 0.00.
  • ReLU: 1.00 ± 0.00.

Interpretation:

Tanh and ReLU demonstrated substantially faster initial optimization progress than Sigmoid under the fixed SGD training protocol.

These observations are consistent with their larger early-layer gradients and greater first-layer weight displacement.

However, epochs-to-threshold measures attainment of a predefined learning milestone, not complete optimization convergence.

Because Tanh and ReLU both reached the threshold during the first epoch, this metric cannot distinguish their subsequent convergence behavior.

Their complete training-loss trajectories and final losses provide additional information.

7.7.6 — Finding 5: Gradient Propagation and Validation Performance Had Different Rankings¶

Primary observation:

At the final epoch, mean validation performance was:

Metric Sigmoid Tanh ReLU
Validation loss 1.2689 0.4301 0.6748
Validation accuracy 46.63% 86.21% 81.70%
Validation macro-F1 0.3377 0.8441 0.7946

Tanh achieved the lowest final validation loss and the highest validation accuracy and macro-F1.

However, ReLU exhibited a slightly higher mean first-to-last gradient ratio and final normalized first-layer weight displacement than Tanh.

In addition, ReLU had higher mean validation accuracy at epochs 1 and 5, while Tanh performed better at epochs 10 and 20.

Interpretation:

The activation with the highest relative gradient ratio did not achieve the strongest final validation performance.

This shows that relative gradient propagation and parameter displacement are not interchangeable with classification performance.

Activation functions affect forward representations and the optimization trajectory as well as the gradients calculated during backpropagation.

Better relative gradient preservation may support optimization, but it does not guarantee superior generalization.

The observed Tanh advantage in final validation performance should be interpreted within the tested training configuration and three random seeds.

7.7.7 — Evaluation of H3: Activation Effect¶

H3 — Activation Effect:

Under a common controlled initialization, Sigmoid and Tanh may show stronger depth-dependent gradient attenuation than ReLU; the magnitude of this difference may depend on initialization.

Evidence supporting H3:

  1. The three activation functions exhibited substantially different layer-wise RMS gradient profiles under the same D5 architecture.
  2. Sigmoid exhibited much stronger early-layer gradient attenuation than both Tanh and ReLU.
  3. ReLU showed slightly higher mean first-to-last gradient ratios than Tanh at epoch 1 and the selected later epochs.
  4. Tanh and ReLU produced substantially larger first-layer weight displacement than Sigmoid.
  5. Tanh and ReLU achieved much faster training-loss reduction and stronger validation performance than Sigmoid.
  6. The major Sigmoid-versus-Tanh/ReLU differences were consistent across the three random seeds.

Evidence boundaries:

  • The activation-function comparison was conducted at only one fixed network depth, D5.
  • Therefore, the experiment directly evaluates activation-dependent gradient differences at D5, not how those differences vary systematically as depth increases.
  • All activation conditions used the same Xavier Uniform initialization.
  • The experiment does not evaluate whether changing initialization alters the magnitude or ordering of activation effects.
  • The ReLU-versus-Tanh difference in relative gradient ratio was modest compared with the much larger difference between Sigmoid and the other activations.
  • The small seed set does not support a general statistical claim that ReLU consistently provides better gradient propagation than Tanh across other configurations.

H3 Assessment: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED AS ORIGINALLY FORMULATED.

The experiment provides substantial empirical support for activation-dependent differences in gradient attenuation, early-layer weight displacement, optimization, and validation performance under the tested D5 configuration.

The especially strong attenuation observed with Sigmoid relative to Tanh and ReLU supports the principal activation-effect finding.

However, the depth dependence of these differences and their sensitivity to initialization were not directly tested.

Therefore, the broader depth-dependent and initialization-related aspects of H3 remain unresolved.

This assessment does not weaken the validity of the controlled D5 comparison; it identifies the precise scope of the evidence collected.

7.7.8 — Connections to Stage A, H1, and H2¶

Connection to H1 — Depth Effect:

Stage A investigated increasing MLP depth under a fixed Sigmoid + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration.

It showed substantially stronger early-layer gradient attenuation as network depth increased from D2 to D20.

Stage B complements this result by demonstrating that gradient attenuation can also vary considerably with activation choice when network depth is fixed.

Together, these observations indicate that gradient propagation depends on the network architecture and the specific training configuration.

Connection to H2 — Early-Layer Trainability:

Stage A found that stronger early-layer gradient attenuation was associated with smaller first-layer weight displacement and slower training-loss reduction across increasing network depths.

Stage B observed a similar association across activation conditions at D5.

Sigmoid exhibited stronger early-layer attenuation, smaller cumulative first-layer weight displacement, and slower training-loss reduction than Tanh and ReLU.

These results are consistent with the proposed relationship between gradient attenuation and early-layer trainability.

However, neither stage independently isolates gradient attenuation as the sole causal mechanism affecting learning.

Combined Interpretation:

Stage A and Stage B provide complementary evidence for the central research question.

Stage A shows how gradient attenuation and trainability vary with network depth under the Sigmoid baseline.

Stage B shows how activation choice affects gradient propagation and optimization at one selected depth under common initialization.

The combined findings support the importance of analyzing gradient measurements, early-layer parameter displacement, and learning dynamics together rather than relying solely on final classification accuracy.

7.7.9 — Limitations¶

The Stage B findings should be interpreted within the following limitations:

  1. Single dataset: Only BloodMNIST was evaluated. The results cannot automatically be generalized to other datasets or biomedical applications.

  2. Single fixed depth: Stage B evaluated activation functions only at D5. Activation-by-depth interactions were not directly tested.

  3. Architecture: The models were constant-width MLPs rather than CNNs, ResNets, Transformers, or GNNs.

  4. Common initialization: All activation functions used Xavier Uniform (gain = 1). This controlled the main comparison but did not necessarily provide optimal initialization for each activation.

  5. Fixed optimizer and learning rate: SGD with learning rate 0.1 was used throughout Stage B. Other optimization settings could produce different results.

  6. Limited training duration: Each run used 20 epochs. Longer training might change the observed convergence and performance differences.

  7. Three random seeds: Mean ± sample standard deviation summarizes the observed variability, but three seeds provide limited information about broader variability.

  8. Gradient measurements: Layer-wise RMS weight gradients and their ratios summarize parameter-gradient magnitudes. They do not fully characterize the propagation of all activation gradients or Jacobian transformations.

  9. Weight-change measurement: Cumulative normalized first-layer weight change measures displacement from initialization, not total SGD update magnitude or representation quality.

  10. No mechanism-specific diagnostics: Activation saturation, dead-neuron behavior, and initialization sensitivity were not directly measured because they were outside the agreed project scope.

  11. Validation-based evaluation: The reported comparisons use the validation split. They are not independent held-out test-set performance estimates.

These limitations identify the boundaries of the conclusions without requiring additional experiments within the current project.

7.7.10 — Stage B Conclusion¶

The controlled activation-function experiment demonstrated substantial differences in gradient propagation, early-layer parameter displacement, optimization, and validation performance across Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.

Under the fixed D5 + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration:

  • Sigmoid exhibited severe early-layer gradient attenuation during early training, smaller cumulative first-layer weight displacement, slower training-loss reduction, and weaker validation performance.
  • Tanh exhibited substantially larger early-layer gradients, faster optimization, greater parameter displacement, and the strongest observed final validation performance.
  • ReLU also exhibited substantially less gradient attenuation than Sigmoid, with slightly higher relative first-to-last gradient ratios and final normalized first-layer weight displacement than Tanh.

The results show that gradient propagation, cumulative parameter displacement, and classification performance are related but distinct aspects of network trainability.

The findings support an activation-dependent effect on gradient attenuation and learning behavior at D5.

However, they do not establish universal superiority of any activation function, activation-by-depth interactions, or sensitivity to alternative initialization methods.

Overall Stage B Assessment:

H3 is partially supported as originally formulated, with substantial evidence for activation-dependent differences under the tested conditions and unresolved broader claims about depth dependence and initialization sensitivity.

Stage B Status: COMPLETE

All nine Stage B runs have been trained, verified, organized, aggregated, and analyzed.

The completed results are ready for integration with Stage A in the final project report.

Part 8 — Final Analysis & Scientific Reporting¶

1. Overview & Research Objective¶

Part 8 integrates the completed Stage A and Stage B experiments to evaluate how network depth and activation choice are associated with gradient attenuation, early-layer trainability, and optimization behavior in MLPs trained on BloodMNIST.

The objective is to verify the experimental records, consolidate the principal figures and summary tables, and evaluate the three research hypotheses:

  • H1 — Depth Effect: Increasing network depth is expected to produce stronger relative attenuation of early-layer weight gradients.
  • H2 — Trainability Effect: Stronger gradient attenuation is expected to be associated with smaller first-layer weight displacement and slower training-loss reduction.
  • H3 — Activation Effect: Activation choice is expected to influence gradient propagation and trainability under controlled conditions.

The final analysis combines experimental measurements with the established theoretical background while distinguishing observed associations from unverified causal explanations.

2. Experimental Evidence & Reporting Protocol¶

Part 8 uses the results generated in Parts 6–7 under the experimental protocol finalized in Part 5.

Component Stage A — Network Depth Stage B — Activation Functions
Independent variable Network depth Hidden-layer activation
Experimental conditions D2, D5, D10, D20 Sigmoid, Tanh, ReLU
Fixed activation / depth Sigmoid D5
Initialization Xavier Uniform Xavier Uniform
Optimizer SGD, learning rate = 0.1 SGD, learning rate = 0.1
Training duration 20 epochs 20 epochs
Random seeds 0, 1, 2 0, 1, 2
Main hypotheses H1, H2 H3

Both stages use the same BloodMNIST preprocessing, gradient-measurement definitions, and training/validation protocol.

Experimental run accounting:

  • Stage A: 12 completed depth–seed runs.
  • Stage B: Nine activation–seed result entries, including three D5 + Sigmoid baseline runs reused from Stage A and six additional Tanh/ReLU runs.
  • Total: 18 unique main training runs, with 21 stage-level result entries.

Debugging and learning-rate pilot runs are excluded from the main experimental results.

Data sources: The final analysis reuses stage_a_runs, stage_b_runs, the corresponding numerical summary DataFrames, and the figures generated in Part 6. No additional training or gradient measurements are performed in Part 8.

Principal quantitative results are reported as mean ± sample standard deviation across three random seeds, where applicable.

4. Scientific Interpretation & Reporting Principles¶

The final analysis uses the measurement definitions established in Part 4 and the multi-seed summaries calculated in Parts 6–7.

Evidence Primary Role
Figure 1 — Gradient Magnitude vs. Layer Compare absolute and relative RMS weight-gradient magnitudes across network depths.
Figure 2 — Gradient Evolution During Training Examine layer-wise gradient behavior throughout D20 training.
Figure 3 — Training Loss vs. Epoch Compare optimization progress across D2, D5, D10, and D20.
Table 1A — Stage A Summary Consolidate depth-dependent gradient, weight-displacement, convergence, and validation results.
Table 1B — Stage B Summary Compare activation-dependent measurements at fixed D5 depth.

The following distinctions guide the interpretation:

  • RMS weight gradients summarize parameter-gradient magnitudes; they do not directly measure activation Jacobians or prove a specific gradient-attenuation mechanism.
  • Normalized first-layer weight displacement measures net parameter movement from initialization, not the sum of individual SGD updates.
  • Epochs-to-threshold measures attainment of a predefined training-loss milestone, not complete optimization convergence.
  • Validation accuracy and macro-F1 evaluate classification performance but do not independently establish the presence or absence of vanishing gradients.
  • Activation comparisons are restricted to D5 under the common Xavier Uniform initialization and SGD training protocol.

The study evaluates empirical associations among gradient attenuation, parameter displacement, and learning behavior. Causal interpretations and generalization beyond the tested experimental conditions require additional evidence.

5. Final Research Outputs¶

Part 8 consolidates the completed study into:

  • Three principal scientific figures with descriptive captions.
  • Two final summary tables reporting Stage A and Stage B results.
  • An integrated evaluation of H1, H2, and H3.
  • A discussion of methodological limitations and future research directions.
  • A final conclusion addressing the primary and secondary research questions.

The accompanying technical report presents the theoretical background, experimental methodology, quantitative results, and scientific interpretation in a standalone research format.

Objective:

Verify that the completed Stage A and Stage B experiments are complete, internally consistent, and ready for inclusion in the final technical report.

Confirm that all required depth–seed and activation–seed combinations were executed under the finalized experimental protocol, that the three-seed summaries are available, and that the D5 + Sigmoid baseline was correctly reused between the two stages.

This section performs a final experiment-level integrity check without retraining models or recalculating experimental measurements.

Procedure:

  1. Verify the finalized experimental configuration:

    • Confirm the three Stage B activations: Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.

    • Confirm the common random seeds: 0, 1, and 2.

  2. Verify the completeness of Stage A and Stage B:

    • Confirm 12 Stage A depth–seed combinations (4 depths × 3 seeds).
    • Confirm 9 Stage B activation–seed combinations (3 activations × 3 seeds).
    • Check that all expected combinations are present without missing or unexpected run keys.

  3. Verify the main-run configurations and measurement records:

    • Read the saved run_config for each completed run.
    • Confirm the expected depth, activation, seed, initialization, learning rate, batch size, optimizer settings, and training duration.
    • Confirm that max_batches=None, indicating full-dataset main training rather than a shortened debugging or pilot run.
    • Verify 20 epoch-history records per run.
    • Verify the first-100-step gradient records, layer-wise epoch-gradient records, and first-layer weight-change records.
    • Confirm that the existing epoch-level gradient protocol uses 10 sampled training batches per epoch.

  4. Verify the multi-seed summary tables:

    • Confirm that stage_a_summary_df contains four unique network depths.
    • Confirm that stage_b_summary_df contains three unique activation conditions.
    • Confirm exactly three completed seeds per experimental condition.
    • Reuse the previously calculated mean ± sample standard deviation without performing additional aggregation.

  5. Verify D5 + Sigmoid baseline reuse:

    • Compare the D5 + Sigmoid results in stage_a_runs with the corresponding Sigmoid results in stage_b_runs for seeds 0, 1, and 2.
    • Verify that run configurations, training histories, early-step gradients, epoch-level gradients, and weight-change records are identical.
    • Compare the corresponding aggregated D5 + Sigmoid summary metrics across Stage A and Stage B.
    • Confirm consistency of the epoch-1 first-to-last hidden-layer gradient ratio between Stage A Figure 1 and Stage B.

  6. Confirm experiment readiness:

    • Report the number of completed Stage A and Stage B result entries.
    • Confirm the number of unique completed training runs after accounting for reused Sigmoid baseline results.
    • Display a concise final verification summary.
    • Preserve all existing experimental results without modification.

Purpose:

Ensure that the final project conclusions are based on complete and consistent experimental evidence.

Although Parts 6 and 7 already verified their training runs and calculated multi-seed statistics independently, the final report requires a cross-stage verification.

In particular, the reused D5 + Sigmoid baseline must remain consistent across both stages to maintain a valid connection between the depth experiment and the activation-function experiment.

    reused = stage_b_runs[("sigmoid", seed)]               # Corresponding baseline result in Stage B.

    for field in ("run_config", "history", "step_records", "epoch_gradients", "weight_changes"):
        assert original[field] == reused[field], (
            f"D5 Sigmoid baseline mismatch: seed={seed}, field={field}"
        )                                                  # Every recorded component must match exactly.


# Compare the aggregated D5 + Sigmoid metrics calculated independently in Sections 6.3 and 7.5.
stage_a_d5 = stage_a_summary_df.set_index("depth").loc[stage_b_depth]
stage_b_sigmoid = stage_b_summary_df.set_index("activation").loc["sigmoid"]

shared_metrics = (
    "train_loss_mean",
    "val_loss_mean",
    "val_accuracy_mean",
    "val_macro_f1_mean",
    "grad_rms_l1_epoch1_mean",
    "weight_change_l1_final_mean",
    "epochs_to_threshold_mean",
    "seeds_reached_threshold"
)

for metric in shared_metrics:
    assert np.isclose(
        stage_a_d5[metric],
        stage_b_sigmoid[metric],
        equal_nan=True                                   # Allow matching missing threshold values if applicable.
    ), f"Aggregated D5 Sigmoid mismatch: {metric}"


# Cross-check the epoch-1 first-to-last gradient ratio from Stage A Figure 1 and Stage B.
stage_a_d5_ratio = fig1_summary.loc[
    (fig1_summary["depth"] == stage_b_depth)
    & (fig1_summary["layer"] == 1),
    "ratio_mean"
]

assert len(stage_a_d5_ratio) == 1                         # Exactly one D5 first-layer ratio is expected.
assert np.isclose(
    stage_a_d5_ratio.iloc[0],
    stage_b_sigmoid["first_to_last_gradient_ratio_mean"]
)                                                        # Both stages must use consistent gradient ratios.

print("\n=== D5 Sigmoid Baseline Consistency ===")
print(f"Reused baseline seeds: {len(cfg.seeds)} / {len(cfg.seeds)}")
print("Recorded run results: MATCH")
print("Aggregated performance and trainability metrics: MATCH")
print("First-to-last gradient ratio: MATCH")


# Count unique training runs only after confirming the baseline is reused consistently.
# The 9 Stage B entries include three Sigmoid results already present in Stage A.
unique_runs = len(stage_a_runs) + len(stage_b_runs) - len(cfg.seeds)

assert unique_runs == 18                                # 12 Stage A runs + 6 new Stage B runs.

print("\n=== Final Experiment Summary ===")
print(f"Stage A result entries: {len(stage_a_runs)}")
print(f"Stage B result entries: {len(stage_b_runs)}")
print(f"Reused D5 Sigmoid results: {len(cfg.seeds)}")
print(f"Unique completed training runs: {unique_runs}")
print("Final experiment verification: COMPLETE")

Verification Boundaries:

The checks verify recorded configurations, expected record counts, run-key coverage, selected summary consistency, and baseline reuse.

They do not independently recompute all metrics, assess statistical significance, or validate whether any observed gradient magnitude constitutes a harmful optimization mechanism.

Figure Main Measurement Multi-Seed Aggregation Research Role

All figures use the recorded Stage A measurements under the fixed Sigmoid + Xavier Uniform + SGD configuration.

Figure 1 — Gradient Magnitude vs. Layer¶

Final Scientific Caption:

Figure 1. Layer-wise RMS weight-gradient magnitudes for constant-width MLPs with 2, 5, 10, and 20 hidden layers trained on BloodMNIST using Sigmoid activations, Xavier Uniform initialization, and SGD (learning rate = 0.1).

(a) Absolute RMS weight-gradient magnitude versus hidden-layer index. (b) Relative RMS gradient normalized by the last hidden layer within each depth–seed run. Measurements are averaged over the first 10 training batches of epoch 1. Curves represent the mean across three random seeds (0, 1, 2), with shaded regions indicating ±1 sample standard deviation where supported by the logarithmic scale. Both panels use logarithmic y-axes. Hidden Layer 1 is closest to the input; output-layer and bias gradients are excluded.

The figure illustrates progressively stronger early-layer gradient attenuation as network depth increases under the tested Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

Scientific Interpretation & Role:

Figure 1 provides the primary direct gradient-based evidence for H1 — Depth Effect.

The absolute RMS measurements describe the magnitude of weight gradients at each hidden layer, while the normalized measurements quantify relative differences between earlier layers and the last hidden layer.

The results indicate that early-layer gradient attenuation becomes substantially more severe as depth increases.

The normalized ratios summarize relative weight-gradient magnitudes; they do not represent exact percentages of backpropagated gradient signals preserved.

Figure 2 — Gradient Evolution During Training¶

Final Scientific Caption:

Figure 2. Evolution of layer-wise RMS weight-gradient magnitudes in the 20-hidden-layer MLP (D20) throughout 20 training epochs on BloodMNIST under the fixed Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

The heatmap displays Hidden Layers 1–20 on the vertical axis and training epochs 1–20 on the horizontal axis. Each cell represents the base-10 logarithm of the mean RMS weight-gradient magnitude across three random seeds, using the first 10 training batches of the corresponding epoch. Hidden Layer 1 is positioned at the bottom, closest to the input, and Hidden Layer 20 is at the top, closest to the output.

The color scale represents log10(mean RMS gradient), rather than the mean of log-transformed gradients. The heatmap does not display sample-standard-deviation shading.

Extremely small early-layer gradients remain evident throughout the observed training period in D20.

Scientific Interpretation & Role:

Figure 2 extends the gradient analysis from a single early epoch to the complete 20-epoch training period.

It shows that the severe early-layer gradient attenuation observed in D20 is persistent during the evaluated training budget rather than being limited to the initial epoch.

This finding strengthens the descriptive evidence for H1 and provides context for the limited optimization progress observed in the deeper networks.

However, the heatmap displays aggregated means and does not independently establish the variability across seeds or the causal contribution of gradient attenuation to optimization difficulties.

Figure 3 — Training Loss vs. Epoch¶

Final Scientific Caption:

Figure 3. Training-loss trajectories of constant-width MLPs with 2, 5, 10, and 20 hidden layers trained on BloodMNIST using Sigmoid activations, Xavier Uniform initialization, and SGD (learning rate = 0.1) over 20 epochs.

Each curve represents mean training CrossEntropyLoss across three random seeds, with shaded regions indicating ±1 sample standard deviation. Training losses are recorded as the model parameters are updated throughout each epoch. The horizontal dashed line marks the predefined training-loss threshold of 1.50, used as a comparative optimization milestone rather than an early-stopping criterion.

D2 exhibits rapid training-loss reduction, whereas D5 shows delayed improvement. D10 and D20 remain near a high-loss plateau throughout the 20-epoch training budget. Their nearly overlapping trajectories reflect similar observed optimization behavior.

Scientific Interpretation & Role:

Figure 3 provides the primary training-loss evidence for the convergence-related component of H2 — Early-Layer Trainability.

The results show that increasing network depth is associated with slower or more limited training-loss reduction under the tested configuration.

Together with the gradient measurements in Figures 1–2 and the normalized first-layer weight-change measurements in Section 6.7, the figure supports an association between stronger early-layer gradient attenuation and reduced optimization progress.

However, training-loss curves do not directly measure gradients or establish gradient vanishing as the sole cause of optimization difficulties.

The epochs-to-threshold metric is calculated separately for each training run and should not be inferred solely from the mean loss curve crossing the threshold.

Combined Figure Interpretation — Connections to H1, H2, and H3:

H1 — Depth Effect:

Figures 1 and 2 provide complementary evidence of depth-dependent gradient attenuation under the fixed Sigmoid baseline.

Figure 1 demonstrates that increasing depth is associated with smaller relative early-layer gradient magnitudes.

Figure 2 shows that severe early-layer gradient attenuation persists throughout the observed D20 training period.

Together, these observations support H1 within the tested network architectures and training conditions.

H2 — Early-Layer Trainability:

Figure 3 shows that deeper Sigmoid networks experience slower or more limited training-loss reduction.

Combined with the normalized first-layer weight-change measurements in Section 6.7, the figures support the observed association between strong early-layer gradient attenuation, limited parameter displacement, and reduced optimization progress.

These results provide empirical support for the trainability-related findings of H2 without establishing a unique causal mechanism.

H3 — Activation Effect:

Figures 1–3 do not directly evaluate H3 because all Stage A models use Sigmoid.

H3 is investigated separately in Stage B, where Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU are compared at fixed D5 depth under common experimental settings.

The activation-related findings are reported through the numerical analyses and summaries in Sections 7.5–7.7 and the final Stage B summary table in Section 8.3.

Reporting Considerations:

The figures use the original recorded Stage A measurements and do not involve the BloodMNIST test split.

Mean ± sample standard deviation describes variability across the three evaluated random seeds; it does not constitute a confidence interval or statistical-significance test.

Figure 2 displays logarithmically transformed mean gradients rather than uncertainty bands.

The three figures should be interpreted together with the numerical gradient, normalized weight-change, convergence, and validation-performance summaries rather than as independent proof of a causal mechanism.

Conclusion:

All six Stage A figure files passed the implemented file-availability checks.

The three principal figures provide complementary visual evidence of depth-dependent gradient attenuation, gradient evolution, and training-loss convergence under the tested Sigmoid–Xavier–SGD configuration.

Their measurement protocols, aggregation methods, axis interpretations, scientific roles, and reporting limitations have been documented for the final technical report.

    • Create final_stage_a_table and final_stage_b_table.
    • Display both tables in the notebook.
    • Export each formatted table as a CSV file under results/final_report/.
    • Retain the original full-precision statistics in the existing source DataFrames.

Purpose:

Provide a compact quantitative summary of the central experimental findings for the final technical report.

The tables allow readers to compare the relationships among gradient attenuation, first-layer weight displacement, convergence, and validation performance without examining every training history or gradient record.

Using consistent formatting and metric definitions also facilitates comparisons between Stage A and Stage B while preserving their different independent variables.

Expected Results:

Table 1A — Stage A: Network Depth Experiment

  • Four rows representing D2, D5, D10, and D20.
  • One set of previously calculated mean ± sample standard deviation measurements for each depth.
  • Correct reporting of the training-loss threshold outcomes.
  • D10 and D20 displayed as "Not reached" for epochs-to-threshold.
  • Very small gradient and first-layer weight-change measurements preserved through scientific notation.

Table 1B — Stage B: Activation Function Experiment

  • Three rows representing Sigmoid, Tanh, and ReLU.
  • Identical metric definitions to Table 1A.
  • Mean ± sample standard deviation across three seeds.
  • Consistent D5 + Sigmoid baseline measurements with Stage A.
  • No new experimental measurements or statistical calculations.

Role in the Experiment:

Section 8.3 implements Step 48 of the experimental roadmap and prepares the principal quantitative tables for the final report.

It connects:

  • Part 4: Gradient RMS and normalized first-layer weight-change definitions.
  • Section 6.3: Stage A multi-seed statistics.
  • Section 6.4: Relative gradient measurements for the depth experiment.
  • Section 6.8: Stage A validation and convergence summary.
  • Section 7.5: Stage B multi-seed statistics.
  • Section 8.1: Final experiment completeness and baseline-consistency verification.

The resulting tables will support the integrated interpretation of H1, H2, and H3 in Section 8.4 and the final conclusions in Section 8.5.

Notes:

This section performs presentation, formatting, consistency checking, and export only.

No model training, gradient recording, metric recalculation, statistical hypothesis testing, additional figures, or experimental conditions are introduced.

Only two final summary tables are created, one for each experimental stage.
